Life Assurance
A type of insurance contract covering a person's life, wherein incorrect particulars or misstatements regarding the age of the life assured do not render the assurance void unless the true age exceeds the limit specified in the table of rates; the insurer who pays the sum assured is not entitled to subrogation against the person who caused the insured event.

Insurer
The Insurer is the party that undertakes, in consideration of a premium, to pay the assured or the beneficiary a sum of money, annuity, or other pecuniary prestation upon the occurrence of a specified risk.<SEP>The party providing insurance coverage who is liable for damages as specified in the insurance contract, entitled to subrogation rights in fire insurance but not in life assurance, and required to refund excess premiums without interest in life assurance.

Fire Insurance
A type of insurance in which the insurer is liable for all damage resulting from fire, including damage from salvage measures, measures to prevent extension of fire, and loss or disappearance of insured things during fire, unless proven to be caused by theft; the insurer is liable even if fire originated from a defect in the insured thing.

Suretyship
Suretyship encompasses real and personal guarantees as well as joint and several suretyship, which are transferred to the new obligation only with the consent of the sureties and co-debtors.<SEP>A contract whereby a person guarantees the performance of an obligation by giving an undertaking to the creditor to fulfil the obligation should the debtor fail to do so; it must be established in writing and is valid only if the underlying obligation is valid.<SEP>A legal arrangement in which a surety guarantees the debt of a debtor, governed by Articles 788–801 of the Egyptian Civil Code, with specific rules on proceedings, multiple sureties, and subrogation.

Insured
The party covered by insurance who is entitled to compensation for insured events, responsible for providing correct particulars, and whose unintentional fault is covered by the insurer while deliberate or fraudulent acts are excluded from coverage.

Surety
A person who provides a guarantee, whether real or personal, for a debt, and who does not remain bound to the creditor in an assignment of debt unless he has agreed to the assignment.<SEP>A Surety is a guarantor of the debt who is released from obligation when the Debtor's tender is accepted or declared valid by judgment, but is not freed if the Debtor retracts the tender beforehand.<SEP>The surety is a person who provides a personal or real guarantee for the lessee's obligations. The suretyship does not transfer to a tacitly renewed lease unless the surety consents.<SEP>A person who guarantees the performance of a debtor's obligation, must be solvent and reside in Egypt, is discharged simultaneously with the debtor, and is entitled to avail himself of all defenses open to the debtor except the debtor's lack of legal capacity if the surety was aware of it at the time of contracting.<SEP>A person who guarantees the debt of a debtor, with legal rights including demanding that the debtor's property be distrained first and being subrogated to the creditor's rights upon payment of the debt.<SEP>A surety is a guarantor of an inscribed debt who has the right to apply for the sale of property that a third party holder wishes to purge.

Beneficiary
A third party in whose favor a stipulation is made; may be a future person or institution not yet identified at the date of the contract, provided identification is possible when the contract takes effect.<SEP>The third party who acquires direct rights under a stipulation for their benefit and may demand performance from the promisor; the beneficiary's consent is effective only from the time it is given unless retroactive effect is indicated.<SEP>The person entitled to benefit from wakf property who cannot independently grant a lease without authorization from the Nazir or constituent.<SEP>The Beneficiary is the person for whose benefit the insurance is contracted and who is entitled to receive payments such as the sum assured, annuity, or other pecuniary prestation from the insurer.<SEP>The Beneficiary is the person entitled to receive life annuity payments, who may demand due performance or resiliation of the contract if the grantor fails to fulfil the obligation.<SEP>The person designated to receive the sum assured in a life assurance policy, whose rights against the person causing the insured event cannot be subrogated by the insurer.

Premium
A Premium is a pecuniary payment made by the assured to the insurer as consideration for the insurance coverage provided under the contract.<SEP>The payment agreed upon for insurance coverage, which may be adjusted based on the true age of the life assured; if the agreed premium is less than what should have been paid, the sum assured is reduced proportionally, and if higher, the insurer must refund the excess without interest.

Sum Assured
The Sum Assured is the monetary amount the insurer undertakes to pay to the assured or beneficiary under a life insurance policy upon occurrence of the insured event or maturity.<SEP>The amount payable under an insurance contract, which may be reduced in proportion to the ratio between the agreed premium and the premium that should have been paid on the basis of the true age of the life assured.

Egypt
Egypt is the sovereign state whose law serves as the primary reference for characterizing legal relationships in conflicts of law and governs various civil matters within its territory.<SEP>Egypt is a country where the legal provisions described in the text apply, including standards of public policy and morality.<SEP>The country where a surety must reside when a debtor undertakes to offer a surety, as specified in the suretyship provisions of the law.

Table of Rates
A schedule specifying age limits and premium rates for life assurance; if the true age of the life assured exceeds the limit specified in the table, the assurance may be rendered void.

Pledge
A Pledge is a security mechanism whereby a debtor who leaves a pledge in the hand of his creditor as security for his debt is deemed to have tacitly acknowledged the debt, thereby interrupting prescription.<SEP>A security mechanism whose preservation rules apply by analogy to a person exercising the right of retention over a thing.<SEP>A real security or warranty that may encumber an insured thing; when the insured thing is encumbered, rights transfer to the insurance compensation due to the debtor.<SEP>A Pledge is a contract by which a person undertakes, as security for a debt, to hand over a thing to the creditor or a third party, granting the creditor a real right to retain the thing until repayment and to obtain payment from its sale proceeds in preference to other creditors.<SEP>A Pledge (الرهن الحيازة) is a possessory security right. Privileges are extinguished in the same way and in accordance with the same rules as a pledge, as stated in Article 1136.

Mortgage
A real security encumbering property, whose rights transfer to the insurance compensation due to the debtor by virtue of the insurance contract, and whose transfer formalities are borne by the surety in suretyship arrangements.<SEP>A contract by which a creditor acquires a real right over an immovable property appropriated to the payment of a debt, granting preference over ordinary creditors in satisfaction of the claim from the price of the property.<SEP>A mortgage is a real right security over property that ranks from the date of its inscription and secures debts including conditional, future, or contingent obligations.<SEP>A legal security mechanism over immovable property to secure debt repayment. A mortgage may be granted to secure a conditional, future, or contingent debt, and may also secure an opened credit or current account. The mortgage cannot be separated from the debt it secures and depends on it for validity and extinction.<SEP>A Mortgage is a legal right over immovable property as security for a debt, which is extinguished when the secured debt is extinguished or when purge formalities are completed.<SEP>A Mortgage is a legal security right over property whose provisions on inscription, renewal, radiation, indivisibility, effect, and extinguishment apply equally to the judgment charge and pledge.<SEP>A Mortgage (الرهن الرسمي) is a formal security right over immovable property. Provisions relating to mortgages apply to privileged rights over immovable property where not incompatible with the nature of those rights. Privileges are extinguished in the same way as a mortgage, as stated in Articles 1134, 1135, and 1136.

Subrogation
The legal substitution of a third party into the rights of a creditor who has been paid off, including all attributes, accessories, securities, and defenses attached to the debt, arising by law or by agreement.<SEP>Subrogation is the right of a joint and several debtor who has paid the full debt to exercise the creditor's action against the other co-debtors, though recovery is limited to each co-debtor's respective share.<SEP>A legal principle under Article 494 whereby a donee, in case of dispossession, is subrogated into the rights and actions of the donor.<SEP>The legal right of the insurer to step into the position of the insured to pursue claims against third parties; applicable in fire insurance but expressly excluded in life assurance.<SEP>The legal right of a surety who has paid the debt to step into the position of the creditor and exercise all rights against the debtor.<SEP>The legal or contractual substitution of one creditor into the rights of another creditor holding a right secured by an inscription. Subrogation is enforceable against third parties only if inscribed in the margin of the original inscription.<SEP>A legal mechanism by which the Third Party Holder is substituted into the rights of creditors discharged by payment, including guarantees furnished by the Debtor but excluding those furnished by a party other than the Debtor.

Bankruptcy
Bankruptcy is a legal declaration that causes a debtor to forfeit the benefit of the term on obligations, as referenced in Articles 273 and 274.<SEP>A legal condition of the debtor, along with insolvency, that constitutes grounds under Article 547 for compelling the debtor to redeem an annuity.<SEP>A legal proceeding involving a debtor that requires the creditor to prove the debt in the bankruptcy estate, failing which the creditor loses the remedy against the surety to the extent of the loss suffered.<SEP>A legal status subject to special provisions that affect the enforceability and priority of mortgages against third parties. The effectiveness of a mortgage against third parties is subject to the provisions laid down for bankruptcy.

Commercial Debt
A debt arising from commercial transactions; suretyship in respect of a commercial debt is deemed a civil act even if the surety is a trader, except when arising from guarantees or endorsements on negotiable instruments.

Salvage Measures
Actions taken to rescue insured property or prevent the extension of fire; damage caused to insured things by such measures is included in the insurer's liability under fire insurance.

Force Majeure
Unforeseeable circumstances or irresistible force beyond a person's control that exempt liability for injury, alongside unforeseen circumstances, the fault of the victim, or the fault of a third party.<SEP>Unforeseen events beyond the control of the debtor that may excuse non-performance. A debtor may by agreement accept liability for force majeure.<SEP>Unforeseen circumstances beyond the control of either party that may excuse performance, reduce rent, or relieve obligations under a lease.<SEP>Force Majeure is an unforeseeable and unavoidable event not imputable to the operation of a service that may excuse the concessionaire from responsibility for abnormal service interruptions.<SEP>Force Majeure is a cause beyond the control of the worker that prevents the continuation of work and serves as grounds for dissolution of the contract of service, alongside death or prolonged illness of the worker.<SEP>An unforeseeable and unavoidable event; the insurer is liable for damage resulting from a fortuitous event of force majeure under fire insurance provisions.<SEP>Force Majeure is an unforeseeable and uncontrollable event for which the pledgor is held responsible if the thing pledged is lost or deteriorated as a result.

Future Debt
A debt that has not yet been created; suretyship may be entered into for a future debt if the guaranteed amount is fixed beforehand, and the surety who has not fixed the duration of the guarantee may revoke it at any time provided the guaranteed debt has not yet arisen.

Conditional Liability
A liability dependent on the occurrence of a specified condition; suretyship may be entered into in respect of a conditional liability as provided under Article 778.

Negotiable Instruments
Commercial papers whose guarantee by backing signatures or endorsements is always deemed a commercial act, as distinguished from the general rule that suretyship for a commercial debt is deemed a civil act.

Real Security
Property assigned by law or agreement as a guarantee for a debt, which must be realized before the surety's property can be seized when both real security and suretyship exist for the same debt.<SEP>An adequate security interest in property that a debtor may offer as an alternative to producing a surety, and which includes securities assigned to guarantee a debt even if provided after the suretyship was entered into.

Right of Retention
A legal means of security allowing a possessor or holder of a thing to refuse returning it until the amount due is repaid, subject to specific conditions and extinguishment rules.<SEP>Right of Retention is the vendor's legal right to withhold delivery of the thing sold until the purchaser pays the amount due, even if the purchaser offers a mortgage or security. The vendor may also exercise this right before the payment term falls due if the purchaser loses the benefit of the term under Article 273. If the thing sold perishes during retention, the purchaser bears the loss unless caused by the vendor's act.<SEP>A legal right allowing the creditor to retain possession of a movable property as security for a debt; the creditor must surrender such right to the surety upon discharge of the debt.

Judicial Deposit
Judicial Deposit is a court-supervised procedure allowing the Debtor to deposit the thing due when the Creditor refuses payment, is unknown, incapable, or when the debt is disputed.<SEP>A legal measure whereby an insured thing is placed under court supervision; when the insurer is duly notified of such deposit, the insurer shall not pay any sum due to the insured.<SEP>Judicial Deposit is a legal remedy available to the pledgor, allowing the thing pledged to be placed under court-supervised custody when the pledgee mismanages or commits gross negligence, as stated in Article 1106.

Theft
The unlawful taking of property; the insurer under fire insurance is not liable for loss or disappearance of insured things during a fire if the insurer can establish that the loss was occasioned by theft.

Accessories of Debt
Supplementary obligations attached to a principal debt, including expenses of the first demand for payment and expenses incurred after notice has been given to the surety, which are covered by suretyship in the absence of an express agreement to the contrary.

Depositor
The Depositor is a person who entrusts property to another (the Depository) for safekeeping, and who may be required to pay remuneration and reimburse preservation expenses.

Depository
The Depository is a person who receives and undertakes to safeguard property entrusted by the Depositor, and who must return it upon demand, may not appoint a substitute without authority, and is entitled to reimbursement of preservation expenses.

Deposit
The Deposit is a contract whereby one person entrusts a thing to another for safekeeping; it is presumed gratuitous unless remuneration is stipulated, and it is governed by Articles 721 through 728.

Heir of Depository
The Heir of Depository is a successor of a depository who may sell or dispose of the deposited thing and is liable to refund the price received or pay its value depending on whether the alienation was for consideration or gratuitous.

Owner
The owner is the person who holds title to the thing sold; if the owner ratifies a sale made by a non-owner, the contract becomes binding and valid as regards the purchaser.<SEP>The owner of an animal, building, or thing, who may be distinct from the person in charge and may be called upon to take preventive measures or indemnify third parties.<SEP>The Owner is the rightful proprietor of the deposited thing, entitled to reclaim it or receive compensation from the heir of a depository who has disposed of it.<SEP>A person holding full ownership rights over property, including the right to compel neighbors to place boundary marks, use party walls, heighten party walls, and exercise rights of way.<SEP>A person who holds legal title to property, who is entitled to restitution and bears obligations toward the possessor for certain expenditures.

Hotel Proprietor
The Hotel Proprietor is the owner or operator of a hotel, inn, or similar establishment, responsible for safeguarding effects brought by travelers, with liability limited to L.E. 50 for money, securities, and valuables unless special conditions apply.<SEP>The Hotel Proprietor (صاحب الفندق) is the owner of a hotel who has a privilege over the effects brought into the hotel by travellers for sums due for accommodation, provisions, and expenses incurred on the traveller's account, as established in Articles 1133 and 1144.<SEP>A hotel proprietor who is owed sums for accommodation, food, and expenses by a traveller and holds a privilege over the effects brought by the traveller to the hotel or its annexes.

Traveller
The Traveller is a person who stays at a hotel or inn and brings effects into the establishment, and who must promptly report theft, loss, or damage to the proprietor under penalty of forfeiting rights.<SEP>The Traveller (المسافر) is a guest at a hotel whose effects brought into the hotel are subject to the hotel proprietor's privilege for unpaid accommodation and related charges, as referenced in Articles 1133 and 1144.<SEP>A guest at a hotel who owes sums for accommodation, food, and expenses, and whose effects brought to the hotel are subject to the hotel proprietor's privilege.

Receiver
The Receiver (also called Custodian or "Harees") is a person appointed either by agreement of all interested parties or by judicial order to safeguard, manage, and return property under judicial custody, with obligations including keeping regular books of account and rendering annual accounts.<SEP>A Receiver is a person appointed by the Judge Des Referes to manage abandoned or mortgaged property during expropriation proceedings; the third party holder may be appointed as receiver.

Judicial Custody
Judicial Custody is a court-ordered safekeeping arrangement for immovable property or things intended to remain in place, requested by the Debtor when the Creditor fails to take delivery.<SEP>Judicial Custody is a contract whereby parties entrust a third party with movable or immovable property that is subject to litigation or unestablished legal rights, for safeguarding, management, and return to the person whose right is established, as governed by Articles 729 through 738.<SEP>Judicial Custody (الحراسة) is a legal procedure whereby movables charged with a privilege may be placed under court supervision. A creditor who has reasonable grounds to fear misappropriation of such movables may apply for them to be placed in judicial custody, as provided in Article 1133.

Nazir
The administrator or supervisor of wakf property who holds the exclusive right to grant leases and collect rent for such property.<SEP>The Nazir is the administrator of wakf property who cannot lease wakf for more than three years without the judge's authority, unless the Nazir is also the founder or sole beneficiary.<SEP>The Nazir is the administrator of Wakf property whose vacancy, disputed appointment, removal proceedings, wrongful administration, or bad faith may trigger the imposition of judicial custody over the Wakf.

Wakf Property
Islamic religious endowment property governed by special lease rules, administered by a Nazir, with restrictions on rent adequacy and lease duration.<SEP>Wakf property is property held in Islamic trust whose lease is governed by special rules, including a three-year lease limit without judicial authorization and the applicability of general lease provisions where not incompatible.<SEP>Wakf Property is endowed property that may be placed under judicial custody in cases such as vacancy of the Nazir, indebtedness of the Wakf, or insolvency of a beneficiary.<SEP>Wakf property is a category of property that requires thirty-three years of possession for acquisition by prescription under Article 970.<SEP>Wakf Property is religious endowment property on which discovered treasure belongs specifically to the founder of the wakf or to his heirs.<SEP>A type of endowed property for whose benefit a servitude is established, subject to an extended thirty-three-year non-user period for extinguishment of the servitude.

Gaming and Betting
Gaming and Betting are agreements relating to games of chance or bets that are declared void under the law; a loser may reclaim payments within three years, with exceptions for sports bets between participants and legally authorized lotteries.

Life Annuity
A Life Annuity is a periodic payment obligation settled for the lifetime of a designated person, created by contract or will, either gratuitously or for valuable consideration, and valid only if made in writing.

Grantor
The Grantor is the party obligated under a contract who must fulfil his obligation; if he fails, the beneficiary may demand due performance or resiliation of the contract with damages.<SEP>The Grantor is a person who binds themselves to pay a life annuity to another person, and who must fulfil the obligation or face demands for performance or contract resiliation.

Contract of Loan for Consumption
The Contract of Loan for Consumption is the legal characterization that a deposit takes when its object is consumable property and the depository has been authorized to make use of it.

Contract of Insurance
The Contract of Insurance is referenced as the subject of Section III under Chapter IV on Aleatory Contracts in the civil code.

Aleatory Contracts
Aleatory Contracts form Chapter IV of the civil code, encompassing three categories of speculative agreements: Gaming and Betting, Life Annuities, and Contracts of Insurance.

Creditors
Creditors are persons whose rights must be protected against the wrongful administration or bad faith of the Nazir of a Wakf, and judicial custody may be ordered as the sole means of safeguarding their claims.<SEP>Creditors are persons to whom the estate owes debts, entitled to payment from estate assets, who may hold security on estate property, and whose approval is required for non-auction sales when the estate is insolvent.

Hotel Staff
Hotel Staff are employees of a hotel, inn, or similar establishment whose gross negligence can trigger the full liability of the Hotel Proprietor for loss of a Traveller's valuables beyond the standard L.E. 50 limit.

Interested Parties
Interested Parties are all persons with a legal stake in property under judicial custody, whose unanimous consent is required for the appointment of a Receiver and for certain acts beyond routine administration.

Sports Participants
Sports Participants are persons who take part personally in athletic competitions and are permitted under the law to make bets among themselves, though the Judge may reduce excessive stakes.

Will
A Will (الوصية) is a legal disposition taking effect after death, governed by the national law of the testator at the time of death, while its form is governed by the national law of the testator at the time of making the will or the law of the country where the will is made, as stated in Article 17.<SEP>A will is a testamentary disposition whose execution by a person placed under interdiction for prodigality or imbecility is valid if duly authorized by the court, as provided in Article 116.<SEP>A Will is a testamentary instrument that may create a Life Annuity obligation, alongside contracts, as an alternative mode of establishing periodic payment commitments.<SEP>A testamentary document that may contain an inalienability clause restricting the disposition of property, subject to validity requirements of legitimate reason and reasonable duration.<SEP>A Will (Wasiya) is a testamentary disposition by which a testator may divide estate property among heirs, setting out the share of each heir, which is revocable during the testator's lifetime and becomes irrevocable upon death.<SEP>A legal instrument by which the right of usufruct may be bequeathed to successive persons alive at the time of the bequest or to an unborn child.

Contract of Gift
A Contract of Gift is a form of gratuitous transfer referenced in Article 743, whose special formal requirements under the law must be satisfied in addition to the writing requirement for annuity contracts.

Usufruct
A real right to use and enjoy the property of another, mentioned in Article 511 as a type of contribution a partner may make to a partnership, governed by sale warranty provisions.<SEP>Usufruct is a legal right that terminates at the end of the fixed time or, if no time is fixed, upon the death of the usufructuary. It is extinguished by loss of the property, though it may transfer to property obtained in lieu of the destroyed property, and is extinguished by non-user during a period of fifteen years.

Right of User and Occupation
The Right of User and Occupation is a legal right whose extent is determined by the personal requirements of the beneficiary and his family, subject to conditions laid down in the creating deed. It may only be transferred to third parties by virtue of a formal provision or for serious reasons.

Hekr
Hekr is a legal right related to bare property where the bare owner holds preemption rights if the hekr is sold, and the beneficiary of the hekr holds preemption rights if the bare property is sold.<SEP>Hekr is a legal right over land that cannot be concluded for a period exceeding sixty years. It may only be established for reasons of necessity or expediency with court permission and must be formalized by a deed. The grantee may dispose of the right, which is transmissible by inheritance.

Idjaratein
Idjaratein is a contract by which a wakf creates a hekr on land with buildings in need of repair, in consideration of an immediate payment equal to the value of the buildings and an annual rent equal to the rental value of similar lands.

Kholou-el-intifaa
Kholou-el-intifaa is a contract by which a wakf grants a lease of a property even without the permission of the Judge, in consideration of a fixed rent for an indefinite period. The lessee must render the property fit for exploitation, and the wakf may resiliate the contract at any time with due notice.

Servitudes
A servitude is a right which limits the enjoyment of a property for the benefit of another property belonging to another owner. It may be imposed on State property if not incompatible with its intended use. Servitudes are acquired by legal disposition or inheritance, and only apparent servitudes including rights of way can be acquired by prescription.<SEP>Servitudes are easement rights and other real rights that the third party holder had on the property before acquiring it, which are re-vested in the third party holder after expropriation.

Wakf
A wakf is an Islamic endowment whose constitution by a person placed under interdiction for prodigality or imbecility is valid if duly authorized by the court, as provided in Article 116.<SEP>A Wakf is a religious endowment or trust that is explicitly prohibited from exercising the right of preemption under Article 939.<SEP>Wakf is a religious endowment property status. Land constituted in wakf is a prerequisite for establishing hekr, and the cessation of wakf status on land may cause termination of hekr rights, unless the cessation results from revocation by the founder.

Charie Court of First Instance
The Charie Court of First Instance is the court that must grant permission for hekr to be concluded, specifically the court in the district where the land or its most valuable part is situated. The President of the Court or a delegated Judge or notary must draw up the hekr deed.

Usufructuary
A person holding a right of usufruct who may grant leases that end when the usufruct is extinguished unless ratified by the bare owner.<SEP>A person who holds the right of usufruct, entitled to use property and collect its fruits while being bound by duties of preservation, good management, and maintenance.<SEP>The Usufructuary is the holder of usufruct rights who holds the right of preemption in case of a sale of all or part of the bare property which produces the usufruct.<SEP>The usufructuary is the holder of the usufruct right. Upon termination or death, the usufructuary or his heirs may retain possession of the land until standing crops are ripe for harvesting, provided rent is paid for that period.

Grantee of Hekr
The grantee of the hekr holds the right to dispose of his right, owns constructions and plantations absolutely, must pay agreed rent to the grantor, and must take necessary measures to make the land suitable for exploitation.

Grantor of Hekr
The grantor of the hekr receives rent payments from the grantee and may demand resiliation of the contract if rent is not paid for three consecutive years. Upon termination, the grantor may claim removal or maintenance of buildings and plantations.

Article 989
Article 989 is a referenced legal provision whose paragraph 2 applies when the owner restores destroyed property and the usufruct is re-created in favor of the usufructuary.

Article 179
Establishes that a person, even one lacking discretion, who enriches himself without just cause to the detriment of another is liable to compensate for the loss sustained, and this obligation persists even if the profit later disappears.<SEP>Article 179 is a referenced legal provision governing the compensation of a lessee for expenses when a Kholou-el-intifaa contract is resiliated by the wakf.

Article 1008
Article 1008 governs the termination of hekr rights, including termination at the end of the fixed period, upon death of the grantee before building or planting, and upon cessation of wakf status on the land.

Lessee of Kholou-el-intifaa
The lessee under a Kholou-el-intifaa contract undertakes to render the property fit for exploitation and is entitled to compensation for expenses if the wakf resiliates the contract.

Original Owner
The original owner of two separate properties may create apparent servitudes between them by establishing an apparent distinction indicating a relationship of subordination.

Article 993
Article 993 governs the termination of usufruct at the end of the fixed time or upon the death of the usufructuary, and provides that standing crops on the land shall be left with the usufructuary or heirs until ripe for harvesting, provided rent is paid for that period.

Article 994
Article 994 provides that usufruct is extinguished by loss of the property but is transmitted to any property obtained in lieu of the destroyed property, and addresses re-creation of usufruct if the owner restores the property.

Article 995
Article 995 states that the right of usufruct is extinguished by non-user during a period of fifteen years.

Article 999
Article 999 provides that hekr cannot be concluded for a period exceeding sixty years, and if a longer period is fixed or no period is fixed, the hekr is deemed concluded for sixty years.

Article 1000
Article 1000 provides that hekr may only be concluded for reasons of necessity or expediency with permission of the Charie Court of First Instance, and must be established by deed drawn up by the President of the Court or a delegated official, and published under the law relating to the publication of real rights.

Article 1003
Article 1003 states that the grantee of the hekr must pay the agreed rent to the grantor, and in the absence of a contrary provision, the rent is payable at the end of each year.

Article 1004
Article 1004 provides that hekr cannot be concluded at a rent less than that paid for similar lands, and the rent is adjusted when the rental value of similar lands changes by more than one fifth, provided eight years have passed since the last valuation.

Article 1005
Article 1005 governs the estimation of rent increases or decreases based on the rental value of the land at the time of valuation, taking into account its marketable value and demand, while disregarding improvements or deteriorations caused by the grantee.

Article 1007
Article 1007 requires the grantee of the hekr to take necessary measures to make the land suitable for exploitation, considering agreed conditions, the nature of the soil, intended use, and local custom.

Article 1009
Article 1009 provides that the grantor of the hekr may demand resiliation of the contract if the rent is not paid for three consecutive years.

Article 1010
Article 1010 provides that upon resiliation or termination of the hekr contract, the grantor may claim removal or maintenance of buildings and plantations against payment of the lesser of their existing value or removal value, and the Court may grant time for payment in exceptional circumstances.

Article 1011
Article 1011 states that the right of hekr is extinguished by non-user during fifteen years, or thirty-three years if the hekr is constituted in wakf.

Article 1012
Article 1012 provides that no hekr may be established on non-wakf land from the date the law comes into force, while existing hekrs on non-wakf land remain subject to the preceding articles.

Article 1015
Article 1015 defines a servitude as a right limiting the enjoyment of a property for the benefit of another property belonging to another owner, and provides that a servitude may be imposed on State property if not incompatible with its intended use.

Article 1016
Article 1016 provides that the right to a servitude is acquired by legal disposition or inheritance, and that only apparent servitudes including rights of way can be acquired by prescription.

Article 1018
Article 1018 provides that restrictions limiting an owner's right to build on a property, such as height or area limitations, constitute servitude rights on that property for the benefit of the properties for which the restrictions were imposed.

President of the Court
The judicial officer of the court competent to declare insolvency, empowered to grant alimentary allowances to debtors from attached revenues upon application.<SEP>The President of the Court is the judge who reviews applications, considers the amount of the debt and value of properties, and issues orders authorizing judgment charges.<SEP>The President of the Court is the official who may draw up the hekr deed, or delegate a Judge or notary for this purpose, as provided under Article 1000.

Notary
A notary may be delegated by the President of the Court to draw up the hekr deed, as provided under Article 1000.

State Property
State property and public entity property cannot be acquired by prescription, and any encroachment may be removed administratively by the competent Minister.<SEP>State property refers to public property belonging to the State upon which a servitude may be imposed provided it is not incompatible with the use for which such property is intended.

Apparent Servitudes
Apparent servitudes are servitudes that are visible or manifest, which may be created by the intention of the original owner and are the only type of servitudes that can be acquired by prescription, including rights of way.

Rights of Way
Rights of way are a type of apparent servitude that can be acquired by prescription, as referenced in Article 1016.

Founder of Wakf
The founder of a wakf is the person who established the wakf endowment and may revoke or reduce its period, as referenced in Article 1008.

data.entity_name: Law Relating to the Publication of Real Rights
data.content:
Law Relating to the Publication of Real Rights
The law relating to the publication of real rights governs the publication requirements for hekr deeds, as referenced in Article 1000.

Heirs of Grantee of Hekr
The heirs of the grantee of the hekr may request the maintenance of the hekr if the grantee dies before building on or planting the land, as provided under Article 1008.

Worker (العامل)
The Worker is a person employed under a contract of service who must personally perform the work, exercise the care of a reasonable person, obey the master's orders, preserve entrusted things, safeguard industrial or commercial secrets, and carry out obligations imposed by special laws.

Master (رب العمل)
The Master (employer) is a person who employs a worker under a contract of service, owes obligations including paying the worker's salary at the agreed time and place, rendering accounts of profit-sharing or commission, and complying with obligations imposed by special laws.

Contract of Service
A Contract of Service is a legal agreement between a worker and a master that ends at the expiration of its fixed term or upon completion of the work, and may be dissolved by the death of the worker but not necessarily by the death of the master.<SEP>A Contract of Service is a legal arrangement whereby one party undertakes to work under the supervision or control of another party in exchange for remuneration, which may be fixed-term, indefinite, or for specific work.

Tips
Tips are amounts given by customers of a commercial establishment to employees, collected in a common fund for distribution to workers by or under the supervision of the employer; in some industries a worker's salary may consist solely of tips and food.<SEP>Tips are gratuities given by customers to employees that may be deemed part of salary in industries where customary and subject to regulation, particularly when collected in a common fund and distributed under employer supervision.

Non-Competition Agreement
A Non-Competition Agreement is a contractual stipulation preventing a worker, after termination of the contract, from competing with the master or participating in a competitive undertaking, valid only if the worker has attained majority and the restriction is limited as to time, place, and kind of work.

Penalty Clause
A Penalty Clause is a contractual provision applicable in the event of breach of a non-competition condition; it is void if so onerous as to compel the worker to remain in the master's service longer than agreed, and its voidness extends to the entire non-competition condition.

Invention
An Invention is a new discovery made by a worker during service; the master generally has no rights to it unless the nature of the worker's duties requires inventive effort or the contract expressly reserves such rights to the master, in which cases the worker may claim special remuneration if the invention has serious economic importance.

Trade Secrets
Trade Secrets are the industrial or commercial secrets of the work that the worker is obligated to safeguard even after the end of the contract; actions relating to their disclosure or enforcement of protective conditions are not subject to the special one-year prescription period.

Special Laws
Special Laws are laws that impose additional obligations on both the worker and the master beyond those laid down in the contract of service articles, including provisions on salary payment, notice periods, and dissolution of contracts.<SEP>Special Laws are legal enactments that regulate provisions relating to insurance contracts not specifically mentioned in the Code.

Salary
Salary is the payment owed by the master to the worker at the time and place agreed upon in the contract or established by custom, and may include profit-sharing, a percentage of gross receipts or production, or other remuneration of a similar nature.

Compensation for Dismissal
Compensation for Dismissal is a remedy that may be granted to a worker even if the master has not directly dismissed the worker, particularly when the master's vexatious treatment or breach of contract conditions forces the worker to appear to have terminated the contract; it also applies to unjustified transfers to less suitable posts.

Prescription Period
Prescription Period is a one-year limitation period from the time of delivery of the thing sold within which a warranty action must be brought, even if the defect is discovered after the period expires. The vendor cannot invoke this prescription if fraudulent concealment of the defect is proven.<SEP>The Prescription Period is a one-year limitation period from the termination of the contract for actions arising out of a contract of service, except for commission and profit-sharing actions which begin when the master provides a statement, and for trade secrets-related actions which are not subject to this limitation.

Mandate (الوكالة)
Mandate is a contract whereby a mandatary binds himself to perform a judicial act on behalf of a mandator; it must be executed in the same form as that required for the juridical act it concerns.<SEP>A legal contract whereby one person (the mandator) authorizes another (the mandatary) to perform acts on their behalf. A general mandate confers only the power to perform acts of management, while a special mandate is required for acts beyond management such as sale, mortgage, gifts, arbitration, and court representation. A mandate is presumed gratuitous unless agreed otherwise, and it terminates by completion of work, expiration of period, or death of either party.

Mandatary (الوكيل)
The Mandatary is the person who undertakes to perform a judicial act on behalf of the mandator under a mandate contract; under a general mandate, the mandatary is only conferred the power to perform acts of management.<SEP>The person appointed to perform a mandate. The mandatary is bound to execute the mandate without exceeding its limits, must exercise due care (varying by whether the mandate is gratuitous or remunerated), must inform the mandator of progress, render accounts, and may not use the mandator's property for personal benefit. Multiple mandataries may be jointly and severally liable under certain conditions.

Mandator (الموكل)
The Mandator is the person on whose behalf the mandatary performs a judicial act under a mandate contract.<SEP>The person who gives a mandate to another. The mandator may revoke or restrict the mandate at any time, must repay expenses incurred by the mandatary with interest, is responsible for injury sustained by the mandatary in normal performance, and when several mandators appoint a sole mandatary for a common purpose, they are jointly and severally liable.

Acts of Management
Acts of Management are acts carried out by a creditor that retain their validity notwithstanding the realization of a resolutory condition, as stated in Article 269.<SEP>Acts of management are legal acts related to the administration of property, which are valid when performed by a minor possessing discretion who has attained the age of eighteen and has been authorized to take possession of his property, or by a person under interdiction for prodigality who has been authorized to take possession of his property, within the limits provided by law, as set out in Articles 112 and 116.<SEP>Acts of Management are the acts that a mandatary is authorized to perform under a general mandate, including granting leases of no more than three years, acts of preservation and maintenance, recovery of rights, payment of debts, and disposal actions necessary for management such as selling crops or goods.<SEP>Acts that a mandatary may perform under a general mandate without special authorization, including granting leases of no more than three years, acts of preservation and maintenance, recovery of rights, discharge of debts, sale of perishable crops, goods or movables, and purchase of things necessary for preservation and exploitation of the mandate object.

Common Fund
The Common Fund is a collection mechanism where tips given by customers of a commercial establishment are pooled for distribution to workers by or under the supervision of the employer.

Notice Period
The Notice Period is the required delay that must precede termination of an indefinite contract of service; its manner and duration are defined by special laws, and failure to observe it obligates the terminating party to compensate the other.

Profit Sharing
Profit Sharing is a contractual arrangement whereby the worker is entitled, in addition to or in lieu of agreed salary, to a share of the master's profits, a percentage of gross receipts, production amount, value of savings effected, or other remuneration of a similar nature.

Balance Sheet
The Balance Sheet is an accounting document after each rendition of which the master is bound to render the worker an account of the profit-sharing amount payable.

Simulated Contract
A simulated contract is a legal concept referenced in Article 244, involving an ostensible contract that conceals a hidden contract, which creditors and good faith successors may challenge.<SEP>A legal arrangement where parties create an apparent (ostensible) contract to conceal a genuine agreement between them, governed by specific rules regarding creditor and successor rights.

Ostensible Contract
The visible or apparent contract used to conceal the real agreement between contracting parties; in conflicts of interest, parties relying on the ostensible contract have preference.

Hidden Contract
The genuine or real agreement between parties concealed behind an ostensible contract, which binds the contracting parties and their universal successors.

Insolvency
Insolvency refers to the state where a debtor's liabilities exceed assets, triggering special protections for creditors including the right to challenge alienations and exercise the debtor's rights.<SEP>A legal state declared when a debtor's assets are insufficient to pay due debts, governed by court procedures, registration requirements, and specific effects on debts and creditor rights.<SEP>Insolvency is a legal state that may be declared by judgment and automatically ceases upon the expiration of five years from the date of registration of the judgment declaring insolvency. Cessation does not prevent creditors from attacking acts of the debtor.<SEP>Insolvency of the lessee does not render immediately payable rents that have not become due, but the lessor may claim resiliation of the lease unless adequate securities are provided within a reasonable time.<SEP>Insolvency is the financial inability of a joint and several debtor to pay his share of the debt; the insolvent debtor's share is borne pro rata by the co-debtor who effected payment and all other solvent co-debtors.<SEP>The inability of a debtor to satisfy debts, for which the creditor becomes responsible to the surety if the creditor fails to take necessary proceedings in due time under Article 790.

Court of First Instance
The judicial court situated in the district of the debtor's domicile that has authority to declare insolvency and adjudicate related proceedings.<SEP>The Court of First Instance is the judicial body to which the Summary Court refers disputes that fall outside its competence during partition proceedings.<SEP>The Court of First Instance is a court with jurisdiction over mortgage and property matters, receiving declarations of abandonment and applications for judgment charges.

Minister of Justice
The Minister of Justice (وزير العدل) is the official responsible for executing and implementing the Egyptian Civil Code, which came into force on October 15, 1949.<SEP>The government official who issues regulations (Arrêté) governing the organization of the general register of insolvency declarations.

Cairo Court
The court that maintains a general register of insolvency registrations and marginal entries received from all courts for centralized record-keeping.<SEP>The Cairo Court is a judicial body whose registrar receives a copy of the judgment ending insolvency for the purpose of making a similar registration entry.

Greffier
The court registrar responsible for registering insolvency suits, recording judgments, making marginal entries, and transmitting copies to the Cairo Court.<SEP>The Greffier is a court clerk or registrar responsible for recording judgment charge orders, notifying the debtor, endorsing copies of judgments, and informing relevant court offices on the same day the order is rendered.

Article 1119
A referenced legal provision governing the judicial sale procedure for perishable or deteriorating things.<SEP>A legal provision authorizing the pledgee or pledgor to apply to the Judge for authority to sell the pledged thing by public auction or at market value if it is in danger of perishing, deteriorating, or diminishing in value, with the creditor's right transferring to the sale price.

Article 244
Article 244 provides that creditors and particular successors in good faith may invoke a hidden contract and establish the simulation of a prejudicial contract by any means; in case of conflict, those relying on the ostensible contract have preference.<SEP>A legal provision allowing creditors and particular successors in good faith to avail themselves of the hidden contract in simulated contracts and establish simulation by any means.

Article 245
A legal provision stating that the genuine contract binds contracting parties and their universal successors when a genuine contract is hidden behind an ostensible contract.

Article 246
A legal provision establishing the right of retention, allowing a person to refrain from performing obligations until the creditor performs connected obligations or provides adequate security.

Article 247
A legal provision stating that the right of retention does not imply a privilege, requiring the retainer to preserve the thing according to pledge rules and to account for its fruits.

Article 248
A legal provision stating that the right of retention is extinguished when the thing ceases to be in the hands of the possessor or holder, with a 30-day claim period for restitution.

Article 249
A legal provision allowing a debtor to be declared insolvent when assets are insufficient to pay due debts.

Article 250
A legal provision stating that insolvency is declared by judgment of the Court of First Instance upon petition of the debtor or a creditor, heard as a matter of urgency.

Article 251
A legal provision requiring the court to consider all circumstances surrounding the debtor, including future resources, personal ability, and creditor interests, before declaring insolvency.

Article 252
A legal provision setting an eight-day period for opposition and a fifteen-day period for appeal in insolvency judgments, calculated from the date of notification.

Article 253
A legal provision requiring the greffier to register insolvency suits in a special register, record judgments and marginal entries, and send copies to the Cairo Court for a general register.

Article 254
A legal provision requiring a debtor who changes domicile to notify the greffier of the former court, which must transmit records to the new court at the debtor's expense.

Article 255
A legal provision rendering all debts immediately due upon insolvency declaration, with allowance for the judge to maintain or extend payment deadlines in the interests of both debtor and creditors.

Article 256
A legal provision stating that insolvency does not bar individual creditor proceedings, but charges on debtor property registered after the insolvency petition are void against prior creditors.

Article 257
A legal provision rendering void, as against creditors, any debtor acts after insolvency registration that diminish assets or increase liabilities, including debt payments.

Article 258
A legal provision allowing a debtor to dispose of property at normal price with proceeds deposited at the court treasury; sales below normal price require the purchaser to deposit the difference.

Article 259
A legal provision allowing the court president to grant an alimentary allowance to the debtor from attached revenues, subject to three-day opposition periods.

Article 260
A legal provision imposing misappropriation penalties on debtors who willfully become insolvent in fraud of creditors or who conceal property or fabricate fictitious debts after insolvency judgment.

Article 261
A legal provision governing cessation of insolvency by court judgment when liabilities no longer exceed assets or when the debtor pays debts that were due before the declaration.

Article 262
A legal provision providing for automatic cessation of insolvency upon the expiration of five years from the date of registration of the insolvency judgment.

Article 263
A referenced legal provision governing the restoration of original payment terms for debts after the state of insolvency ceases.

Misappropriation
A penal offense applicable to debtors who willfully render themselves insolvent or conceal property in fraud of creditor rights.<SEP>Misappropriation is a legal penalty applicable to any person, including an heir, who fraudulently appropriates a part of the assets of the estate.

Possessor
A person who holds or possesses a thing and may exercise the right of retention, having incurred necessary or useful expenditure on the thing, and is required to preserve it according to pledge rules.<SEP>A possessor is a person who exercises actual control over a right or thing, and whose rights and obligations are governed by these articles.<SEP>A person who holds physical possession of property, whose rights and obligations vary depending on whether possession is held in good faith or bad faith.

Caisse du Tribunal
The Caisse du Tribunal is the court treasury where proceeds from public auction sales are deposited by order of the judge.<SEP>The court treasury where purchase prices from debtor property dispositions are deposited for distribution to creditors in accordance with the procedure for distribution.

Alimentary Allowance
A living allowance that the President of the Court may grant to a debtor from attached revenues during insolvency proceedings, subject to opposition within three days.<SEP>An Alimentary Allowance is a financial provision authorized by the Juge de Service for heirs who were supported by the deceased, paid from estate assets pending final winding up and deductible from each heir's inheritance share under Article 882.

Particular Successors in Title
Legal successors who, if in good faith, may avail themselves of the hidden contract and establish the simulation of a contract by which they were prejudiced.

Universal Successors in Title
Legal successors who are bound by the genuine (hidden) contract when a genuine contract has been concealed behind an ostensible contract.

Obligation
An Obligation is a legal duty or commitment that is extinguished through extinctive prescription after fifteen years unless a special provision specifies otherwise.<SEP>An Obligation is a legal bond that is definitely created as a liability of the Debtor, requiring performance, payment, or abstention, and may be extinguished by payment or equivalent means.<SEP>A binding duty that must be performed by a debtor under a contract; its object must be determinate as to kind and quantity, and when the quality is not specified, the debtor must supply an article of average quality.

Contract
A legal agreement between parties creating reciprocal obligations; may be rescinded upon non-performance, impossibility of performance, or by mutual agreement, with reinstatement of parties to their former position.<SEP>A binding agreement between parties that constitutes the law governing their relationship; it must be performed in good faith and cannot be revoked or altered except by mutual consent or for reasons provided by law.<SEP>A contract is created, subject to any special formalities required by law, from the moment two persons exchange two concordant intentions. Contracts may be formed in person, between absent parties, by telephone, or through conduct.<SEP>A contract is a legal agreement whose validity may be affected by legal capacity, defects of consent such as mistake, fraud, duress, or lesion, and the nature of its object, as governed throughout Articles 109 to 134.<SEP>A legal instrument that may contain an inalienability clause restricting the disposition of property, subject to validity requirements of legitimate reason and reasonable duration.<SEP>A Contract is the legal mechanism through which ownership of movables and immovables and other real rights are transferred, provided the contract refers to an object belonging to the person disposing of it.

Consideration
The legal reason or cause for an obligation; an obligation is presumed to have lawful consideration even if not expressed, and a contract is void when assumed without consideration or with consideration contrary to public policy or morality.

Nullity
The legal state of invalidity of a void contract; it may be invoked by any interested person and ordered by the court on its own initiative, cannot disappear by ratification, and proceedings are prescribed after fifteen years from the conclusion of the contract.

Avoidance
The legal remedy allowing a contracting party to annul a voidable contract; the right to avoidance belongs exclusively to the designated party, is extinguished by ratification, and is prescribed if not invoked within three years.

Ratification
The act by which an owner confirms a sale made by a non-owner, making the contract binding and valid; ratification also applies in the context of sales during last illness where heirs may ratify a sale exceeding one third of the inheritance.<SEP>Express or implied confirmation of a voidable contract that extinguishes the right to avoidance and is retroactive to the date of the contract without prejudice to the rights of third parties.

Contract of Adhesion
A contract containing leonine conditions, where the judge may modify these conditions or relieve the adhering party of the obligation to perform them in accordance with the principles of equity.

Public Policy
Fundamental legal and societal principles; a contract is void if its object or consideration is contrary to public policy.<SEP>Public policy in Egypt serves as a ground for refusing to apply foreign law provisions that are contrary to it.<SEP>A fundamental legal principle that constrains natural obligations; no natural obligation can ever be contrary to public policy.<SEP>A fundamental legal principle that constrains the creation of natural obligations; a natural obligation cannot exist if it is contrary to public policy, as stated in Article 200.<SEP>Matters touching the status of individuals or general legal principles on which a compromise cannot be made, though proprietary interests arising from personal status or penal offences may be compromised.

Morality
Standards of moral conduct recognized by law; a contract is void if its object or consideration is contrary to morality.<SEP>Morality in Egypt serves as a ground, alongside public policy, for refusing to apply foreign law provisions that are contrary to it, as stated in Article 28.

Legal Incapacity
The state of lacking legal capacity to contract; it serves as grounds for avoidance of a contract, with the prescription period running from the date of cessation of such incapacity.<SEP>Legal incapacity refers to a condition under which a person may be declared totally or partially incapable of concluding contracts, including minors, persons suffering from insanity, mental derangement, imbecility, and prodigals.

Mistake
An error affecting contract validity that serves as grounds for avoidance; the right to avoidance must be invoked within three years from the date the mistake is discovered.

Fraudulent Misrepresentation
Deliberate deception that serves as grounds for avoidance of a contract; the right to avoidance must be invoked within three years from the date the misrepresentation is discovered.<SEP>Fraudulent misrepresentation consists of artifices or intentional silence by a party or their representative of such gravity that, but for them, the other party would not have concluded the contract, as defined in Article 125.

Duress
Coercion that serves as grounds for avoidance of a contract; the right to avoidance must be invoked within three years from the date the duress ceases.<SEP>Duress is unlawful pressure whereby a person contracts under the stress of justifiable fear instilled by the other party, involving serious and imminent danger to life, limb, honor, or property, as described in Article 127.<SEP>A circumstance under which a payor makes a payment, which constitutes an exception to the rule barring restitution; a payor who paid under duress may recover the payment even if he knew he was not obligated, as provided in Article 181.

Stipulation for Third Party
A contractual provision by which a person stipulates that an obligation be performed for the benefit of a third party, giving the beneficiary a direct right against the promisor; the beneficiary may be a future or unspecified person identifiable at the time the contract takes effect.

Stipulator
A party who makes a stipulation in favor of a third party in a contract; may revoke the stipulation before the beneficiary claims it, substitute a new beneficiary, or retain the benefit for himself.<SEP>The contracting party who stipulates that an obligation be performed for the benefit of a third party; the stipulator may revoke the stipulation before the beneficiary accepts it, substitute a new beneficiary, or retain the benefit.

Universal Successor in Title
A general successor, such as an heir, who acquires the rights and obligations of a contracting party, subject to the rules relating to successions.

Particular Successor in Title
A specific successor who acquires property along with associated obligations and rights, provided such obligations constitute essential elements of the property and the successor had knowledge at the time of transfer.

Leonine Condition
Unfair or oppressive terms found in contracts of adhesion that the judge may modify or relieve the adhering party from performing.

Promisor
The person who undertakes to perform an obligation for the benefit of a third party; the promisor may set up against the beneficiary the defenses arising out of the contract and is liable to indemnify the other contracting party if the third party refuses to perform.

Equity
A legal principle referenced as a standard for contract performance and for the modification of leonine conditions in contracts of adhesion, requiring fairness and just outcomes between the parties.

Contract Interpretation
The process of ascertaining the common intention of the contracting parties; when contract wording is clear it cannot be deviated from, but when interpretation is needed, the search goes beyond the literal meaning of words to account for the nature of the transaction and commercial usage.

Reinstatement
The legal remedy by which parties to a void or annulled contract are restored to their prior positions; if reinstatement is impossible, equivalent damages may be awarded.

Damages
Compensation for injury or loss awarded by a judge; may consist of a money payment paid in installments, a regular periodical payment, restoration of the original position, or performance of a specific act connected to the unlawful act.<SEP>Compensation awarded to a party when reinstatement to the position prior to a void or annulled contract is impossible, equivalent to the loss suffered.<SEP>Monetary compensation awarded for non-performance or delayed performance of obligations, including losses suffered by the creditor, profits deprived, and moral prejudice, assessed by the judge if not fixed by contract or law.<SEP>Financial compensation payable by the lessor to the lessee for losses caused by defects, disturbances, or government authority acts imputable to the lessor, or payable by the lessee for unauthorized alterations or unlawful retention of the property.

Contracting Party
A person who enters into a contract; the effects of a contract apply to the contracting parties, and a contract binds them not only to expressed conditions but also to everything deemed a necessary sequel according to law, usage, and equity.

Property Owner
A person who holds the exclusive right to use, enjoy, and dispose of property within the limits of the law, including rights to all fruits, products, and accessories of the property.

Neighbor
An owner of adjoining property who has rights and obligations related to neighboring properties, including nuisance claims, right of way, and shared costs for canals and boundary marks.<SEP>An adjoining property owner bound by specific obligations regarding shared walls, views, boundary marks, and rights of way, and who may become a co-proprietor of a heightened party wall by contributing to costs.

Joint and Several Liability
A form of liability arising when several persons are responsible for an injurious act; they are jointly and severally obligated to make reparation, with liability shared equally unless the judge fixes individual shares.<SEP>A form of liability where each party is individually responsible for the entire obligation, applicable to sureties either by contract stipulation or by operation of law in judicial and legal suretyship.

Right of Ownership
The exclusive legal right to use, enjoy, and dispose of a thing within the limits of the law, encompassing all essential elements of the thing owned and extending to what is above and below land.<SEP>The fundamental property right from which other real rights such as usufruct, use, and occupation are derived, forming the subject of Chapter II of the legal text.

Right of Way
A legal easement allowing an owner whose land is cut off from a public road to pass over neighboring land, subject to fair compensation and the condition of least possible damage.<SEP>A legal easement allowing a landowner to pass through neighboring property when the land is cut off from a public road, subject to payment of fair compensation and exercised where it causes the least possible damage.

Private Canal or Drain
A privately constructed waterway or drainage system built in conformity with regulations, granting the builder exclusive usage rights, while neighboring owners may use it for irrigation or drainage after the owner's needs are met.

Boundary Marks
Physical markers placed along the boundaries of adjoining properties, with the cost of delimitation shared between neighboring owners.<SEP>Markers placed along the boundaries of adjoining properties, whose cost of delimitation is shared between neighboring owners.

Egyptian Territory
The geographic boundaries of Egypt; property situated outside Egyptian territory is not taken into account when indicated by a surety under Article 789.

Egyptian Civil Code
The Egyptian Civil Code (القانون المدني المصري) is a comprehensive legislative document governing civil matters in Egypt, including laws, rights, legal capacity, conflicts of law, and various civil obligations.<SEP>The body of civil law containing provisions governing suretyship relationships and real property rights in Egypt, as reflected in Articles 788–814.

Debt
A financial obligation owed by a debtor to a creditor, the central subject of the suretyship provisions, including capital, interest, and expenses, as governed by Articles 788–801.

Sub-Surety
A person who guarantees the obligation of a principal surety, as provided under Article 797; the creditor may not proceed against the sub-surety before acting against the principal surety unless the sub-surety is jointly and severally liable with the principal surety.

Public Road
A public thoroughfare referenced in Article 812; an owner whose land is cut off from or lacks adequate access to a public road is entitled to a right of way over neighboring land.<SEP>A road accessible to the public, referenced as the access route for which a right of way may be claimed when land is cut off, and as an exception allowing an oblique view prohibition to cease when the view is simultaneously a direct view over a public road.

Land
A form of property whose ownership extends to what is above and below it to the extent of useful enjoyment, and which is subject to rules on water passage, irrigation, drainage, right of way, and boundary demarcation under Articles 802–814.

Fair Compensation
Compensation payable to a neighbor when a right of way is exercised over the neighbor's land.<SEP>A payment required by law when an owner is deprived of property under Article 805, when water passage is permitted across land under Article 809, and when a right of way is exercised over neighboring land under Article 812.

Bilateral Contract
A contract binding both parties to correlative obligations (contrats synallagmatiques); either party may abstain from performing his obligation if the other party does not perform.

Rescission
The dissolution of a contract; may be demanded after formal summons, agreed to as automatic (ipso facto) upon non-performance, or occur automatically upon impossibility of performance.

Formal Summons
A legal notice that must be served on a debtor before demanding performance or rescission of a contract, unless the parties expressly agree to dispense with it.<SEP>A legal procedure to notify a debtor of default, served through the court or by equivalent act, including by post in accordance with the Code de Procedure, or resulting from a stipulation in an agreement.<SEP>A Formal Summons is the official notification issued by the Vendor or Purchaser to the prospective preemptor, which must contain an adequate description of the property, the price, costs, conditions of sale, and the identities of the Vendor and Purchaser, on pain of nullity, as prescribed in Articles 940 and 941.

Reward
A prize promised to the public in exchange for a specified service; the promisor is bound to pay whoever performs the service, even without knowledge of the promise, and may withdraw the promise by public notice.

Unlawful Act
A fault causing injury to another that imposes an obligation of reparation on the person who committed it; forms the basis for tort liability and may give rise to a damages action prescribed after three years.<SEP>An illegal action for which any contractual clause discharging a person from responsibility is void. Formal summons is not required when the object of the obligation is payment of damages for an unlawful act.<SEP>An act that gives rise to liability regardless of legal capacity; a voluntary agent who is not legally capable is still liable if his liability results from an unlawful act, as stated in Article 196.

Legitimate Defense
Self-defense of one's own person or property, or that of a third party; exempts a person from liability for causing injury, provided the defensive measures do not exceed what is necessary.

Public Official
A government employee who is not liable for causing injury if acting in pursuance of a superior's order that he was obliged to obey, provided he had reasonable grounds to believe the act was lawful and acted with care.

Victim
A person who suffers injury from an unlawful act and may claim damages; the right of action is prescribed after three years from knowledge of the injury and the responsible person, or fifteen years from the unlawful act.

Supervisor
A person entrusted by law or agreement with the supervision of a person requiring care due to minority or mental or physical condition; liable for injuries caused by the supervised person and may escape liability by proving due diligence.

Minor
A person under fifteen years of age or still under the care of a guardian; deemed to require supervision, which transfers to schoolteachers or craft supervisors while under their care.<SEP>A minor is a person who has not attained majority. A minor who has attained eighteen years has a special domicile for acts the law considers the minor capable of performing.

Master
A person who has actual powers of supervision and control over a servant; liable for damage caused by the servant's unlawful acts performed in the course of or as a result of employment.<SEP>The Master (Employer) commissions works, is obligated to take delivery and pay the price, may terminate the contract before completion provided compensation is paid, and has rights regarding contract resiliation in cases of significant cost overruns.

Servant
A person under the employment and control of a master; the master-servant relationship exists when the master has actual powers of supervision and direction over the servant.

Animal Keeper
A person in charge of an animal, even if not its owner, who is liable for harm caused by the animal even if it strays or escapes, unless the harm resulted from a cause beyond the keeper's control.

Animal
A living creature under the care of an animal keeper; harm caused by the animal gives rise to the keeper's strict liability.<SEP>A living creature for whose harm a person in charge is liable even if not the owner, even if the animal strays or escapes, unless the accident was due to a cause beyond control, as established in Article 176.

Building Keeper
A person in charge of a building, even if not its owner, who is liable for damage caused by the building's collapse.

Penal Offence
A criminal offense from which a damages claim may arise; when the penal action has not yet prescribed, the civil damages action is only prescribed when the penal action itself is prescribed.

Necessity
A legal defense where a person causes injury to another in order to avoid a greater injury threatening himself or a third party; the person is only responsible for such equitable damages as the judge deems appropriate.

Security
A guarantee that a debtor may be ordered to provide when damages are paid by installments or in the form of a regular periodical payment, as determined by the judge.<SEP>Security refers to the special guarantee or collateral given to a creditor by a debtor, whether by subsequent act or by virtue of law. The debtor must not diminish the security, and if it is reduced, the debtor may forfeit the benefit of the term unless adequate replacement security is provided.<SEP>Security refers to guarantees on movable or immovable property given to creditors of the estate, which must be published in accordance with provisions for judgment charges on real property if granted on immovable property.<SEP>A guarantee or surety that may be demanded from the possessor or usufructuary to protect the rights of the owner, including in contexts of installment repayments, endangered ownership rights, and movable property subject to usufruct.

Right of Redress
The legal right of a person held responsible for the act of another to claim compensation from that other person to the extent that the other person is responsible for reparation of the injury.

Restoration
A method of making good damage ordered by the judge upon the demand of the victim, whereby the original position before the unlawful act is restored.

Special Mandate
A mandate required for any act that is not an act of management, in particular for sale, mortgage, gifts, compromise, admission, arbitration, tendering of an oath, and court representation. It only confers power to act in specified matters and matters necessarily incidental thereto according to prevailing custom.

Substitute (نائب الوكيل)
A person nominated by the mandatary to perform the mandate in the mandatary's place. If appointed without authorization, the mandatary is responsible for the substitute's acts as if they were their own, and both are jointly and severally liable. If authorized, the mandatary is only liable for faulty choice or faulty instructions.

Third Party (الغير)
An external person who deals with the mandatary or in whose interest a mandate may be granted. When a mandate is given in the interest of a third party, the mandator may not revoke or restrict it without the third party's consent. Articles 104 to 107 regarding representation apply to the relationship with third parties.

Heirs (ورثة)
The heirs of a deceased mandatary who, if they possess legal capacity and knowledge of the mandate, are bound to inform the mandator of the death and take necessary steps to protect the mandator's interests.

Judge (القاضى)
The judicial authority who assesses the remuneration agreed for a mandate, unless the remuneration has been voluntarily paid after performance of the mandate.

Deposit (الوديعة)
A contract whereby one person (the depository) agrees to take delivery from another person (the depositor) a thing which the depository undertakes to keep in safe custody and return in kind. The depository may not use the deposited thing without authority or appoint a substitute except in cases of urgent necessity.

Depository (المودع عنده)
The person who receives the deposited thing and is bound to keep it in safe custody and return it. In a gratuitous deposit, the depository must exercise the care used in their own affairs; in a remunerated deposit, the diligence of a reasonable person is required. The depository must return the thing upon the depositor's request.

Depositor (المودع)
The person who delivers a thing to the depository for safe custody. The depositor has the right to demand return of the deposited thing at any time, unless the contract specifies a term fixed in the interests of the depository.

Articles 104 to 107
Legal provisions regarding representation that apply to the relationship of a mandator and a mandatary with third parties dealing with the mandatary, as referenced in Article 713.

Joint and Several Liability (التضامن)
A legal concept whereby multiple mandataries appointed under the same mandate, or multiple mandators who appoint a sole mandatary for a common purpose, share collective responsibility. Applies when the mandate is indivisible, when damage results from common fault, or when a mandatary appoints an unauthorized substitute. Mandataries are not responsible for acts by co-mandataries exceeding mandate limits or involving wrongful use.

Reasonable Person (الرجل المعتاد)
The legal standard of care and diligence used as a benchmark for obligations under both mandate and deposit contracts. Under a remunerated mandate, the mandatary must always exercise the diligence of a reasonable person; under a remunerated deposit, the depository must exercise the same standard. Under gratuitous arrangements, the standard is the care one gives to their own affairs, without exceeding the reasonable person standard.

Renunciation of Mandate
The right of the mandatary to resign from the mandate at any time, even contrary to agreement, by notifying the mandator. In a remunerated mandate, the mandatary must indemnify the mandator for loss from untimely or unjustified renunciation. A mandatary may not renounce a mandate given in the interest of a third party without serious justification and must notify the third party.

Revocation of Mandate
