The right of the mandator to revoke or restrict the mandate at any time, notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary. In a remunerated mandate, the mandator must indemnify the mandatary for loss from untimely or unjustified revocation. The mandator cannot revoke a mandate granted in the interest of a third party without that party's consent.

Servitude
Servitude is a type of encumbrance or right affecting the thing sold, which the vendor is presumed not to warrant if it was apparent or disclosed to the purchaser, as provided under Article 445.<SEP>A legal right constituting a relationship of subordination between two properties, where the dominant tenement benefits from rights over the servient tenement, including use, preservation, and specific restrictions on building or land use.

Dominant Tenement
The property that benefits from a servitude, whose owner is entitled to carry out works necessary to use and preserve the right of servitude and must use it in the least harmful manner possible.

Servient Tenement
The property that bears the burden of a servitude, whose owner may not diminish the use of the servitude or make it more inconvenient, but may demand its transfer or cessation under certain conditions.

Mortgagor
The person who grants a mortgage over property; may be the debtor or a third party, and must be the owner of the mortgaged property with legal capacity to dispose of it.<SEP>The mortgagor is the party who bears the cost of inscription, its renewal, and its radiation of the mortgage, unless an agreement provides otherwise.<SEP>The person who grants a mortgage over their property. The mortgagor may dispose of and manage the mortgaged property and collect its fruits until they become incorporated in the immovable. The mortgagor may be a person other than the debtor, and in such case only the mortgaged property may be proceeded against. The mortgagor is the guarantor of the effectiveness of the mortgage.

Mortgagee Creditor
The creditor in whose favor a mortgage is constituted, acquiring a real right of preference over ordinary and subordinate creditors for payment of the claim from the proceeds of the mortgaged immovable property.

Immovable Property
Immovable Property (العقار) refers to real estate whose possession, ownership, and real rights are governed by the law of the place where the immovable is situated, as stated in Article 18.<SEP>Immovable property includes things fixed in place that cannot be removed without damage, real rights over immovable property including ownership, and movables placed by their owner in an immovable to serve or exploit it.<SEP>Immovable property is real estate belonging to a person, including a legally incapable person, whose value is assessed at the time of sale to determine whether lesion exceeds one fifth.<SEP>Immovable Property refers to real estate whose ownership and other real rights are not transferred unless the rules laid down in the law regulating the publication of real rights are observed, and which may be subject to preemption.<SEP>Property on which a mortgage may only be constituted; it must be marketable, capable of being sold by public auction, and specifically described as to its nature and situation.<SEP>A category of property that is fixed or attached to land, including real estate and buildings, which serves as the subject of special privileges established in Articles 1147 through 1149.

Authentic Document
A formal official instrument required for a valid gift of immovable property and for a binding promise to make a gift; absence of such a document renders the gift void unless it is disguised under another contract.<SEP>An official instrument required for the valid constitution of a mortgage, the costs of which are borne by the mortgagor unless otherwise agreed.

data.entity_name: Book IV: Accessory Rights Or Real Securities
data.content:
Book IV: Accessory Rights Or Real Securities
The fourth book of the legal code governing accessory real rights and real securities, including mortgages and related provisions.

Chapter I: Mortgages
The first chapter of Book IV, governing the constitution, effects, and rules applicable to mortgages over immovable property.

Article 1148
A referenced legal provision granting a privilege to sums due to contractors or architects, preserved without prejudice when a mortgage extends to accessories of the mortgaged property.<SEP>Article 1148 provides that sums due to contractors and architects entrusted with erection, reconstruction, repair, or maintenance of buildings or other works have a privilege over such works limited to the increase in value, and such privilege must be inscribed.

Co-Owners In Common
Joint owners of a dominant tenement who share servitude rights; use of the servitude by one co-owner interrupts prescription in favor of all others.

Deed Of Creation
The document by which a servitude is created, containing the rules that govern the servitude as stated in Article 1019.

Local Custom
The customary practices of a locality that serve as one of the governing sources for servitudes alongside the deed of creation and statutory provisions.

Prescription
Prescription (التقادم) refers to legal time limits, with new legislative provisions applying from the time they come into force for incomplete prescription periods.<SEP>The legal time limit for bringing claims, generally set at three years from knowledge of the right and fifteen years from when the right arose for enrichment, restitution, and voluntary agency claims.<SEP>Prescription is the extinction of a debt through the passage of a legally prescribed time period; it benefits other co-debtors only to the extent of the contributing debtor's share, and interruption or suspension as to one debtor does not affect others.<SEP>A legal mechanism by which a neighbor may acquire the right to a direct view over another's property at a distance of less than one meter through long-term continuous use, preventing the other neighbor from building within one meter along the length of the building in which the view was opened.<SEP>A legal mechanism by which a right of servitude can be extinguished through non-user over a prescribed period, or by which the manner of exercising the servitude can be modified, as stated in Article 1027.

Non-User
The failure to exercise a servitude right over a specified period, leading to its extinguishment: fifteen years in general and thirty-three years for servitudes benefiting wakf property.

Fruits And Revenues
The produce and income generated by a mortgaged property, which from the date of transcription of the formal summons to pay are assimilated to the immovable and distributed in the same manner as the price of the property.

Formal Summons To Pay
An official notice whose transcription triggers the assimilation of the fruits and revenues of the mortgaged property to the immovable, making them distributable in the same manner as the property price.

Future Property
Property that does not yet exist at the time of the gift, a gift of which is declared void under Article 492.<SEP>Property not yet owned or in expectancy; a mortgage on future property is declared void under Article 1033.

data.entity_name: Section I: The Constitution Of Mortgages
data.content:
Section I: The Constitution Of Mortgages
A subdivision of Chapter I within Book IV, specifically addressing the requirements and rules for the valid creation and formation of mortgages.

Lessor
The party in a lease contract who is bound to deliver the leased property, maintain it in good condition, carry out necessary repairs, and abstain from disturbing the lessee's enjoyment.<SEP>The property owner who grants a lease to the lessee. The lessor is obligated to abstain from disturbing the lessee's enjoyment, warrants against disturbances and defects, and has rights including lien on movables, rent collection, and objecting to alterations. The lessor is liable for compensation when defects or disturbances cause damage to the lessee.<SEP>The lessor is the property owner who grants a lease to the lessee. The lessor has rights of retention and recovery over movables, is entitled to receive rent, may agree to or object to improvements, and may terminate the lease under certain conditions such as personal need or the lessee's insolvency.<SEP>The party who grants a lease and owns or controls the leased property, with rights to receive rent and obligations to hand over property and perform major repairs.<SEP>The Lessor (المؤجر) is a person who leases property. The lessor is deemed a holder of furniture in leased premises for purposes of privilege enforcement. The lessor has a privilege over attachable movables and crops on the leased property belonging to the lessee for rent and other sums due under the lease, as governed by Article 1143.<SEP>A person who leases property and holds a lessor's privilege, which has the same rank as a hotel proprietor's privilege.

Lessee
The party in a lease contract who enjoys the use of the leased property in return for paying rent and may demand resiliation or rent reduction under certain conditions.<SEP>The party who rents and occupies the leased property from the lessor. The lessee is obligated to use the property as agreed, carry out lessee's repairs, pay rent at agreed times, notify the lessor of issues requiring intervention, restitute the property upon lease expiration, and is responsible for fire damage and deterioration not resulting from normal use.<SEP>The lessee is the party who rents the leased property from the lessor. The lessee is obligated to restitute the leased property upon expiration, maintain it in good condition, pay rent, and may assign the lease or sublet subject to agreement. The lessee may make improvements and claim reimbursement for them.<SEP>The party who rents and occupies leased property, with obligations including proper cultivation, maintenance of land and equipment, and payment of rent.<SEP>The Lessee is the party who leases wakf property and is bound, under penalty of resiliation of the contract, to make up the rent to the level of rent for similar properties if the agreed rent is grossly inadequate.<SEP>The Lessee (المستأجر) is a person who rents property from a lessor. The lessee's movables and crops on the leased property are subject to the lessor's privilege, as stated in Article 1143.

Sub-Lessee
A sub-lessee is a person who rents the leased property from the principal lessee under a sub-lease arrangement. The sub-lessee is directly answerable to the lessor for amounts owed to the principal lessee after a summons is served.<SEP>The Sub-Lessee (المستأجر من الباطن) is a person who rents property from the principal lessee. The lessor's privilege extends to movables and crops belonging to the sub-lessee if sub-letting was expressly prohibited, or up to the amount due by the sub-lessee to the principal lessee if sub-letting was not prohibited, as governed by Article 1143.

Assignee
The assignee is the person to whom a right is assigned, who may exercise a right of recourse in warranty against the assignor, and whose assignment is preferred if it is first effective as regards third parties in cases of multiple assignments.<SEP>The assignee is the person to whom the lease is transferred by the principal lessee. The principal lessee remains guarantor for the assignee's obligations unless the lessor formally accepts the assignment.

Heirs of Lessee
The heirs of the lessee may claim termination of the lease upon the death of the lessee if the burden of the lease has become too heavy for their resources or exceeds their needs, provided they act within six months of the death.<SEP>The successors of a deceased lessee who may claim reimbursement of expenses or continue cultivation of the land until crops ripen in the case of amodiation.

New Owner
The new owner is a third party to whom ownership of the leased property is voluntarily or forcibly transferred. The new owner is bound by the lease only if it has an established date prior to the transfer, and may evict the lessee only after providing proper notice and compensation.

Leased Property
The specific thing that is the subject of a lease contract, which must be delivered in a condition suitable for its intended purpose.<SEP>The property subject to the agreement of lease, which the lessee is entitled to use and enjoy. It may be an immovable property such as a house, warehouse, shop, or agricultural land, and may contain defects or be subject to third-party claims and government authority actions.<SEP>The leased property is the subject of the lease contract. It must be restituted by the lessee upon expiration in the condition it was received, subject to permissible loss or deterioration.

Lease Contract
The lease contract is the agreement between the lessor and lessee governing the use of the leased property. It ends at the expiration of the agreed term and may be renewed tacitly, assigned, or sublet subject to conditions established in the applicable articles.

Assignment of Lease
Assignment of lease is the transfer of the lessee's rights under the lease to an assignee. The principal lessee remains guarantor for the assignee's obligations unless the lessor formally agrees to the assignment.

Sub-Lease
A sub-lease is an arrangement where the lessee rents out the whole or part of the leased property to a sub-lessee. A prohibition of sub-letting implies a prohibition of assignment and vice versa.

Compensation
Compensation is a payment owed by the lessee to the lessor for unlawful retention of the leased property, for damage caused by removal of unauthorized improvements, or owed by the lessor to the lessee for early eviction or termination of the lease.<SEP>Damages that the lessee may be entitled to claim when the leased property is unfit for use, its usefulness is appreciably diminished, or the lessor fails to fulfill obligations.<SEP>Compensation is the legal mechanism by which mutual debts between a creditor and a co-debtor are offset; a joint and several debtor cannot set up compensation with regard to that which a creditor owes to another co-debtor, except in respect of that other co-debtor's share.<SEP>Compensation refers to amounts due on account of the destruction of a building, which shall be set aside for the costs of reconstruction without prejudice to the rights of registered creditors, per Article 868.

Improvements
Improvements include buildings, plantings, or other additions made by the lessee to the leased property that increase its value. The lessor is bound to reimburse the lessee for improvements unless they were made without knowledge or despite objection.

Rent
The payment due under a lease, which may consist of money or any other prestation, and is determined by agreement or based on current rent for similar properties.<SEP>The payment owed by the lessee to the lessor for use of the leased property, payable at agreed times or, in the absence of agreement, at times established by local custom. Payment is presumed to cover prior terms unless proven otherwise.<SEP>Rent is the payment owed by the lessee to the lessor for use of the leased property. Advance rent payments cannot be set up against a new owner if the lessee knew of the ownership transfer at the time of payment.

Notice of Evacuation
Notice of evacuation is a formal notification given by one party to the other to terminate the lease and vacate the leased property, governed by the periods specified in Article 563.<SEP>The formal notice required to terminate a lease of undetermined duration, with specific notice periods varying by property type: three months for agricultural and uncultivated land, two months for houses, shops, offices, and warehouses, and one month for apartments and furnished rooms.

Tacit Renewal
Tacit renewal occurs when the lessee continues to enjoy the leased property after expiration with the knowledge and without objection of the lessor. It is deemed a new lease on the same conditions but for an indefinite duration.

Article 563
Article 563 is a referenced legal provision that prescribes the periods of notice of termination applicable to lease agreements and is cited throughout Articles 599 through 608.<SEP>A referenced legal provision governing notice periods required for lease termination.

Real Securities
Real securities are property-based guarantees provided by the debtor for the original obligation, which may be transferred to the new obligation under specific conditions depending on the type of novation.<SEP>Real securities are guarantees supplied by the lessee in connection with the lease. They transfer to a tacitly renewed lease subject to the rules of publication applicable to real property.

Industrial or Commercial Establishment
An industrial or commercial establishment is a business entity created by the lessee on the leased immovable property. Its sale by the lessee may trigger judicial exceptions to sub-letting prohibitions under Article 594.

Movables
Movables are personal property items present on the leased property over which the lessor holds rights of retention and recovery, except when removed to meet the professional requirements of the lessee in accordance with customary requirements of daily life.<SEP>Furniture, goods, crops, cattle, or implements found in the leased property that serve as security for rent payment and are subject to the lessor's lien, even when they do not belong to the lessee.

Proces Verbal
A proces verbal is a formal written record or inventory setting out particulars of the leased property drawn at the time of delivery. Its absence creates a legal presumption that the lessee received the property in good condition.

Transfer of Ownership
Transfer of ownership is the voluntary or forced conveyance of the leased property to a third party, which affects the enforceability of the lease against the new owner depending on whether the lease has an established date prior to the transfer.

Resiliation of Lease
The termination of a lease contract that the lessee may demand if the leased property is unfit for use, poses a serious health danger, or is partially or totally destroyed.<SEP>The termination of the lease agreement, available as a remedy to the lessee when enjoyment is deprived by third-party claims, government authority acts, trespass, or defects warranting such action.<SEP>Resiliation of lease is the judicial cancellation of the lease contract, distinct from normal termination. The lessor may claim resiliation due to the lessee's insolvency unless securities are provided, and the lessee may claim resiliation if not authorized to assign or sublet, upon payment of equitable compensation.

Party Wall
A wall shared between two adjoining properties that co-proprietors may use for its intended purpose, including supporting roof beams, provided the wall is not overloaded; repairs and reconstruction costs are borne proportionally by co-proprietors.

Direct View
A legal concept restricting a neighbor from having a straight-facing opening over a neighbor's property at a distance of less than one meter, measured from the outside face of the wall or the edge of a balcony.

Oblique View
A legal concept restricting a neighbor from having an angled opening over a neighbor's property at a distance of less than fifty centimeters from the outside edge of the opening, unless the view also constitutes a direct view over a public road.

Light Shaft Opening
An opening whose base is above normal human height, intended solely for the passage of air and light, not providing a view over neighboring property, and exempt from distance requirements.

Inalienability Clause
A clause in a contract or will stipulating that a property cannot be alienated; valid only if based on a legitimate reason, such as protecting a lawful interest, and limited to a reasonable duration, which may extend for the life of a relevant party.

Joint Ownership
Joint ownership refers to the legal state in which multiple persons hold undivided shares in common property, governed by statutory provisions regarding alienation, partition, and management.<SEP>A form of property ownership in which two or more persons own the same undivided thing, with their respective shares presumed equal in the absence of proof to the contrary.

Co-owner
A person who holds an undivided share in jointly owned property, with absolute ownership of their share, rights to alienate it, collect its fruits, participate in management, and take preservation measures even without consent of others.<SEP>A person who holds an undivided share in an immovable property held in common. A co-owner may grant a mortgage on their undivided share or on a divided part of the immovable. If as a result of partition a different property is attributed to the co-owner, the mortgage transfers to an equivalent portion of the new property.<SEP>A person who shares ownership of property with others and has partitioned it, holding a privilege over the partitioned property for remedies and repayment of differences.

Manager
A person entrusted with directing partnership affairs whose powers cease upon dissolution and who is deemed a liquidator toward third parties until a formal liquidator is appointed.<SEP>A person appointed by majority of co-owners or by the Court to manage property held in common; a co-owner who manages without objection from others is considered a mandatory of the rest.<SEP>A Manager is one or more persons appointed by co-owners holding the majority in value of shares to administer family joint ownership, with authority to introduce changes to improve enjoyment of the property, and who may be discharged by the Court or by the appointing co-owners.

Majority Decision
A decision binding on all co-owners when taken by a majority calculated on the basis of the value of their shares, applicable to ordinary acts of management of commonly held property.

Article 813
A legal provision granting every owner the right to compel neighbors to place boundary marks on adjoining properties, with delimitation costs shared between them.

Article 814
A legal provision governing the use of party walls for intended purposes and the proportional sharing of repair and reconstruction costs among co-proprietors.

Article 815
A legal provision permitting an owner to heighten a party wall for good reason, bearing all costs, provided no serious prejudice is caused to the co-owner, and requiring full reconstruction at the owner's cost if the wall cannot support heightening.

Article 816
A legal provision allowing a neighbor who did not contribute to heightening expenses to become a co-proprietor of the heightened part by paying half the cost and half the value of any increased thickness ground area.

Article 817
A legal provision establishing the presumption that a wall separating two buildings at the time of construction is a party wall up to the point where it ceases to be common.

Article 818
A legal provision preventing an owner from compelling a neighbor to assign part of a wall or land except as provided in Article 816, and prohibiting demolition of a wall that injures a neighbor without good reason.

Article 819
A legal provision requiring a minimum distance of one meter for direct views over a neighbor's property, with rights preserved by prescription.

Article 820
A legal provision requiring a minimum distance of fifty centimeters for oblique views, with the prohibition lifted if the view is simultaneously a direct view over a public road.

Article 821
A legal provision exempting light shaft openings from distance requirements when the opening is above normal human height and intended only for air and light.

Article 822
A legal provision requiring factories, wells, steam engines, and establishments injurious to neighbors to be constructed at distances and under conditions laid down by regulations.

Article 823
A legal provision governing the validity of inalienability clauses in contracts or wills, requiring a legitimate reason and reasonable duration.

Article 824
A legal provision declaring that any alienation contrary to a valid inalienability clause in a contract or will is void.

Article 825
A legal provision defining co-ownership as ownership by two or more persons of the same undivided thing, with shares presumed equal.

Article 826
A legal provision granting each co-owner absolute ownership of their share including alienation and collection of fruits, with provisions for transfer of rights upon partition.

Article 827
A legal provision stating that management of property held in common belongs jointly to all co-owners unless otherwise agreed.

Article 828
A legal provision making majority decisions binding on all co-owners for ordinary management, allowing the Court to appoint a manager, and deeming unobjected managing co-owners as mandatories of the others.

Article 829
A legal provision allowing co-owners holding at least three-quarters of common property to make essential modifications exceeding normal management, with dissenting co-owners having two months to challenge in Court.

Article 830
A legal provision allowing any co-owner to take necessary preservation measures for common property without the consent of other co-owners.

Article 831
A legal provision requiring all co-owners to bear management, preservation, tax, and other costs of common property proportionally to their shares.

Article 832
Article 832 provides that co-owners possessing at least three-quarters of common property may decide to alienate it based on serious grounds, with notification to other co-owners and a right of action before the Court within two months for dissenting co-owners.<SEP>A legal provision allowing co-owners holding at least three-quarters of common property to decide on its alienation based on serious grounds, with Court determination if partition is contrary to co-owners' interests.

Establishments Injurious to Neighbors
A category encompassing factories, wells, steam engines, and all similar establishments that must be constructed at distances and under conditions prescribed by regulations due to their potential to cause harm to neighboring properties.

Regulations
Legal rules that prescribe the distances and conditions under which factories, wells, steam engines, and establishments injurious to neighbors must be constructed, as referenced in Article 822.

Acquirer
A person who acquires a share or specific part of property held in common from a co-owner, whose right transfers to the portion that falls to the settler upon partition, or who may demand cancellation of the alienation if unaware the settler lacked ownership of the specific part alienated.

Partition
Partition refers to the legal process of dividing property held in common among co-owners into separate parts, which may be carried out in kind, by sale, or by provisional arrangements.<SEP>The division of property held in common among co-owners into separate individual portions, referenced in the context of transferring acquirer rights to the part devolving upon the settler, and as a factor in determining whether alienation of jointly owned property should proceed.<SEP>The division of co-owned immovable property. A mortgage granted by all co-owners remains effective regardless of the result of partition. A mortgage on an individual co-owner's share transfers to equivalent property attributed upon partition, with the portion fixed by judicial order.

Common Movable Property
Movable property or a collection of property held in common by co-owners, referenced in Article 833 in the context of a co-owner's right of recovery of a common share before partition is effected.

Article 833
Article 833 grants a co-owner of movable property or property consisting of movables and immovables the right to repurchase an undivided share sold by another co-owner to a third person within thirty days of knowledge or notification of the sale.<SEP>A partially visible legal provision concerning a co-owner's right to recover a common share in movable property or a collection of property before partition.

Solidarity
Solidarity (Joint and Several Obligation) is a relationship between multiple creditors or multiple debtors that is not presumed but created by agreement or by law. Payment by one debtor liberates all others, and a creditor may pay any one of several joint creditors.<SEP>Solidarity is the legal principle under which multiple debtors are jointly bound for the same obligation, such that payment by one debtor liberates all others, and a creditor may take action against all debtors jointly or severally.

Joint and Several Creditor
A joint and several creditor is a creditor in a solidary obligation who receives payment on account of the debt that reverts to all creditors and is divided proportionally or equally among them, subject to contrary agreement or legal provision.

Joint and Several Debtor
A joint and several debtor is a debtor in a solidary obligation who is liable for the entire debt, is only responsible for his own acts in performance, and has a right of recourse against co-debtors for their respective shares after full payment.

Co-debtor
A Co-debtor is a person sharing joint responsibility for a debt, whose obligation is not discharged if the Debtor retracts a tender before acceptance or judgment.<SEP>A co-debtor is a fellow debtor in a joint obligation who shares liability and against whom other co-debtors may claim contribution for their respective shares, including shares of insolvent co-debtors.

Novation
Novation is the replacement of an existing obligation with a new one, effected by a change of the debt, a change of the Debtor, or a change of the Creditor through agreement of the parties.<SEP>Novation is a legal mechanism that extinguishes an original obligation with its accessories and substitutes a new obligation in its place, requiring that both obligations be free from grounds of nullity.<SEP>Novation is the replacement of an existing debt with a new obligation; when occurring between a creditor and one joint and several debtor, it releases other co-debtors unless the creditor reserves his rights against them.

Merger
Merger is a legal mechanism whereby the qualities of creditor and debtor in the same debt are united in one person, extinguishing the debt to the extent of the merger, with revival possible if the cause of merger disappears retroactively.<SEP>Merger occurs when the capacities of creditor and debtor unite in the same person, which does not extinguish the debt as regards other co-debtors except to the extent of the merged share of the co-debtor.

Release of Debt
Release of debt is the creditor's voluntary discharge of a debtor from obligation, which does not release other co-debtors unless the creditor expressly declares such; the creditor may claim the balance from remaining co-debtors after deducting the released debtor's share.

Indivisibility
Indivisibility is a legal principle whereby an obligation cannot be divided, either because its object is naturally indivisible or because the parties intended that performance should not be divided.

Assignment of a Right
The assignment of a right is the transfer of a creditor's claim to a third party, valid without the debtor's consent, subject to conditions of notification, attachability, and comprising all associated warranties, securities, privileges, mortgages, and accrued interest.

Transmission of an Obligation
Transmission of an obligation is the broader legal framework covering the transfer of rights and obligations between parties, organized under Chapter IV of the civil code.

Chapter IV
Chapter IV, titled "Transmission of an Obligation," is a structural division of the civil code encompassing provisions on the assignment of rights and the transfer of obligations.<SEP>A chapter titled "Privileged Rights" introducing priority rights established by law for certain claims.

Section I
Section I, titled "The Assignment of a Right," is a subdivision within Chapter IV specifically addressing the legal rules governing the assignment of a creditor's right to a third party, including validity, effectiveness, warranties, and notification requirements.<SEP>Section I, titled "Elements of a Pledge," is the first section of Chapter III covering the essential requirements, elements, and conditions for a valid pledge, including the object of the pledge and applicable mortgage provisions.<SEP>A section titled "General Provisions" under Chapter IV, appearing at the end of the text and introducing the rules on privileged rights.

Article 298
Article 298 provides that if a joint and several debtor becomes insolvent, the insolvent debtor's share is borne by the co-debtor who effected payment and all other solvent co-debtors pro rata to their respective shares.

Article 300
Article 300 defines when an obligation is indivisible: when its object is by nature not susceptible to division, or when the parties' intention or the purpose of the obligation requires indivisible performance.

Article 303
Article 303 establishes that a creditor may assign his right to a third party provided the claim is not impossible to assign by law, agreement, or nature, and the assignment is valid without the debtor's consent.

Transaction
A transaction is a settlement entered into between a creditor and one joint and several debtor that benefits other co-debtors if it involves remission of the debt or release of liability, but is only binding on other co-debtors if they consent when it creates or increases obligations.

Assignor
The assignor is the person who transfers or assigns a right to another party, warrants the existence of the right at the moment of assignment, and is responsible for personal acts even if the assignment is without consideration or warranty.<SEP>The assignor is the original creditor who transfers his right to a third party; in an assignment for valuable consideration the assignor warrants the existence of the right at the time of assignment, but does not warrant the debtor's solvency unless specifically stipulated.

Attachment
A legal seizure served upon the debtor of an assigned debt, which, if served before the assignment becomes effective against third parties, makes the assignment equivalent to an attachment against the distrainer.<SEP>Attachment is a legal constraint on a creditor's right limiting its transferability; a right can only be assigned to the extent to which it can be attached, as provided under Article 304.

Formal Demand
A formal demand is a procedural act directed at a debtor; a formal demand by the creditor to one joint and several debtor has no effect against other co-debtors, but a formal demand issued by one co-debtor against the creditor benefits all other co-debtors.

Acknowledgement of Debt
An acknowledgement of debt is a debtor's recognition of the obligation; when made by one joint and several debtor, it does not bind the other co-debtors.

Oath
An oath is a sworn statement used in judicial proceedings; if one joint and several debtor refuses an oath or tenders it to the creditor, it does not prejudice other co-debtors, but if the creditor tenders an oath to one co-debtor who takes it, the oath benefits all other co-debtors.

Judgment
A judgment is a court decision that, upon becoming final, replaces a contract when a party who promised to enter into a contract refuses to do so and legal proceedings are brought to enforce the promise, provided the conditions for conclusion of the contract are met.<SEP>A judgment is a court decision in relation to a joint and several obligation; a judgment against one co-debtor has no effect against others, while a judgment in favor of one co-debtor benefits all others unless based on a ground personal to that co-debtor.

Mortgagee
A mortgagee is a secured creditor who holds a mortgage on property and is paid before unsecured creditors out of the proceeds of sale of the mortgaged property, in the order of the rank of their inscriptions.<SEP>The creditor who holds the mortgage right. The mortgagee may oppose any act or omission that appreciably diminishes their security, take protective measures in emergencies, and claim expenses from the mortgagor. The mortgagee has the right of preference over ordinary creditors and the right of tracing into substituted assets.<SEP>The Mortgagee is a creditor who holds a mortgage on property and has the right to initiate expropriation proceedings against the third party holder or debtor to recover the secured debt.

Mortgaged Property
The immovable property subject to a mortgage, which may include constructions erected on third-party land. Every part of the mortgaged property secures the whole of the debt. The mortgaged property may be disposed of by the mortgagor, but such disposal does not affect the right of the mortgagee. If the property perishes or deteriorates, the mortgage transfers to compensation, insurance monies, or expropriation payments.<SEP>Mortgaged Property is immovable property subject to a mortgage that may be sold by auction, purged of inscriptions, abandoned, or expropriated.

Inscription
Inscription refers to the registration of a mortgage, its renewal, and its radiation, governed by the law regulating the publication of real rights.<SEP>The formal registration of a mortgage deed or judgment to establish its legal effect against third parties. Inscription procedures, renewal, radiation, and annulment are governed by the law regulating the publication of real rights. The cost of inscription, its renewal, and its radiation is borne by the mortgagor unless otherwise agreed.<SEP>A legal requirement for registration of certain privileges over immovables, which determines the rank of the privilege by the date of its registration.<SEP>Inscription (القيد) is a legal registration procedure applicable to privileged rights over immovable property. The provisions relating to inscription, its effects, renewal, and radiation are applicable to privileges over immovables, as stated in Article 1134.

Right of Preference
Right of preference is a legal priority right held by certain creditors over others, recognized in Articles 234 and 242, which grants privileged standing in the distribution of the debtor's assets.<SEP>The Right of Preference is the legal principle by which mortgagees are paid before unsecured creditors out of the proceeds of the mortgaged property according to the rank of their inscriptions.<SEP>The right of mortgagees to be paid before ordinary creditors from the proceeds of the mortgaged property or from the property that has replaced it, according to their order of rank.

Right of Tracing
The Right of Tracing allows mortgagees to pursue their claims against the mortgaged property or any monies obtained in substitution thereof.<SEP>The right of the mortgagee to follow the mortgage into substituted assets such as compensation, insurance monies, or expropriation payments when the mortgaged property perishes or deteriorates.<SEP>The Right of Tracing (حق التتبع) is a legal concept allowing a creditor to follow privileged property into the hands of subsequent holders. General privileges, even over immovables, do not confer a right of tracing, as stated in Article 1134.

Code of Procedure
The Code of Procedure is the legal code prescribing the manner in which deposits are to be made following a tender of the thing due.<SEP>The Code of Procedure is the body of procedural law that governs the manner of sale of common property that cannot be divided in kind.<SEP>The law governing the procedural aspects of expropriation and sale of mortgaged property, prescribing the delays and formalities for such proceedings.<SEP>The Code of Procedure is the procedural law governing expropriation proceedings and legal processes related to mortgage enforcement.

data.entity_name: Law Regulating the Publication of Real Rights
data.content:
Law Regulating the Publication of Real Rights
The Law Regulating the Publication of Real Rights is the legislation that governs the publication of acts, judgments, and instruments related to immovable property, determining which must be published and the rules for such publication.<SEP>The Law Regulating the Publication of Real Rights is the governing legislation that controls inscription, renewal, radiation, and annulment of radiation of mortgages.<SEP>The law governing the procedures for inscription, its renewal, radiation, annulment of radiation, and all effects related to the formal registration of real rights including mortgages.

Formal Summons to Pay
A formal notification to the debtor requiring payment. From the date of its transcription, the fruits and revenues of the mortgaged property are assimilated to the immovable. Its transcription also triggers time limits for lease enforceability against the mortgagee.<SEP>A Formal Summons to Pay is a legal notice served by a mortgagee upon the debtor or third party holder demanding payment of the secured debt, and its transcription benefits all other creditors.<SEP>A legal document transcribed and served in connection with mortgage enforcement proceedings, in whose margin the declaration of abandonment by the Third Party Holder must be entered.

Lease
A contract by which the lessor undertakes to enable the lessee to enjoy a specific thing for a certain time in return of a fixed rent.<SEP>A legal agreement for renting property, including fixed-period leases that may be terminated under serious circumstances with equitable compensation.<SEP>A rental agreement entered into by the mortgagor over the mortgaged property. A lease cannot have effect against the mortgagee unless it has an established date before the transcription of the formal summons to pay. Leases exceeding nine years are enforceable against the mortgagee only for nine years unless transcribed before the inscription of the mortgage.

data.entity_name: Section II: Effects of a Mortgage
data.content:
Section II: Effects of a Mortgage
A legal section covering the effects of mortgage as between the parties with respect to the mortgagor and the mortgagee, and the effects of mortgage as regards third parties, including rights of preference and tracing.

Pactum Commissorium
An agreement that authorizes the creditor to acquire the mortgaged property at a fixed price upon non-payment or to sell it without legal formalities. Such agreements are void even if entered into after the constitution of the mortgage. However, the debtor may transfer the property in payment of the debt after it has fallen due.

Rules of Accession
Legal rules governing the right of a landowner to keep constructions erected on their land by a third party, requiring the landowner to pay compensation. Referenced in Article 1038 in connection with the mortgage on constructions built on land belonging to another person.

Mortgage Deed
The formal document in which the mortgage is constituted. The mortgage deed must specify the amount of the secured debt or the maximum amount the debt may attain, particularly when the mortgage secures a conditional, future, or contingent debt, an opened credit, or a current account.

Ordinary Creditors
Creditors who do not hold a mortgage or preferential right. Mortgagees are paid from the proceeds of the mortgaged property before ordinary creditors according to their order of rank.

Assignment of Rent
The advance receipt or transfer of rent from the mortgaged property. An assignment of rent for a period not exceeding three years is not valid against the mortgagee unless it has an established date prior to the transcription of the formal summons to pay. For periods exceeding three years, transcription before the inscription of the mortgage is required.

Expropriation
Expropriation is a legal process of forcibly depriving an owner, third party holder, or receiver of ownership of mortgaged property through compulsory sale by public auction.<SEP>The legal process by which the mortgagee, upon summons to the debtor to pay, may proceed with the forced sale of the mortgaged property within the delays and formalities prescribed by the Code of Procedure. Expropriation for public utility also generates payments to which a mortgage may transfer under the right of tracing.

Abandonment of Mortgaged Property
A procedure by which a mortgagor who is not the debtor may avoid proceedings against them by surrendering the mortgaged property, following the procedures and rules laid down for the abandonment of an immovable by a third party holder.

Article 834
Article 834 establishes that every co-owner may demand partition of property held in common unless bound by law or agreement, and prohibits agreements preventing partition for more than five years.

Article 835
Article 835 allows co-owners in unanimous agreement to divide common property in any manner they deem fit, with legal formalities required when a co-owner is subject to legal incapacity.

Article 836
Article 836 provides that if co-owners disagree on partition, a co-owner wishing to withdraw may summon others before the Summary Court, which may delegate experts for valuation and division.

Article 837
Article 837 states that the expert will compose separate parts based on the smallest share, and if a co-owner cannot obtain all his share in kind, he shall be compensated by payment equal to the shortage.

Article 838
Article 838 grants the Summary Court jurisdiction over disputes relating to the composition of separate parts and referral of other disputes to the Court of First Instance.

Article 839
Article 839 provides that once disputes are resolved and lots allocated, the Summary Court gives judgment assigning each co-owner his divided part, with partition by drawing lots if no direct allotment was made.

Article 840
Article 840 requires Court ratification of a final partition judgment when one of the co-owners is absent or under legal incapacity.

Article 841
Article 841 provides that when property cannot be divided in kind or would suffer serious diminution in value, it shall be sold in the manner laid down by the Code of Procedure, with auction restricted to co-owners if they unanimously request it.

Article 842
Article 842 grants personal creditors of any co-owner the right to oppose partition in kind or sale by auction without their intervention, requiring notification to all co-owners and joinder of inscribed creditors before a partition action.

Article 843
Article 843 deems each co-partitioner to have been the owner of the part falling to him from the date he became co-owner and never to have owned the other parts.

Article 844
Article 844 establishes that co-partitioners warrant each other against interference or eviction due to causes existing before partition, with liability proportional to shares, subject to waiver by express agreement.

Article 846
Article 846 governs provisional partition, whereby co-owners allot enjoyment of divided parts equal to their shares, with a maximum duration of five years and conversion to final partition after fifteen years of continuous possession.

Article 847
Article 847 provides that a provisional partition may also take place when co-owners agree to take turns enjoying all the common property for periods corresponding to their shares.

Article 848
Article 848 states that provisional partition is governed by provisions relating to contracts of lease insofar as they are not incompatible with its nature.

Article 849
Article 849 allows co-owners to agree on a provisional partition during final partition proceedings, and permits the Summary Judge to order it upon application of one co-owner if agreement cannot be reached.

Article 850
Article 850 prohibits co-owners from demanding partition of common property when the purpose for which it is intended requires it to remain permanently in common ownership.<SEP>Article 850 establishes that co-owners of property held in common cannot demand its partition if the intended use requires it to always remain in common.

Article 851
Article 851 permits members of the same family with a common occupation or interest to create a family joint ownership in writing, consisting of inherited property or any other property they agree to include.<SEP>Article 851 provides that members of the same family with a common occupation or interest may agree in writing to create a family joint ownership from inherited or other property.

Co-Owner
A co-owner is a person who holds an undivided share in property held in common with others, possessing rights to demand partition, repurchase shares, and participate in decisions regarding the property.

Provisional Partition
Provisional partition is a temporary arrangement in which co-owners agree to allot each other the enjoyment of divided parts of common property, which may convert to a final partition after fifteen years.

Obligatory Joint Ownership
Obligatory joint ownership arises when the purpose of the common property requires it to remain permanently undivided, preventing co-owners from demanding partition.

Family Joint Ownership
Family joint ownership is a form of joint ownership created by written agreement among members of the same family who share a common occupation or interest, comprising inherited or other property.<SEP>Family Joint Ownership is a legal arrangement whereby members of the same family who share a common occupation or interest agree in writing to hold property jointly, consisting either of an inheritance left wholly or partly in joint ownership or any other property they agree to place in joint ownership, for a period not exceeding fifteen years.

Right of Repurchase
The right of repurchase allows a co-owner to buy back an undivided share sold by another co-owner to a third person within thirty days of knowledge or notification.

Summary Court
The Summary Court is the judicial body with competence to hear partition disputes, appoint experts, allocate divided parts, and refer matters outside its competence to the Court of First Instance.<SEP>The Summary Court is the court within whose jurisdiction the deceased was domiciled, and on whose notice board estate-related announcements must be posted under Article 886.

Summary Judge
The Summary Judge is the judicial officer empowered to order a provisional partition upon the application of a co-owner when agreement cannot be reached among co-owners.

Expert
The expert is a person delegated by the Court to proceed with the valuation of common property and to divide it into separate parts based on the smallest share.<SEP>An Expert is a person with special experience who may be employed by the Administrator for the preparation of the inventory and the estimation of the value of the estate property.<SEP>The Expert is a person with special knowledge who may be engaged by the administrator to assist in preparing the inventory and estimating the value of estate assets under Article 888.

Right of Action
The right of action allows a dissenting co-owner to challenge an alienation decision before the Court within two months from the date of notification.

Warranty Against Eviction
The warranty against eviction is an obligation among co-partitioners to indemnify each other against interference or eviction caused by reasons predating the partition, unless waived by express agreement.

Article 845
Article 845 allows rescission of partition by agreement if a co-partitioner proves injury exceeding one fifth of his share, provided the action is commenced within one year following the partition.

Personal Creditor
A personal creditor of a co-owner has the right to oppose a partition in kind or a sale by auction without their intervention, and must be notified and joined in all proceedings.

Contract of Lease
A contract of lease is the legal framework referenced in Article 848 as governing provisional partition in terms of validity against third parties, capacity, rights, obligations, and means of proof.

Representative
The Representative is a person authorized to receive payment on behalf of the Creditor, and payment made to the Representative is deemed valid.<SEP>A representative is a person who enters into a contract on behalf of a principal within the limits of his authority. The representative, not the principal, is the person examined for vices of consent or effects of knowledge of special circumstances.

Payment
The fulfillment of an obligation which may be made by the debtor, his representative, or any interested or uninterested third party, subject to certain conditions including ownership and capacity to dispose, and which extinguishes the obligation.<SEP>Payment is the fulfillment of a debt obligation, which must be made with the very thing due, at the proper time and place, and carries specific rules regarding imputation, partial payment, and expenses.

Receipt
A Receipt is a document issued by the Creditor as proof of discharge of payment, which qualifies the bearer to receive payment unless personal payment was agreed upon.

Document of Title of Debt
The Document of Title of Debt is a legal instrument evidencing the existence of a debt, which the Debtor has the right to have annotated, restituted, or cancelled upon payment.

Giving in Payment
Giving in Payment is a method of extinguishing an obligation whereby the Creditor accepts another prestation in place of what is due, governed by provisions of sale and payment.

Delegation
Delegation is the transfer of a debt obligation to a third party, where a third party agrees to take the place of the original Debtor with the Creditor's consent.<SEP>Delegation is a legal mechanism whereby a debtor procures the acceptance by the creditor of a third party who undertakes to pay in the debtor's stead, and does not necessarily require a prior debt between the debtor and the third party.

Summons
A Summons is a formal legal notice served on the Creditor, after which the Creditor becomes responsible for loss or deterioration of the thing and interest ceases to run.

Interest
Interest is a financial charge accruing on the debt that ceases to run from the time a summons has been served on the Creditor.<SEP>The agreed charge payable by the borrower on a loan, falling due at agreed dates; absence of an interest agreement renders the loan gratuitous and without consideration.

Actual Tender
Actual Tender is the formal offering of the thing due by the Debtor, which is equivalent to payment when followed by a deposit or equivalent measure, provided it is accepted by the Creditor or recognized as valid by a final judgment.

Final Judgment
Final Judgment is a conclusive court decision that recognizes the validity of a tender or deposit, after which the Debtor may not retract the tender without releasing co-debtors and sureties.

Expenses
Expenses are costs in connection with payment that are at the charge of the Debtor unless otherwise agreed, and are the first to be deducted from an insufficient payment before interest and principal.

Voidable Contract
A voidable contract is a contract susceptible to annulment, and if the original obligation arises from one, novation is valid only if the new obligation aims to confirm the contract and replace the original.<SEP>A Voidable Contract is a contract susceptible to annulment; novation of an obligation arising from a voidable contract is only valid if the new obligation is intended to ratify the original contract and replace it.

Principal
The Principal is the main amount of the debt to which payment is imputed last, after expenses and interest have been deducted.<SEP>The principal is the person on whose behalf a representative acts. Rights and obligations from contracts concluded by a representative within authority are binding upon the principal.<SEP>The person on whose behalf a voluntary agent acts, who is bound to carry out obligations, indemnify the agent, reimburse expenses, and compensate for loss when the agent acted with reasonable care.

Third Party Holder
A third party holder is any person who acquires ownership of a mortgaged property or any real right over it capable of being mortgaged, without being personally responsible for the debt secured by the mortgage.<SEP>The Third Party Holder is a person who holds mortgaged property and has rights and obligations including payment of inscribed debts, purge of the property, abandonment, participation in auctions, warranty claims against preceding owners, and subrogation into the rights of discharged creditors.

Unsecured Creditor
An unsecured creditor is an ordinary creditor who is paid after mortgagees from the proceeds of sale of the mortgaged property.

Former Owner
The former owner is the previous owner of the mortgaged property from whom the third party holder acquired the property.

Purchaser by Auction
The purchaser by auction is the person who acquires the property at public auction and is liable for the price of adjudication, the cost of formalities for the purge, and refunding costs to the disposed third party holder.

Inscribed Creditor
An inscribed creditor is a creditor whose rights are registered on the mortgaged property and who may compel payment or apply for the sale of the property.

Purge
Purge is the legal process by which a third party holder clears the mortgaged property of all inscriptions, requiring formal summons to inscribed creditors and potentially leading to a public auction.<SEP>Purge is a legal procedure by which a third party holder clears mortgaged property of all inscriptions and encumbrances by paying creditors or depositing funds.

Rank Assignment
Rank Assignment determines the order in which mortgagees are paid and is calculated from the date of inscription of the mortgage, even if it secures a conditional, future, or contingent debt.

Rank Assignment by Subrogation
A mortgagee may assign his rank in favor of another creditor having a mortgage inscribed on the same property, within the limits of his secured debts.

Applicant
The applicant is an inscribed creditor or surety who applies for the sale of the property during the purge process, must deposit a sum sufficient to cover auction costs at the Court, and may not renounce the application without consent of all inscribed creditors and sureties.

Compulsory Expropriation
Compulsory Expropriation is the formal legal process that must be followed when an application is made for the sale of a mortgaged property, as prescribed in the purge and auction procedures.

Greffier of the Court
The Greffier of the Court is the official responsible for recording the judgment that puts an end to the state of insolvency in the margin of the registration and for sending a copy of the judgment to the Registrar of the Cairo Court.

Registrar of the Cairo Court
The Registrar of the Cairo Court is the official who makes a registration entry similar to that of the greffier upon receiving a copy of the judgment ending insolvency.

Conditional Obligation
A Conditional Obligation is an obligation whose existence or extinction depends on a future and uncertain event, as defined in Article 265.

Suspensive Condition
A Suspensive Condition is a condition upon which the existence of an obligation depends, and the obligation does not become executory until the condition is realized. The obligation is void if the condition is impossible, contrary to morality or public order, or depends solely on the will of the obligor.<SEP>A suspensive condition is a legal condition under which a sale upon trial is deemed to have been made, requiring acceptance of the thing sold before the sale becomes effective.

Resolutory Condition
A Resolutory Condition is a condition upon which the extinction of an obligation depends. When realized, the obligation is extinguished and the creditor must restitute what has been received. Acts of management by the creditor remain valid.<SEP>A resolutory condition is an alternative condition under which a sale upon trial may be made, as opposed to a suspensive condition, unless the agreement or circumstances indicate otherwise.

Time Clause
A Time Clause (term) is a provision where the performance or extinction of an obligation depends on a future certain event, as defined in Article 271.

Alternative Obligation
An Alternative Obligation is one whose object includes numerous prestations and the debtor is entirely freed by the performance of one of them. The option belongs to the debtor unless agreed or provided otherwise by law.

Facultative Obligation
A Facultative Obligation is one whose object consists of a single prestation but the debtor may free himself by performing another prestation in its place. The nature of the obligation is determined by the principal prestation promised.

Retroactive Effect
Retroactive Effect refers to the legal principle by which the fulfillment of a condition is effective retroactively to the day the obligation was contracted, unless the will of the parties or the nature of the contract indicates otherwise, as defined in Article 270. The extinction of an obligation at the end of a resolutory term has no retroactive effect.

Restitution
The legal obligation to return what was received without proper cause, governed by rules on good faith, bad faith, legal capacity, and prescription.<SEP>Restitution is the obligation of a creditor to return what has been received upon the realization of a resolutory condition, as stated in Article 269. If restitution is impossible due to a cause for which the creditor is responsible, the creditor is liable in damages.<SEP>The obligation of the lessee to return the leased property to the lessor upon expiration of the lease. Unlawful retention of the property obliges the lessee to pay compensation based on the rental value of the property and any harm suffered by the lessor.

Protective Measures
Protective Measures are legal actions a creditor may take to safeguard his rights before the realization of a suspensive condition or before the expiration of a suspensive term, as referenced in Articles 268 and 274.

Vendor
The Vendor is a party to a sale contract who is bound to transfer ownership of a thing or propriety right to the purchaser and must allow the purchaser to trial the thing sold in applicable cases.<SEP>The seller of mortgaged immovable property who may agree with the purchaser to assign the mortgage debt, triggering the requirement for creditor notification and ratification.<SEP>The vendor is the seller in a sale contract who transfers ownership of goods or property and has the right to demand payment; the vendor may dissolve the sale if the purchaser fails to pay on the due date.<SEP>The vendor is a party to a sale contract who is obligated to transfer ownership of the thing sold, deliver it in its proper state, and provide warranty against disturbance and eviction to the purchaser.<SEP>The Vendor is the seller in a sale contract who bears warranty obligations against dispossession and defects, possesses a right of retention over the thing sold until payment, and may be liable for refunds, compensation, and legal interest. The Vendor remains liable even under warranty exclusion clauses if dispossession results from the Vendor's own acts or fraudulent concealment.<SEP>The Vendor is the seller in a property transaction who is required to issue or receive formal summons regarding preemption and is bound by the effects of preemption.<SEP>A seller of movable or immovable property who is owed the price and accessories and holds a privilege over the property sold.

Sale Upon Trial
A sale upon trial is a type of sale deemed made subject to a suspensive condition of acceptance, where the purchaser's silence after the agreed or reasonable time for trial constitutes acceptance of the thing sold.

Sale Subject To Tasting
A sale subject to tasting allows the purchaser to accept the thing sold at their discretion, but acceptance must be declared within the time fixed by agreement or custom, and the sale is complete only from the date of such declaration.

Price Determination
The method of establishing the price may be confined to indicating the basis on which the price will ultimately be fixed, including reference to the market price at the place and time of delivery.

Market Price
The market price is the prevailing trade price used to determine the price of the thing sold when the parties have not fixed a specific price, evaluated at the place and time of delivery or at a place where prices are customarily deemed applicable.

Lesion
Lesion refers to a disadvantage or loss exceeding one fifth of the value of an immovable property sold by a legally incapable person, giving rise to a right of action to supplement the price to four fifths of the normal price.<SEP>Lesion refers to a situation where the obligations of one contracting party are out of all proportion to the advantages obtained, due to exploitation of obvious levity of character or unbridled passion, allowing the judge to annul the contract or reduce obligations, as set out in Article 129.

Legally Incapable Person
A legally incapable person is an individual lacking full legal capacity whose immovable property, if sold with lesion exceeding one fifth, entitles the vendor or representative to seek a supplement of the price.

Supplement Of Price Action
A legal action to make up the price to four fifths of the normal value when an immovable belonging to a legally incapable person is sold with lesion exceeding one fifth, prescribed within three years from the cessation of incapacity or the death of the owner.

Obligations Of The Vendor
The vendor is bound to perform everything necessary to transfer the right to the thing sold to the purchaser and to abstain from all acts that might render the transfer impossible or difficult, including proper delivery and warranty.

Ownership Transfer
Ownership transfer is the conveyance of property rights from the vendor to the purchaser, which may occur upon sale in bulk, upon full payment in a credit sale, or upon delivery depending on the terms agreed.

Sale In Bulk
A sale in bulk transfers ownership to the purchaser in the same manner as ownership of a definite and ascertained thing, even when the price depends on the extent, weight, or measure of the goods.

Credit Sale
A credit sale is a deferred-price sale in which the vendor may stipulate that ownership transfer is subject to full integral payment of the price, even after delivery of the thing sold.

Installment Payment
Installment payment is a method of paying the price in parts, where the parties may agree that the vendor retains a portion as damages if the sale is cancelled for non-payment, and ownership is deemed transferred from the date of sale when all installments are paid.

Delivery
Delivery consists in placing the thing sold at the disposal of the purchaser so that the purchaser can take possession and enjoy it without hindrance, including all accessories and permanent appurtenances.

Deficiency And Excess
Deficiency or excess in the quantity of the thing sold relative to the contract gives rise to rights of the purchaser to demand price reduction or contract cancellation, or rights of the vendor to claim a supplement of the price, prescribed within one year of actual delivery.

Perishment Before Delivery
Perishment of the thing sold before delivery due to a cause beyond the vendor's control results in the dissolution of the sale and refund of the price to the purchaser, unless the purchaser was summoned to take delivery before the loss.

Deterioration Before Delivery
Deterioration of the thing sold before delivery gives the purchaser the option to cancel the sale if the diminution is substantial or to uphold the sale at a reduced price.

Warranty Against Disturbance
The vendor warrants the purchaser against disturbance in enjoyment of the thing sold, whether caused by the vendor's own act or by a third party having a right over the thing sold enforceable against the purchaser.<SEP>The lessor's legal obligation to protect the lessee against disturbances caused by the lessor, the lessor's servants, other lessees, or successors in title. Any agreement excluding or limiting this warranty is void if the lessor fraudulently concealed the cause.

Revendication Action
An action for revendication is a legal proceeding brought against the purchaser by a third party claiming ownership of the thing sold, requiring the vendor to join as co-defendant or take the purchaser's place upon receiving notice.

Warranty Of Eviction
The vendor's obligation to protect the purchaser against dispossession by a third party, including refunding amounts paid by the purchaser to avoid dispossession, together with legal interest and expenses.

Code Of Procedure
The Code of Procedure governs the procedural aspects of legal actions, including the vendor's obligation to intervene in a revendication action brought against the purchaser.<SEP>The Code of Procedure (Qanun Almurafa'at) is the body of procedural law referenced as governing the recourse against court orders admitting claims related to inventory disputes.

Article 422
Article 422 provides that in a sale subject to tasting, the purchaser may accept the thing sold but must declare acceptance within the time fixed by agreement or custom.

Article 423
Article 423 allows the method of establishing the price to be confined to indicating the basis on which the price will be fixed, with the market price determined at the place and time of delivery in case of doubt.

Article 424
Article 424 provides that a sale is not void for lack of a fixed price if the parties intended to adopt the current trade price or the price usually applied in their dealings.

Article 425
Article 425 grants a right of action to supplement the price to four fifths of the normal price when an immovable belonging to a legally incapable person is sold with lesion exceeding one fifth.

Article 426
Article 426 prescribes the supplement of price action within three years from the cessation of legal incapacity or the death of the owner, protecting third parties in good faith.

Article 427
Article 427 prohibits an action for supplement of price on grounds of lesion in sales conducted by public auction in accordance with the law.

Article 428
Article 428 obligates the vendor to perform everything necessary to transfer the right sold and to abstain from acts that might render the transfer impossible or difficult.

Article 429
Article 429 states that in a sale in bulk, ownership transfers as with a definite and ascertained thing, even when the price depends on measurement of the goods.

Article 430
Article 430 allows the vendor in a credit sale to stipulate that ownership transfer is subject to full payment, with provisions for installment payments, retention of damages, and retroactive ownership transfer upon full payment.

Article 431
Article 431 obligates the vendor to deliver the thing sold in the state it was at the time of the sale.

Article 432
Article 432 defines delivery as including accessories and everything permanently appropriated for the use of the thing sold, in accordance with the nature of things, local custom, and the intention of the parties.

Article 433
Article 433 establishes the vendor's liability for deficiency and the purchaser's obligations for excess in the quantity of the thing sold, with rights to cancel or adjust the price.

Article 434
Article 434 prescribes rights related to deficiency or excess in the thing sold within one year from actual delivery.

Article 435
Article 435 defines delivery as placing the thing sold at the disposal of the purchaser and allows delivery by mere agreement when the thing was already in the purchaser's possession.

Article 436
Article 436 provides that delivery of a thing to be sent to the purchaser is not effective until the thing reaches the purchaser, unless agreed otherwise.

Article 437
Article 437 provides that if the thing sold perishes before delivery due to a cause beyond the vendor's control, the sale is dissolved and the price refunded.

Article 438
Article 438 gives the purchaser the option to cancel the sale or uphold it at a reduced price if the value of the thing sold is diminished by deterioration before delivery.

Article 439
Article 439 imposes on the vendor a warranty against disturbance in the purchaser's enjoyment, whether caused by the vendor or a third party with a right derived from the vendor.

Article 440
Article 440 governs the vendor's obligation to intervene in a revendication action brought against the purchaser, and the consequences of failure to notify or intervene.<SEP>Article 440 is a referenced legal provision regarding the purchaser's obligation to notify the vendor of the action of revendication, referenced in Article 443 as a condition for recovering certain litigation costs.

Article 441
Article 441 preserves the purchaser's warranty right even if the purchaser in good faith acknowledges the third party's claim or compromises with the third party, provided the vendor was duly notified and given the opportunity to intervene.

Article 442
Article 442 allows the vendor to free himself from warranty consequences by refunding to the purchaser amounts paid to avoid dispossession, including legal interest and expenses.

Contracting Parties
The contracting parties are the individuals or entities entering into a sale agreement, including the vendor and purchaser, who may fix the price, agree on installment terms, or describe the contract as a lease.

Contract Of Lease
A contract of lease is a description the contracting parties may give to what is substantively a sale, to which the provisions governing credit sales and installment payments still apply.

Article 224
Article 224 provides that damages fixed by agreement are not due if the debtor establishes that the creditor has not suffered any loss. The judge may reduce these damages if the amount was grossly exaggerated or the principal obligation was partially performed. Any contrary agreement is void.<SEP>Article 224 is a legal provision referenced in Article 430 paragraph 2, under which the judge may reduce the amount of agreed damages according to circumstances.

Co-owners
Co-owners are the members of a family or building who jointly hold shares in property held in common, with rights and obligations regarding partition, disposal of shares, management, and cost participation.<SEP>Co-owners are persons who jointly own parts of a building and are bound to conform to the decisions of the syndicate regarding reconstruction.

Ownership of Storeys in Buildings
Ownership of Storeys in Buildings is a legal framework governing situations where different storeys or apartments of a building belong to different owners, who are considered co-owners of the ground and parts intended for common use.

Building
A structure for whose collapse damage a person in charge is liable even if not the owner, even if the collapse is partial, unless it did not result from negligent maintenance, age, or defect, as established in Article 177.<SEP>A Building is a physical structure divided into storeys or apartments that may belong to different owners, containing common parts and individual parts subject to specific legal rules.

Common Parts
Common Parts are the parts of a building intended for the common use of all owners, including foundations, main walls, main entrances, yards, roofs, lifts, passages, corridors, floor supports, and pipes of all kinds, which cannot be divided and in which each owner holds a share proportional to the value of his part in the building.

Syndicate of Owners
A Syndicate of Owners is an organization that may be formed by owners of storeys or apartments in a building to manage common parts, establish rules, take out collective insurance, authorize works, and make binding decisions regarding the building held in common.

Representative of the Syndicate
The Representative of the Syndicate is a person appointed by majority vote of owners or by the President of the Court of First Instance to execute the decisions of the syndicate, take preservation measures, and represent the syndicate before the courts.

data.entity_name: President of the Court of First Instance
data.content:
President of the Court of First Instance
The President of the Court of First Instance is the judicial officer within whose jurisdiction the building is located, with authority to appoint or discharge the representative of the syndicate when the required majority is not obtained.

Upper Storey
The Upper Storey is the higher storey of a building, whose owner has rights and obligations in relation to the lower storey, including the right to rebuild the lower storey at the lower owner's cost and the obligation not to heighten the building in a way that injures the lower storey.

Lower Storey
The Lower Storey is the lower storey of a building, whose owner is bound to execute works and repairs necessary to prevent the upper storey from falling and to rebuild if the building is destroyed.

Title Deeds
Title Deeds are legal documents that may contain provisions contrary to the default rules regarding co-ownership of the ground and common parts of a building.

Article 852
Article 852 stipulates that a family joint ownership may be created for a period not exceeding fifteen years, with provisions for early withdrawal by court authorization or after six months notice if no period is fixed.

Article 853
Article 853 provides that co-owners cannot demand partition while family joint ownership continues, and no co-owner may dispose of his share to a non-family member without consent of all co-owners.

Article 854
Article 854 governs the appointment and discharge of managers by co-owners holding the majority in value, and the manager's authority to introduce changes for better enjoyment of the property.

Article 855
Article 855 provides that family joint ownership is governed by the provisions relating to joint property and to mandate, subject to the preceding special provisions.

Article 856
Article 856 establishes the rules for ownership of storeys and apartments in a building, defining common parts and proportional shares in relation to the value of each owner's part.

Article 857
Article 857 regulates the use of and modifications to common parts, requiring consent of all owners for modifications except those that facilitate use without changing purpose or causing prejudice.

Article 858
Article 858 obliges every owner to participate in the costs of preservation, maintenance, management, and reconstruction of common parts proportionally, and prohibits renouncing shares to avoid such costs.

Article 859
Article 859 obliges the owner of a lower storey to execute repairs to prevent the upper storey from falling, and authorizes the Judge to order the sale of the lower storey or urgent repairs if the owner refuses.

Article 860
Article 860 provides that if a building is destroyed, the owner of the lower storey must rebuild it, and the owner of the upper storey may rebuild it at the lower owner's cost and withhold occupancy until repayment.

Article 861
Article 861 prohibits the owner of the upper storey from heightening the building in a way that injures the lower storey.

Article 862
Article 862 provides that owners of storeys or apartments in a building may form a syndicate, which may also be formed for the purpose of constructing or acquiring buildings.

Article 863
Article 863 allows a syndicate to establish rules with the consent of all members to ensure better enjoyment and good management of the building held in common.

Article 864
Article 864 provides that in the absence of management rules, the syndicate manages common parts through binding decisions taken by majority of owners based on share value, after summoning all interested parties.

Article 865
