Article 865 authorizes the syndicate to take out collective insurance against risks and to authorize works or installations that increase the building's value.

Article 866
Article 866 provides for the appointment of a representative to execute syndicate decisions, either by majority vote or by the President of the Court of First Instance, with duties including preservation and court representation.

Article 867
Article 867 governs the remuneration and discharge of the representative of the syndicate.

Article 868
Article 868 provides that if a building is destroyed by fire or otherwise, co-owners are bound to conform to the syndicate's reconstruction decision, with compensation set aside for reconstruction costs.

Joint Property
Joint Property is the legal concept of property held in common (الملكية الشائعة), the rules of which govern family joint ownership alongside mandate rules per Article 855.

Mandate
A legal arrangement whose rules apply to voluntary agency when the principal ratifies the agent's act, as referenced in Articles 190 and 193, and which governs the obligations of the mandatary regarding restitution and accounting.<SEP>Mandate is the legal concept of agency (الوكالة), the rules of which govern family joint ownership alongside joint property rules per Article 855.

Non-family Member
A Non-family Member is a person outside the family who may only become a partner in family joint ownership if he and all co-owners consent, as established in Article 853.

Inner Walls
Inner Walls are walls separating two apartments in a building that are owned as party property by the owners of the two adjacent apartments, as specified in Article 856.

Registered Creditors
Registered Creditors are creditors with registered claims against the building whose rights are preserved when compensation for destruction is allocated for reconstruction costs, as stated in Article 868.<SEP>Registered Creditors are persons with registered claims against property whose rights must be preserved during reconstruction or estate winding up.<SEP>Registered Creditors are creditors whose mortgages or charges are registered against the Purchaser and who retain their rights of preference on that portion of the sale price of the property which reverts to the Purchaser, notwithstanding preemption, as provided in Article 947.

Collective Insurance
Collective Insurance is insurance against risks to the building or to the co-owners jointly, which the syndicate may take out with the prescribed majority consent per Article 865.

Abandonment
Abandonment is a legal process by which a third party holder declares relinquishment of mortgaged property through a declaration submitted to the Registrar of the competent Court of First Instance.

Caisse of the Court
The Caisse of the Court is the court's treasury where the third party holder may deposit sums for valuation, auction prices, or debt payments.

Judge Des Referes
The Judge Des Referes is a judge handling urgent matters who has the authority to appoint a receiver for managing property during expropriation proceedings.

Auction
An Auction is a public sale process for mortgaged property, in which the third party holder and other persons may participate, subject to conditions on minimum bid prices.

Judgment Charge
A Judgment Charge is a legal charge on one or more specific immovable properties belonging to a debtor, obtained by a creditor through an enforceable judgment to secure payment of principal, interest, and costs.<SEP>A Judgment Charge is a legal right that a creditor may obtain to secure a debt, governed by the same provisions as a mortgage, including rules on inscription, renewal, radiation, indivisibility, effect, reduction, and extinguishment.

Preceding Owner
The Preceding Owner is the person from whom the third party holder acquired the property and against whom the third party holder has a right of action for warranty.

data.entity_name: Section III: Extinguishment of the Mortgage
data.content:
Section III: Extinguishment of the Mortgage
Section III: Extinguishment of the Mortgage is a legal section covering the termination of mortgage rights, including through extinction of debt, completion of purge, or compulsory sale.

data.entity_name: Chapter II: Judgment Charges upon Immovable Property
data.content:
Chapter II: Judgment Charges upon Immovable Property
Chapter II: Judgment Charges upon Immovable Property is a legal chapter governing the constitution, requirements, and procedures for obtaining judgment charges on immovable property.

Title Deed
A legal document establishing ownership of property that the Third Party Holder transcribes, and which serves as the basis for ownership claims during purge and auction proceedings, including the original title deed referred to in Articles 1073 and 1075.

Enforceable Judgment
A court judgment rendered on the merits of a case condemning the Debtor to a liquidated amount, which serves as a prerequisite for obtaining a Judgment Charge over immovable property.

Judgment of Adjudication
A court judgment that confers ownership rights on a person other than the Third Party Holder who acquires the mortgaged property at auction, deriving the right from the Third Party Holder.

Arbitration Award
A decision issued by arbitrators that cannot serve as a basis for a Judgment Charge until it has been made enforceable.

Foreign Court
A court outside the jurisdiction whose judgments cannot serve as a basis for a Judgment Charge until the judgment has been made enforceable.

Fruits of the Property
The produce or income generated by the mortgaged property that the Third Party Holder is liable to restitute from the date of being summoned to pay or abandon the property, or from a new summons if proceedings are abandoned for three years.

data.entity_name: Section I: The Constitution of a Judgment Charge
data.content:
Section I: The Constitution of a Judgment Charge
A legal section governing the creation, eligibility requirements, and procedural steps for establishing Judgment Charges on immovable property, including the conditions under which judgments may serve as a basis.

Gift
Gift is a legal concept whose substantive rules govern the release of an obligation, as stated in Article 372.<SEP>A contract by which the donor disposes of property belonging to him without consideration; the donor may impose upon the donee the performance of a specific obligation while retaining the intention of making a gift.<SEP>A legal mechanism whereby a donor transfers property to a donee, governed by provisions on delivery, warranties against dispossession and defects, consideration, and revocation rules.

Donor
The person who makes a gift by disposing of property without consideration; the donor may impose obligations on the donee, must execute the gift through an authentic document for immovables, and cannot demand restitution of voluntarily delivered gifts that are null due to formal defects.<SEP>The person who makes a gift, obligated to deliver the gifted thing, subject to limited liability for defects and dispossession, and entitled to revoke the gift under specified conditions.

Donee
The recipient of a gift who must accept the gift or have it accepted by a representative for the gift to be complete; the donee may be subject to obligations imposed by the donor.<SEP>The person who receives a gift, entitled to delivery of the gifted thing, potentially bound to perform consideration, and protected by warranty provisions.

Article 491
A legal provision stating that a gift of a definite and specific thing not belonging to the donor is governed by the provisions of Articles 466 and 467.

Article 492
A legal provision declaring that a gift of future property is void.

Article 493
A legal provision obligating the donor to deliver the gifted thing to the donee, applying the provisions related to the delivery of a sold thing.

Article 494
A legal provision addressing the donor's warranty against dispossession, covering intentional concealment and gifts made for valuable consideration.

Article 495
A legal provision concerning the donor's warranty for defects in the gifted thing, including liability for intentionally hidden defects.

Article 496
A legal provision limiting the donor's liability to intentional acts or gross negligence.

Article 497
A legal provision binding the donee to perform any consideration imposed upon him, whether in favor of the donor, a third party, or the public interest.

Article 498
A legal provision limiting the donee's obligation to perform consideration to the extent of the value of the thing donated.

Article 499
A legal provision regarding the donee's obligation to discharge the donor's existing debts as consideration for the gift.

Valuable Consideration
Compensation or payment provided by the donee in exchange for a gift, affecting warranty obligations and the donor's liability for dispossession.

Revocation of Gift
The legal process by which a donor may cancel a gift, either by mutual consent of the donee or through court authority, subject to specific grounds and obstacles.

Article 500
A legal provision allowing revocation of a gift with the donee's consent or, if the donee does not consent, through court application based on reasonable grounds.

Article 501
A legal provision enumerating reasonable grounds for revocation, including serious ingratitude by the donee, the donor's inability to maintain himself, and the birth of a child after the donation.

Article 502
A legal provision listing obstacles to revocation of a gift, including inherent increase in value, death of a party, alienation by the donee, spousal gifts, and acts of charity.

Article 503
A legal provision stating that a revoked gift is deemed null and void, with rules on restitution of fruits and repayment of necessary and useful expenses.

Article 504
A legal provision addressing the donor's liability for loss if the donor takes back the gifted thing without consent or court decision.

Partnership
A Partnership is a legal business entity formed by partners who contribute capital, services, or other assets, and share in profits and losses according to the partnership deed or statutory provisions.<SEP>A contract by which two or more persons undertake to contribute jointly in a pecuniary undertaking by providing contributions of property or services, with the object of sharing profits or losses.<SEP>A legal business entity formed by partners, subject to dissolution by unanimous agreement or court order, and governed by a partnership deed that defines liquidation and partition procedures.

Partner
A Partner is a member of a partnership who contributes capital, services, or other assets and is entitled to a share of profits while being liable for losses and partnership debts in proportion to his contribution, unless otherwise agreed.<SEP>A person who contributes to a partnership through property, services, or other forms of contribution, and shares in the profits or losses of the undertaking.<SEP>A member of a partnership who holds the right to request dissolution, seek the exclusion of another partner, apply for retirement, and share in the distribution of partnership assets or losses.

Article 505
A legal provision defining partnership as a contract involving contributions of property or services for sharing in profits or losses.

Article 506
A legal provision stating that a partnership is deemed a juristic person upon constitution, with publication formalities required for recognition by third parties.

Juristic Person
A juristic person enjoys all rights within the limits established by law, except those inherent in the nature of an individual. It has its own patrimonium, legal capacity, the right to sue, and its own domicile.<SEP>The legal personality attributed to a partnership upon its constitution, which is enforceable against third parties only after completion of publication formalities.<SEP>A juristic person is a legal entity whose good or bad faith in possession is determined by the intention of its representative, as established by Article 965.

Partnership Deed
The Partnership Deed is the contractual agreement establishing the partnership, defining the shares of partners in profits and losses, the method of management, and other terms governing the partnership.<SEP>The written document required to establish a partnership, which must be in writing under penalty of nullity, along with any modifications to it.<SEP>The contractual document governing the partnership that specifies the manner of liquidation, partition of assets, and the valuation of partners' capital contributions.

Article 507
A legal provision requiring partnership deeds to be in writing under pain of nullity, and addressing the limited effects of nullity among partners and toward third parties.

Article 508
A legal provision presuming partners' contributions to be equal and to consist of ownership of property, unless agreement or custom provides otherwise.

Article 509
A legal provision stating that the influence or credit of a partner cannot alone constitute a contribution.

Article 510
A legal provision making a partner liable for interest on unpaid money contributions from the date the contribution fell due, plus additional compensation for loss.

Article 511
A legal provision applying sale warranty provisions to property ownership contributions and lease provisions to use-of-property contributions.

Article 512
A legal provision governing service contributions, requiring partners to perform promised services and account for profits, while not obligating contribution of patents without agreement.

Article 513
Article 513 provides that if a partner's contribution consists of debts due by third parties, his obligation to the partnership is only extinguished by recovery of those debts, and he is liable for damages if the debts are not paid when due.<SEP>A legal provision addressing contributions consisting of debts due by third parties, where the contributing partner's obligation is only extinguished upon recovery of such debts.

Articles 466 and 467
Referenced legal provisions that govern the gift of a definite and specific thing not belonging to the donor, as cited in Article 491.

Dispossession
The loss of ownership or possession of the gifted thing, addressed in Article 494, which governs the donor's warranty obligations against dispossession and the donee's right to equitable compensation.

Alimony
Alimony (النفقة) refers to obligations for payment of maintenance between relatives, governed by the national law of the person liable for such payment, as stated in Article 15.<SEP>A legal obligation to provide financial support to another person, mentioned in Article 501 as a ground for revocation of a gift if the donor becomes unable to meet this obligation.

Fruits
The produce or profits derived from the gifted thing, addressed in Article 503, which states that the donee is liable for restitution of fruits only from the date of agreement on revocation or commencement of legal proceedings.

Spouse
A marital partner mentioned in Article 502 as a category relating to gifts between spouses, which constitutes an obstacle to the revocation of a gift even after dissolution of the marriage.

National Courts
National Courts (المحاكم الوطنية) are Egyptian judicial bodies that previously operated under an older civil law issued on October 28, 1883.

Mixed Courts
Mixed Courts (المحاكم المختلطة) are Egyptian judicial bodies that previously operated under an older civil law issued on June 28, 1875.

Qasr El-Qubba
Qasr El-Qubba (قصر القبة) is the palace in Cairo where the Egyptian Civil Code was issued on July 16, 1948 (9 Ramadan 1367).

Custom
Custom (العرف) is a source of law applied by judges when no legislative provision exists, serving as a secondary legal reference after statutory law.<SEP>Local practice or general usage governing rent payment times, tolerated defects, lessee's repairs, and other aspects of the lease relationship in the absence of express agreement between the parties.

Islamic Sharia
Islamic Sharia (الشريعة الإسلامية) is a source of law applied by judges in the absence of both legislative provisions and custom, serving as a tertiary legal reference in the Egyptian Civil Code.

Natural Justice
Natural Justice (القانون الطبيعي) is a legal principle applied by judges as a final source of law when no legislative provision, custom, or Islamic Sharia principle is available.

Rules of Equity
The Rules of Equity (قواعد العدالة) are legal principles applied alongside natural justice when no other legal source is available.

Legal Capacity
Legal Capacity (الأهلية) refers to the legal competence of persons as defined by legislative provisions, applicable to all persons fulfilling the conditions embodied in such provisions.<SEP>Legal capacity is the ability to exercise civil rights. Full legal capacity is attained at twenty-one years of age completed in accordance with the Gregorian calendar, provided the person is in possession of mental faculties and not under legal disability.<SEP>Legal capacity is the capacity of a person to conclude contracts. Every person who has not been declared under total or partial legal incapacity has legal capacity.<SEP>Legal capacity is the ability of a person who has not been declared to be under total or partial legal incapacity to conclude a contract, as established in Article 109 of the Civil Code.<SEP>The legal ability to enter into contracts; its absence limits the liability of recipients and voluntary agents to the extent of their enrichment.<SEP>The requirement that parties to a compromise must possess the legal ability to dispose for valuable consideration of the rights that are the objects of the compromise contract.

Gregorian Calendar
The Gregorian Calendar (التقويم الميلادي) is the standard calendar used for calculating periods of limitation under the Egyptian Civil Code unless otherwise specified.

Marriage
Marriage (الزواج) is a legal institution whose validity conditions are governed by the national law of each spouse, and its effects are regulated by the law of the husband's country at the time of conclusion.

Inheritance
Inheritance (الميراث) and wills are governed by the national law of the deceased, testator, or person disposing of property at the time of death.

Contractual Obligations
Contractual Obligations (الالتزامات التعاقدية) are governed by the law of the common domicile of the contracting parties, or by the law of the place where the contract was concluded.

Non-Contractual Obligations
Non-Contractual Obligations (الالتزامات غير التعاقدية) are governed by the law of the state in whose territory the act giving rise to the obligation took place.

Private International Law
Private International Law (القانون الدولي الخاص) applies in cases of conflict of laws for which no specific provision is made in the Egyptian Civil Code.<SEP>Private international law provisions are excluded when a foreign law is deemed applicable; only the internal provisions of such foreign law shall apply.

Official Gazette
The Official Gazette (الجريدة الرسمية) is the official publication in which Egyptian laws, including the Egyptian Civil Code, are published as a legal requirement for promulgation.

Advance Proof
Advance Proof (الأدلة التي تعد مقدماً) refers to evidence prepared in advance, governed by the provisions of the law in force at the time when such proof was or should have been established, as stated in Article 9.

Foreign Juristic Person
A Foreign Juristic Person (الشخص الاعتباري الأجنبي) such as companies, associations, or foundations whose legal status is governed by the law of the state where its actual principal seat of management is located, with Egyptian law applying if principal activities are carried out in Egypt.

Divorce
Divorce (التطليق) is a legal dissolution of marriage governed by the law of the country to which the husband belongs at the time of commencement of legal proceedings, as distinguished from repudiation in Article 13.

Separation
Separation (الانفصال) is a legal concept distinct from divorce and repudiation, governed by the law of the country to which the husband belongs at the time of commencement of legal proceedings, as stated in Article 13.

Guardianship
Guardianship (الولاية والوصاية والقوامة) encompasses natural and legal guardianship, receivership, and other systems for the protection of persons without legal capacity and absent persons, governed by the national law of the person to be protected, as stated in Article 16.

Movable Property
Movable Property (المنقول) refers to movable assets whose possession, ownership, and real rights are governed by the law of the place where the movable was situated at the time of the event resulting in acquisition or loss of such rights, as stated in Article 18.<SEP>Movable property includes all things that are not immovables, and all proprietary rights other than real rights over immovable property.<SEP>Property that can be physically moved, subject to special rules for acquisition by possession under Articles 976 and 977.<SEP>Movable Property refers to personal property whose ownership is transferred by contract upon identification, and which may become mingled with other movables belonging to different owners.<SEP>A category of property that can be moved, including personal effects and items sold by vendors, which serves as the subject of special privileges established in Articles 1144 through 1146.

Real Rights
Real Rights (الحقوق العينية) refer to property rights including possession and ownership, regulated by the law of the location of the property, as stated in Article 18.

Tort
Tort (الفعل الضار) refers to obligations arising from harmful acts, with the exception that acts occurring abroad which are lawful in Egypt are not governed by the law of the place where the act occurred, as stated in Article 21.

International Convention
An International Convention (المعاهدة الدولية) in force in Egypt can override the provisions of the Egyptian Civil Code regarding conflicts of law, as stated in Article 23.

State with Multiple Legal Systems
A State with Multiple Legal Systems refers to a country having several coexisting legal systems, where the internal law of that state determines which legal system applies, as stated in Article 26.

Article 222
Article 222 provides that a judge may award compensation for moral prejudice only to spouses and relatives up to the second degree, by reason of grief caused by the death of the victim.

Article 223
Article 223 states that the parties may fix in advance the amount of damages either in the contract or in a subsequent agreement, subject to the provisions of Articles 215 to 220.

Article 225
Article 225 states that when the loss exceeds the contractually fixed amount, the creditor cannot claim an increased sum unless the creditor proves the debtor committed fraud or gross negligence.

Article 226
Article 226 provides that when the object of an obligation is a sum of money of known amount and the debtor delays payment, the debtor is bound to pay interest at four percent in civil matters and five percent in commercial matters as damages for delay, running from the date of the court claim unless otherwise agreed or provided by law.

Article 227
Article 227 allows the parties to agree on another rate of interest not exceeding seven percent. Any agreed rate exceeding seven percent is reduced to seven percent with surplus refunded. Any commission or consideration exceeding the maximum limit is treated as disguised interest and subject to reduction.

Creditor
A Creditor (الدائن) is a person or party to whom a debt, obligation, or annuity is owed and who is entitled to receive payment or performance from a debtor. The creditor holds a range of rights and powers in relation to the obligation, including the authority to ratify or refuse an assignment of debt, to accept payment, and to demand specific performance of the obligation. Where payment is not due, the creditor may be required to make restitution, with the right to restitution influenced by whether the payment was received in good faith. A creditor may also voluntarily release the debtor or be replaced through novation by a third party.

To protect and enforce their rights, a creditor may take legal proceedings against the debtor, seek court orders for enforcement, and claim damages for losses and lost profits. The creditor may interrupt prescription through legal proceedings, summons, attachment, or other formal acts. A creditor is entitled to require the debtor to provide adequate securities guaranteeing the debt and may take protective measures when there are reasonable grounds to apprehend misappropriation — for instance, under Article 1133, a creditor may apply for movables charged with a privilege in their favor to be placed in judicial custody. The creditor benefits from pledges, mortgages, and other forms of security, and may apply for a judgment charge on the debtor's immovable property, with the right to appeal a rejection of such application to the Court of First Instance. Creditors are ranked by priority for payment from the proceeds of property sales.

In relation to sureties, the creditor receives the guarantee from the surety but must generally first take proceedings against the debtor before pursuing the surety. The creditor is bound to prove the debt in bankruptcy to preserve rights against the surety, and may levy execution on the property of both the debtor and, under certain conditions, the surety.

During insolvency proceedings, creditors retain certain rights, including the ability to bring individual actions against the debtor. These rights are preserved even upon the cessation of insolvency.

Article 228
Article 228 establishes that moratory interest, whether fixed by law or by agreement, is due without the creditor being obliged to prove loss as a result of delay.

Article 229
Article 229 provides that if a creditor in bad faith prolongs litigation, the judge may reduce legal or contractual interest or refuse to allow interest for the period of unjustified prolongation.

Article 230
Article 230 governs the distribution of the price of expropriated property sold by auction, limiting moratory interest for admitted creditors based on whether the purchaser or the Caisse du Tribunal is bound to pay interest, with interest distributed pro rata among all creditors.<SEP>A referenced legal provision governing interest provisions, cited in Article 1111 as limiting the scope of accrued interest secured by a pledge.

Article 231
Article 231 allows a creditor to demand supplementary damages in addition to interest if the creditor establishes that a loss exceeding the interest was caused by the debtor in bad faith.

Article 232
Article 232 prohibits interest on outstanding interest and caps total interest collected by the creditor at the amount of the capital, subject to commercial rules and practices to the contrary.

Article 233
Article 233 states that the legal rate of commercial interest on current accounts varies according to the applicable local market rate, and capitalization on current accounts is effected according to commercial usage.

Section III
Section III covers the means of realizing and securing the rights of creditors, including means of execution and means of guarantee.<SEP>A section titled "Extinguishment of a Pledge" encompassing Articles 1112–1113, governing the termination of pledge rights.

Purchaser
The Purchaser is the buyer in a sale contract who acquires ownership of a thing in consideration of a price. As a party to the sale, the Purchaser is obligated to pay the price and take delivery of the thing sold, bearing the costs of the deed of sale, stamp duties, transcription fees, and delivery expenses unless otherwise agreed. The Purchaser must have sufficient acquaintance with the thing sold and is obligated to inspect it for defects upon delivery, giving timely notice of any discovered defects. In trial or tasting sales, the Purchaser has the right to accept or refuse the thing sold.

The Purchaser is entitled to significant protections under the law. These include warranty protection against defects, disturbance, and dispossession. When disturbed in enjoyment or threatened with dispossession, the Purchaser may retain the price. The Purchaser is also entitled to claim compensation, refunds, legal interest, and reimbursement of expenses in cases of dispossession or defects.

In specific contexts, the Purchaser's role carries additional legal implications. When purchasing mortgaged immovable property, the Purchaser may agree with the vendor to assume the mortgage debt through assignment, with the creditor required to ratify or refuse within six months of notification. When a Purchaser buys an industrial or commercial establishment from a lessee on leased property, the court may maintain the lease in the Purchaser's favor despite a prohibition on sub-letting, provided the Purchaser furnishes adequate security and the lessor suffers no real prejudice. A Purchaser who buys a deposited thing from the heir of a depository in good faith is also recognized as a protected party. In property transactions subject to preemption rights, the Purchaser must be notified of any intention to exercise preemption, and the preemptor may assume the Purchaser's rights and obligations.

Article 234
Article 234 provides that the debts of a debtor are secured by all of the debtor's property, and all creditors are treated equally with respect to this security, subject to any right of preference acquired in accordance with law.

Article 235
Article 235 grants every creditor, even if the claim has not fallen due, the right to exercise in the name of the debtor all the debtor's rights of action except those that are purely personal or cannot be attached, provided the creditor proves the debtor has not exercised such rights and that failure to do so results in or increases insolvency.

Article 236
Article 236 states that a creditor exercising the debtor's rights is deemed to be the debtor's representative, and proceeds from such exercise fall into the patrimonium of the debtor and serve as security to all creditors.

Article 237
Article 237 allows any creditor whose claim has fallen due to demand that a prejudicial act of alienation by the debtor be declared void if it diminished rights or increased obligations resulting in or increasing insolvency, subject to conditions in the following article.

Article 238
Article 238 sets conditions for invalidating debtor acts: acts for valuable consideration require proof of debtor fraud and the other party's knowledge of fraud; gratuitous acts are void against the creditor even without fraud; and subsequent transferees' liability depends on their knowledge of fraud or insolvency.

Article 239
Article 239 provides that a creditor alleging debtor insolvency need only establish the amount of debts, while the debtor must prove that assets equal or exceed liabilities.

Article 240
Article 240 provides that once an act is declared void, the benefits of cancellation shall extend to all creditors prejudiced by the act.

Article 241
Article 241 allows a person who acquired a right from an insolvent debtor without paying the price to escape a creditor's action by depositing the normal price at the Caisse du Tribunal.

Article 242
Article 242 provides that fraud giving unjustified preference to one creditor over another only results in loss of that advantage. Payment by an insolvent debtor to one creditor before the originally fixed date is not valid against other creditors, nor is post-date payment resulting from a fraudulent arrangement.

Article 243
Article 243 prescribes a three-year limitation period for an action to set aside an act of alienation from the date the creditor learns of the grounds, and a fifteen-year absolute limitation from the date of the contested act.

The Judge
The judge is the judicial authority empowered to award compensation, reduce damages, reduce or refuse interest, and declare acts void under various provisions of the law.<SEP>The Judge is the judicial officer who appoints administrators, confirms testamentary executors, may discharge administrators for adequate reasons, and can require periodic accountings of administration.<SEP>The judicial authority who authorizes sales of pledged things, fixes sale conditions, orders deposit of sale prices, and resolves matters related to pledge enforcement.

The Creditor
The creditor is a party owed an obligation who may claim damages, exercise the debtor's rights, demand voiding of prejudicial acts, and receive interest payments under the law.

The Debtor
The debtor is a party bound by an obligation who owes payment or performance to the creditor, whose property secures debts, and whose acts of alienation may be challenged by creditors.

Caisse Du Tribunal
The Caisse du Tribunal is the court treasury where the price of expropriated property may be deposited and which may be bound to pay interest on such deposits.

Contractual Damages
Contractual damages refer to compensation fixed in advance by agreement between parties, subject to judicial reduction if grossly exaggerated or if no loss was suffered.

Moratory Interest
Moratory interest is compensation for delay in payment, fixed either by law or agreement, due without proof of loss, with rates varying for civil and commercial matters.

Paulian Action
The Paulian action allows creditors to challenge and set aside prejudicial acts of alienation by debtors, subject to proof of fraud for valuable consideration acts and a three-year prescription period.

Fraud
Fraud is a legal concept central to creditor-debtor relations, referenced in Articles 225, 238, and 242, encompassing intentional deception by the debtor such as entering into acts with intent to defraud creditors.<SEP>Fraud is a ground on which a purchaser may claim annulment of a sale despite a contractual statement that the purchaser is acquainted with the thing sold, provided fraud by the vendor is proven.<SEP>Intentional deception for which a debtor always remains liable. A debtor cannot be contractually discharged from liability arising from personal fraud.<SEP>Deceptive conduct by the lessor, such as fraudulently concealing the cause of a warranty against disturbance or defects, which renders any agreement excluding or limiting such warranty void.

Bad Faith
Bad faith is a legal concept appearing in two distinct contexts: a creditor's bad faith in prolonging litigation (Article 229) and a debtor's bad faith causing loss exceeding interest (Article 231).<SEP>A legal state of mind in which a recipient of undue payment acts dishonestly; a bad faith recipient must also return interest, profits gained, or profits negligently forfeited.<SEP>Bad Faith is a state attributed to the vendor who, knowing of defects or third-party rights, fails to disclose them to the purchaser, resulting in enhanced liability including responsibility for superfluous expenditures that would not otherwise be recoverable.<SEP>Bad faith arises when a possessor knows of infringement or has usurped possession by violence, and it negatively affects the possessor's legal position.<SEP>A state of awareness of the illegitimacy of one's possession, which increases liability for fruits, loss, and deterioration of the property.

Disguised Interest
Disguised interest refers to any commission or consideration stipulated by the creditor that, together with agreed interest, exceeds the maximum legal limit, as defined in Article 227.

The Syndicate
The Syndicate is the body that decides by majority on the reconstruction of destroyed buildings and provides loans to co-owners secured by a privileged charge on their property.

Privileged Charge
A Privileged Charge is a legal security on a co-owner's divided part and undivided share in common parts of a building, ranking from the date of its registration.

The State
The State is identified as a juristic person under Egyptian law, along with its provinces (mudirias), towns, and villages.<SEP>The State is the governing entity that owns uncultivated land without an owner and authorizes its appropriation or possession in accordance with regulations.

Mohammedan Law
Mohammedan Law is Islamic law governing the establishment of heirs, their hereditary shares, and the devolution of estate property onto them.

The Court
The Court is the judicial authority empowered to order the dissolution of a partnership upon the demand of any partner for non-performance of obligations or other reasons not attributable to the partners.<SEP>The Court is the judicial body that oversees estate administration, appoints administrators, orders preservation measures, and controls the winding up process.

Administrator of an Estate
The Administrator of an Estate is a person appointed to take possession of estate property, wind up the estate under court control, publish notices to creditors and debtors, and file statements of assets and liabilities within prescribed time limits.

Testamentary Executor
The Testamentary Executor is a person appointed by the deceased to manage the estate, subject to confirmation by the Judge, and governed by the same rules as an administrator.

The Greffier
The Greffier is the court clerk responsible for entering day by day the court orders regarding the appointment of administrators and confirmation of testamentary executors in a public register with alphabetical indexes.

Ministere Public
The Ministere Public is the public prosecution office that can request the discharge and replacement of an estate administrator or urgent preservation measures for estate property.

Juge de Service
The Juge de Service, or Judge in Chambers, is the judicial officer who authorizes alimentary allowances to heirs supported by the deceased and resolves disputes regarding such allowances.

Inheritance Certificate
The Inheritance Certificate is a document that must be delivered to an heir before the heir may dispose of estate assets, recover estate debts, or set off personal debts against estate debts.

The Omdah
The Omdah is a local official whose main residence door serves as a mandatory posting location for estate-related notices in towns or villages where estate property is situated.

Estate
The Estate is the total collection of property, assets, rights, and liabilities left by a deceased person, subject to formal administration, debt settlement, and division among heirs according to law.<SEP>The Estate comprises the property, assets, and obligations of a deceased person that are subject to administration, winding up, and distribution to heirs under court supervision.

Heirs
The successors in title of a deceased voluntary agent or principal, who are bound by the same obligations as the deceased under Article 194, specifically referencing the obligations of a mandatary's heirs under Article 717.<SEP>Persons entitled to inherit from a deceased person; in the context of sale during last illness, heirs may ratify a sale exceeding one third of the inheritance value or require the purchaser to pay the amount necessary to make up the two thirds.<SEP>Heirs are the successors of a deceased partner who may continue the Partnership in place of the deceased partner by agreement, even if they are minors, as provided under Article 528.<SEP>Heirs are the persons entitled to inherit from the deceased, obligated to inform the administrator of known estate debts and claims, who receive the residue of the estate property proportionally after settlement of all liabilities.<SEP>Heirs are persons entitled to inherit from the deceased, receive alimentary allowances during the winding up process, and ultimately receive shares of the estate property.

The Deceased
The Deceased is the person whose estate is subject to administration, who may have appointed a testamentary executor, and whose burial and funeral expenses must be paid from the estate.

Buried Treasure
Buried Treasure refers to hidden or buried valuables that no one can establish ownership over, belonging to the owner or bare owner of the property where discovered.

Uncultivated Land
Uncultivated Land is land without an owner that becomes the property of the State and can only be appropriated with state authority, though cultivation or building confers immediate ownership.

Estate Winding Up
Estate Winding Up is the legal process of administering and settling a deceased person's estate, including inventory, preservation, payment of debts, publication of notices, and distribution to heirs.

Movables Without an Owner
Movables Without an Owner refers to property whose owner has abandoned possession with the intention of renouncing ownership, or property that never had an owner, and which can be acquired by taking possession with the intent of appropriation under Article 870.

Wild Animals
Wild Animals are non-domestic animals deemed to have no owner as long as they remain at liberty, and regain ownerless status if the owner does not immediately seek them or ceases pursuit after they regain freedom.

Domestic Animals
Domestic Animals are animals that are tamed and accustomed to return to a designated place, distinguished from wild animals in that they are not automatically considered ownerless when at liberty.

Special Regulations
Special Regulations are legal rules governing the rights of fishing, hunting, things found, and antiquities as referenced in Article 873.

Antiquities
Antiquities are historical objects and artifacts whose ownership and discovery rights are governed by special regulations under Article 873.

Public Register
The Public Register is a court-maintained register recording orders regarding the appointment of administrators and confirmation of testamentary executors, indexed alphabetically by the names of deceased persons under Article 879.

Debtors of the Estate
Debtors of the Estate are persons who owe obligations to the estate and must be called upon by the administrator to submit particulars of their debts within three months of the last publication of notice under Article 886.

Acquisition by Appropriation
Acquisition by Appropriation is a legal method of acquiring ownership of ownerless movables or immovables by taking possession with the intent of appropriation, as described in Articles 870 through 874.

Statement of Assets and Liabilities
The Statement of Assets and Liabilities is a document that the administrator must file with the Court registry within four months of appointment, detailing the assets and liabilities of the estate with an estimate of their value under Article 887.

Constituent of Wakf
The person who established the wakf endowment and may delegate leasing authority to beneficiaries.

Agricultural Land
Land used for agricultural purposes subject to specific lease regulations regarding cultivation methods, crop rotation, and maintenance obligations.

Cattle and Agricultural Implements
Items found on agricultural land that may be included in a lease, requiring the lessee to properly care for and maintain them.

Amodiation
A sharecropping arrangement where agricultural or tree-planted land is granted to a lessee in exchange for a fixed share of the crop as rent.

Article 608
Legal provision allowing either contracting party to terminate a fixed-period lease when serious and unforeseen circumstances render performance too burdensome, subject to notice under Article 563 and equitable compensation.

Article 609
Legal provision permitting officials or employees to terminate dwelling leases when their duties require a change of residence, with contrary agreements being void.

Article 612
Legal provision stipulating that when an agricultural lease is expressed in years, it is deemed to cover annual crop rotations.

Article 614
Legal provision allocating routine repair responsibilities to the lessee and major repairs and building construction to the lessor for agricultural land.

Article 615
Legal provision relieving the lessee from payment of all or part of the rent when force majeure prevents land preparation or sowing.

Article 616
Legal provision allowing rent remission for total crop loss and rent reduction for partial loss due to force majeure, unless compensated by other profits or insurance.

Article 619
Legal provision defining amodiation as granting agricultural or tree-planted land to a lessee in consideration of the lessor receiving a fixed share of the crop.

Article 624
Legal provision governing equal division of produce in amodiation by default and shared bearing of force majeure losses between both parties.

Article 626
Legal provision stating that amodiation does not terminate on the death of the lessor but terminates on the death of the lessee.

Article 628
Legal provision granting the Nazir the exclusive right to lease wakf property, while beneficiaries cannot lease without authorization.

Article 630
Legal provision prohibiting the Nazir from leasing wakf property to himself but permitting leasing to ascendants and descendants at current rent.

Article 633
Legal provision limiting the Nazir's authority to lease wakf property to a maximum of three years without judicial authorization.<SEP>Article 633 limits the Nazir's authority to lease wakf property to three years without the judge's permission, with an exception when the Nazir is also the founder or sole beneficiary.

Article 365
Article 365 provides that compensation takes place only when invoked by the interested party, extinguishes both debts to the extent of the smaller amount, and cannot be renounced before the right arises.<SEP>A referenced legal provision governing notice periods for lease termination.

Article 610
Legal provision stating that when the leased property is agricultural land, the lessor is not bound to hand over cattle and agricultural implements to the lessee unless they are included in the lease.

Article 611
Legal provision obligating the lessee to take proper care of and maintain cattle and agricultural implements belonging to the lessor in the manner required for their customary use.

Article 613
Legal provision requiring the lessee of agricultural land to work the land according to normal agricultural use, maintain it in a good state of production, and prohibiting substantial changes to cultivation methods without the lessor's consent.

Article 617
Legal provision allowing the lessee to remain on agricultural land after the lease ends, upon payment of proportional rent, until the harvest ripens for reasons not imputable to the lessee.

Article 618
Legal provision prohibiting an outgoing lessee from diminishing or retarding the enjoyment of the land by an incoming lessee, and requiring the outgoing lessee to allow the incoming lessee to prepare and sow the land.

Article 620
Legal provision stating that in the absence of contrary agreement or custom, the conditions governing leases apply to amodiation subject to specific subsequent provisions.

Article 621
Legal provision establishing that when no term is fixed, an amodiation is deemed to have been granted for one yearly rotation of crops.

Article 622
Legal provision providing that a lease in case of amodiation includes agricultural implements and cattle belonging to the lessor which are on the land at the time of the agreement.

Article 623
Legal provision requiring the lessee in amodiation to give the same care to cultivation and crop preservation as to his own affairs, holding him responsible for land deterioration unless he proves reasonable care was exercised.

Article 625
Legal provision prohibiting the lessee in amodiation from assigning the lease or subletting the land without the consent of the lessor.

Article 627
Legal provision requiring the lessor to reimburse the lessee or his heirs for expenditures on unripened crops when amodiation ceases before its term, and allowing heirs to continue cultivation until crops ripen if the lessee dies.

Article 629
Legal provision designating the Nazir as the person entitled to receive rent for wakf property, prohibiting payment to the beneficiary without the Nazir's consent.

Article 631
Legal provision rendering a lease of wakf property invalid if the rent is grossly inadequate, unless the lessor is the sole beneficiary with administrative power, in which case the lease binds only the lessor and not succeeding beneficiaries.

Article 632
Legal provision requiring rent estimation for wakf property leases to be made at the time of contract conclusion, and obligating the lessee to supplement inadequate rent under penalty of contract resiliation.

Incoming Lessee
The person who succeeds an outgoing lessee in the use of agricultural land and is entitled to prepare and sow the land before taking possession.

Greffier Of The Court
The Greffier of the Court is the court official who must notify the debtor of the judgment charge order, endorse it on the authenticated copy of the judgment, and inform the greffier of the Court that rendered the judgment.

Court Of First Instance
The Court of First Instance is a judicial body before which the debtor or creditor may appeal orders related to judgment charges.

President Of The Court
The President of the Court is the judicial officer who decides on applications for judgment charges, and whose rejection of such an application may be appealed by the creditor to the Court of First Instance.

Pledgor
The Pledgor is the person who undertakes to deliver the thing pledged as security for a debt, guarantees the pledge and its efficacy, and must not diminish the value of the pledged thing.<SEP>The debtor who grants the pledge and may request restitution of the pledged thing, apply to the Judge for authorization of an advantageous sale, and has the right to be informed of collections made on the pledged debt.

Pledgee
The Pledgee is the creditor who receives the thing pledged, must preserve and maintain it with reasonable care, manage it, and may not derive gratuitous advantage from it; must restitute it upon repayment of the debt.<SEP>The Pledgee is the creditor who holds a pledge and, if unpaid when the pledged debt and secured debt fall due, may collect the pledged debt up to the amount due, demand its sale, or request its allocation in accordance with Article 1121, paragraph 2.<SEP>The creditor who holds the pledge, with rights including collection of interest and periodic payments, enforcement of the pledge through sale or appropriation, and obligations including preservation of the pledged thing, payment of taxes and charges, and protection of the pledged debt.

The Thing Pledged
The Thing Pledged is the movable or immovable property delivered by the pledgor to the pledgee as security for a debt, which must be capable of being sold independently by public auction.

Chapter III
Chapter III, titled "Rights Derived from the Right of Ownership Pledge," is the legal chapter encompassing the rules on pledges including their elements, effects, and the obligations of the pledgor and pledgee.

Section II
Section II covers the effects of a judgment charge, its reduction, and extinguishment, as well as the effects of a pledge between contracting parties and as regards third parties.

Fruits And Revenue
Fruits and Revenue are the produce or income generated by the thing pledged, which the pledgee must apply in reduction of the secured debt in a specific order: first to preservation expenses and repairs, then to expenses and interest, and then to the capital amount of the debt.

Person Assuming the Debt
A third party who undertakes to assume a debt in place of the original debtor through an agreement, who is responsible to effect payment to the creditor until ratification or refusal, and who may raise defenses available to the original debtor.

Original Debtor
The original debtor in an assignment of debt scenario who enters into an agreement with a third party to transfer the debt, and who warrants the solvency of the person assuming the debt at the moment the creditor ratifies the assignment.

Distrainer
A person who serves an attachment upon the debtor of an assigned debt, whose rights are affected by whether the assignment has become effective against third parties.

Assignment of Right
The transfer of a right from an assignor to an assignee, governed by provisions regarding warranties, solvency of the debtor, effectiveness against third parties, and preference among multiple assignments of the same right.

Assignment of Debt
The transfer of a debt obligation from an original debtor to a person assuming the debt, effected by agreement between the parties, requiring creditor ratification to be effective, and governed by provisions on warranties, defenses, and surety obligations.

Warranty of Solvency
A guarantee regarding the financial solvency of the debtor, which the assignor does not provide unless specifically stipulated, and which only applies to the debtor's solvency at the time of assignment.

Right of Recourse in Warranty
The right of an assignee to seek remedy against the assignor, limiting the assignor's liability to restitution of what was received together with interest and expenses.

Defense
Legal arguments that a debtor may raise against an assignee, including those previously available against the assignor at the time the assignment became effective, and those arising from the contract of assignment.

Chapter V: Extinction of Obligations
A chapter of the civil code covering the various ways in which obligations are extinguished, including through payment and subrogation.

Section II: Assignment of Debt
A section of the civil code governing the transfer of debt obligations from an original debtor to a person assuming the debt, including provisions on creditor ratification, warranties, and defenses.

Article 309
A legal provision stating that an assignor does not warrant the solvency of the debtor unless such warranty is specifically stipulated, and if warranted, it only applies to solvency at the time of assignment.

Article 313
A legal provision providing that in the event of several assignments relating to the same right, preference is given to the assignment that is first effective as regards third parties.

Article 316
A legal provision stating that an assignment of debt is not effective against the creditor unless ratified by the creditor, and that silence after a reasonable period constitutes refusal.

Article 326
A legal provision enumerating the cases in which a third party who makes payment is subrogated into the rights of the creditor, including joint liability, prior creditor status, acquisition of mortgaged property, and statutory subrogation.

Article 322
A legal provision governing the sale of mortgaged immovable property, stating that sale does not imply transfer of the mortgage debt unless agreed, and that creditor silence for six months after notification constitutes ratification.

Article 310
A legal provision stating that when an assignee exercises the right of recourse in warranty against the assignor in accordance with the two preceding articles, the assignor is only liable to restitute what he has received together with interest and expenses notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary.

Article 311
A legal provision stating that an assignor is responsible for personal acts, even if the assignment is not for valuable consideration or even if it has been stipulated to be without warranty.

Article 312
A legal provision stating that a debtor may raise against the assignee the defenses he was entitled to raise against the assignor at the moment the assignment became effective, and may also raise defenses arising from the contract of assignment.

Article 314
A legal provision governing the effect of attachment served upon the debtor before an assignment becomes effective against third parties, making the assignment equivalent to an attachment, and providing for pro rata division of debt among the first distrainer, the assignee, and the second distrainer.

Article 315
A legal provision stating that an assignment of debt is effected by an agreement between the debtor and a third party who undertakes to assume the debt in place of the debtor.

Article 317
A legal provision stating that until the creditor ratifies or refuses the assignment, the person assuming the debt is responsible to the original debtor to effect payment on due date to the creditor, and that the original debtor cannot compel payment by the person assuming the debt until he has discharged his own obligation under the contract of assignment.

Article 318
A legal provision stating that the debt assigned is transmitted with all its warranties, but the surety, whether real or personal, does not remain bound to the creditor unless he has agreed to the assignment.

Article 319
A legal provision stating that in the absence of agreement to the contrary, the original debtor warrants the solvency of the person assuming the debt at the moment the creditor ratifies the assignment.

Article 320
A legal provision stating that a person assuming the debt may raise against the creditor the defenses which the original debtor was entitled to raise, as well as defenses arising out of the contract of assignment.

Article 321
A legal provision stating that an assignment of debt may also take place between the creditor and the person assuming the debt by an agreement providing that such person replaces the original debtor in his obligation, with Articles 318 and 320 being applicable.

Article 323
A legal provision stating that payment may be made by the debtor, his representative, or any interested party, and also by a third party who is not interested, even without the knowledge or against the wish of the debtor, subject to the debtor's right to oppose.

Article 324
A legal provision stating that a third party who pays off the debt has a remedy against the debtor up to the amount paid, and that the debtor against whose wish payment was made may contest the claim if he shows interest in opposing the payment.

Article 325
A legal provision stating that payment is only valid if the payer is the owner of that with which he has paid and has the capacity to dispose of it, but payment by a person without legal capacity still extinguishes the obligation provided it does not prejudice the payer.

Article 327
A legal provision stating that a creditor who receives payment from a third party may by agreement subrogate such third party into his rights even without the debtor's consent, provided the agreement is concluded at the time of payment.

Article 328
A legal provision stating that a debtor who has borrowed money to pay the debt may subrogate the lender into the rights of the creditor even without the creditor's consent, provided the contract of loan states the purpose and the receipt identifies the source of funds.

Article 329
A legal provision stating that a third party subrogated by law or agreement in the rights of the creditor is substituted for the creditor as regards the debt to the amount of sums paid, with all attributes, accessories, securities, and defenses attached to the debt.

Article 330
A legal provision governing partial payment and subrogation, stating that a creditor shall not be prejudiced by partial payment and retains priority over the paying third party, and that a further subrogated party shares pro rata with the first.

Article 331
A legal provision stating that a holder of a mortgaged property who has paid all the mortgage debt and been subrogated into the rights of creditors may only claim from the holder of another property mortgaged for the same debt the proportional share based on the value of the immovable held.

Article 332
A legal provision stating that payment shall be made to the creditor or his representative, and that a person producing a receipt in discharge from the creditor is deemed qualified to receive payment unless it has been agreed that payment shall be made to the creditor in person.

Article 333
A legal provision stating that if payment is made to a person other than the creditor or his representative, the debtor is not discharged unless the creditor ratifies the payment or derives benefit from it, to the extent of such benefit.

Section I: Payment
A section of the civil code covering payment as a means of extinguishing obligations, including provisions on who may make payment, conditions of validity, subrogation, and the proper recipient of payment.

Holder of Mortgaged Property
A third party holder of a mortgaged immovable property who has paid all the mortgage debt and has been subrogated into the rights of the creditors, with the right to claim proportional contributions from holders of other properties mortgaged for the same debt.

Lender
A person who lends money to a debtor for the purpose of paying off a debt, and who may be subrogated into the rights of the creditor who received the payment.<SEP>The party to a loan for consumption who must deliver the thing that is the object of the contract to the borrower and bears the loss if the thing perishes before delivery.

Court
The Court is the judicial body vested with broad authority across civil, contractual, property, and estate matters. It serves as the primary judicial authority empowered to authorize deposits, public auctions, and judicial custody, as well as to grant reasonable delays for the performance of obligations. In the realm of contracts, the Court decides points of detail in disputes according to the nature of the transaction, the provisions of law, custom, and equity. It may order the nullity of a void contract on its own initiative and, in cases of economic imbalance caused by exceptional events, it has the authority to reduce compensation due for loss of profit, grant price increases, or order the resiliation of the contract.

The Court exercises significant powers over personal status and capacity. It pronounces or raises interdictions, appoints judicial advisers, and ratifies acts of minors and interdicted persons. It also adjudicates avoidance claims and is authorized to grant revocation of a gift and adjudicate on the nullity of partnership deeds. In partnership matters specifically, the Court may order dissolution, appoint liquidators, and authorize a partner's retirement upon application.

In property and lease matters, the Court authorizes preventive measures against building dangers, adjudicates claims, and its involvement triggers obligations such as restitution of profits. It may maintain a lease despite a prohibition on sub-letting when a commercial or industrial establishment is sold, grant the lessor time for settlement of payments for improvements, and authorize the lessee to carry out repairs and deduct costs from rent when the lessor delays maintenance obligations. The Court also grants damages instead of material redress for breaches of servitude restrictions when it considers there are reasons for doing so, and decides matters in accordance with equity when movables belonging to different owners become mingled. It handles actions in preemption before the district court where the property is situated.

Regarding co-ownership and joint property, the Court resolves disputes among co-owners, appoints managers for commonly held property, orders security for dissenting co-owners, and decides on the alienation of jointly owned property. It may authorize a co-owner to withdraw a share from family joint ownership before the agreed term, discharge a manager, order the sale of a lower storey, and appoint a representative of a syndicate.

The Court oversees the entire estate administration process, including receiving inventory filings, investigating disputes, authorizing debt payments, fixing deadlines, ordering the sale or allocation of property, and issuing inheritance certificates. It is also the body before which conditions of sale are filed and where third party holders or applicants deposit sums to cover costs or satisfy creditors. Additionally, the Court renders orders authorizing judgment charges, and its greffier is responsible for notifying and endorsing such orders. The Court orders judicial custody, stamps receiver account books, and receives copies of accounts from court-appointed receivers.

Receipt in Discharge
A document issued by the creditor that, when produced to the debtor, deems the bearer qualified to receive payment unless it has been agreed that payment shall be made to the creditor in person.

Contract of Loan
An agreement between a debtor and a lender in which the sum borrowed is stated to be for the purpose of effecting payment of a debt, enabling subrogation of the lender into the creditor's rights.

Contract of Assignment
The agreement governing the assignment of a right or debt, from which defenses may be derived and which defines the obligations of the parties involved.

Managing Partner
A Managing Partner is a partner entrusted with the management of the partnership by a special clause in the partnership deed or by subsequent appointment, entitled to perform acts of management and disposition within the objects of the partnership, provided they are not tainted with fraud.

Personal Creditors
Personal Creditors are creditors of an individual partner who may only claim payment from the partner's share in the profits during the continuance of the partnership, and from the partner's share in assets after liquidation and payment of partnership debts.

Article 514
Article 514 establishes rules for profit and loss sharing when the partnership deed does not fix shares, requiring shares to be proportional to capital contributions, and granting additional shares for partners contributing both services and money or property.

Article 515
Article 515 declares the partnership deed void if one partner agrees not to participate in profits or losses, and permits a service-only partner to be relieved from sharing losses provided no remuneration is allowed for his services.

Article 516
Article 516 governs the appointment and removal of managing partners, granting managing partners appointed by the deed authority to act despite objections, while allowing subsequent appointments to be revoked like ordinary mandates.

Article 517
Article 517 regulates the conduct of multiple managing partners, allowing each to act separately unless unanimity or majority decisions are required, with exceptions only for urgent matters involving serious and irreparable loss.

Article 518
Article 518 provides that majority decisions shall be decided by numerical majority in the absence of an agreement to the contrary.

Public Auction
Public Auction is a legally governed sale method conducted in accordance with formal statutory provisions and judicial authorization. It serves as the prescribed or required mechanism in several distinct legal contexts, including the liquidation of movable and immovable property belonging to an estate—carried out following the manner and delays established for forced sales unless all heirs unanimously agree to an alternative method—as well as the forced sale of mortgaged immovable property through compulsory expropriation formalities, which may be initiated either by a creditor's application or by a third-party holder's wish to purge the mortgage. A mortgaged property must be marketable and susceptible to sale by public auction for this mechanism to apply.

Public Auction also functions as a court-authorized method for the sale of pledged property, particularly when the pledged item is deteriorating, in danger of perishing, or when there is a default of payment, as referenced in Articles 1119, 1121, and 1129. Only movables or immovables that can be sold independently may become the object of a pledge under this framework, as stated in Article 1097. Additionally, it is the designated sale method for items of a rapidly perishing nature or movables that incur exorbitant storage costs, with the proceeds from such sales deposited in the Caisse du Tribunal.

Several legal consequences attach specifically to sales conducted by Public Auction. A contract is formed only upon acceptance of the final bid, and any prior bid is nullified from the moment a higher bid is made, even if that higher bid is subsequently found to be void. Because a Public Auction is conducted in conformity with legal provisions, an action for supplement of price on grounds of lesion does not lie. Furthermore, preemption rights cannot be exercised when the sale is made by Public Auction, as explicitly stated in Article 939.

Article 519
Article 519 excludes non-managing partners from management but grants them the right to personally examine the books and documents of the partnership, rendering any agreement to the contrary void.

Article 520
Article 520 provides that in the absence of special provisions on management, each partner is deemed authorized to manage the partnership, subject to the right of other partners to object before completion of any act.

Article 521
Article 521 obliges each partner to abstain from activities prejudicial to the partnership and to exercise the same care as for his own interests, with a higher standard of care for remunerated managers.

Article 522
Article 522 holds a partner liable for interest on partnership money taken or retained, and entitles a partner to interest on private funds advanced to the partnership in good faith.

Article 523
Article 523 makes partners personally liable for partnership debts not covered by partnership assets, each in proportion to his share in losses, and voids any agreement relieving a partner from such liability.

Article 524
Article 524 provides that partners are not jointly or severally liable for partnership debts unless otherwise agreed, but if one partner becomes insolvent, his share is apportioned among the others.

Article 525
Article 525 restricts personal creditors of a partner from claiming against the partner's capital share during the partnership, limiting them to the partner's profit share, while allowing protective attachment before liquidation.

Article 526
Article 526 states that a partnership ends upon expiration of its term or achievement of its object, but is extended year by year if partners continue operations, subject to creditor opposition.

Article 527
Article 527 provides that a partnership ends upon total or substantial loss of its capital, and is dissolved if a specific thing pledged as contribution perishes before delivery.

Article 528
Article 528 provides that a partnership is terminated by death, interdiction, insolvency, or bankruptcy of a partner, but may continue with heirs or remaining partners by agreement, with the departing partner's share valued at the date of the event.

Article 529
Article 529 permits termination of a partnership by retirement of a partner with no fixed term, provided proper notice is given without fraudulent intent or unsuitable timing, or by unanimous agreement of all partners.

Article 530
Article 530 empowers the Court to order dissolution of the partnership for non-performance by a partner of his obligations or for other reasons not attributable to the partners, and voids any agreement to the contrary.

Non-Partner Manager
A Non-Partner Manager is a manager of the Partnership who is not a partner, and who may be discharged from his post at any time, as distinguished from a managing partner appointed under the Partnership Deed.

Partnership Capital
Partnership Capital refers to the total contributions made by partners to the Partnership, forming the financial foundation against which profit shares, loss shares, and partnership debts are measured.

Partnership Liquidation
Partnership Liquidation is the process of winding up the Partnership's affairs, after which personal creditors of a partner may enforce their claims against the partner's share in the Partnership assets.

Partnership Books and Documents
Partnership Books and Documents are the financial records of the Partnership that non-managing partners are entitled to personally examine, with any agreement to the contrary being void.

Agreement of Lease
The contract between the lessor and lessee establishing their respective rights and obligations, including terms on rent, use of the property, warranties, and conditions for resiliation or alteration.

Government Authority
A governmental body whose lawful acts may appreciably diminish the enjoyment of the leased property, entitling the lessee to claim resiliation of the lease or reduction of rent, and potentially damages if the grounds are imputable to the lessor.

Warranty Against Defects
The lessor's obligation to ensure the leased property is free from defects that prevent or appreciably diminish enjoyment, except for defects customarily tolerated or known to the lessee at the time of contract. The lessor is not liable for defects of which the lessee was informed or aware.<SEP>Warranty Against Defects is a legal guarantee obligating the vendor for defects in the thing sold that diminish its value or usefulness at the time of delivery, even if the vendor was ignorant of them. It does not cover defects known to the purchaser, discoverable by reasonable inspection, or customarily tolerated, unless the vendor affirmed the absence of defects or fraudulently concealed them.

Reduction of Rent
A remedy available to the lessee when the enjoyment of the leased property is appreciably diminished due to third-party claims, government authority acts, trespass, or defects in the property.

Lien
The lessor's right to retain and recover attachable movables found in the leased property as security for all amounts due under the lease, even when such movables do not belong to the lessee. This right is limited by professional requirements and customary needs of the lessee.

Servants of the Lessor
Individuals acting on behalf of the lessor whose acts of disturbance or damage are covered by the lessor's warranty to the lessee.

Successor in Title
A person who acquires rights from the lessor and whose lawful claims against the lessee are covered by the lessor's warranty against disturbance.

Lessee's Repairs
Maintenance and repair obligations of the lessee carried out in accordance with general usage, unless otherwise agreed between the parties.

Other Lessee
Another tenant of the same lessor whose disturbances or lawful claims against the primary lessee are covered by the lessor's warranty. When several lessees rent the same property, the one who without fraud first enters into possession has preference.

Fire
An event causing damage to the leased property for which the lessee is responsible unless the cause is proven not imputable to the lessee. When multiple lessees occupy a building, each is responsible in proportion to the part occupied, unless the fire started in one specific part.

Alteration
Changes or modifications made by the lessee to the leased property, requiring the lessor's permission unless no damage is thereby occasioned to the lessor. Unauthorized alterations may compel the lessee to reinstate the property and pay compensation.

Security for Rent
The obligation of the lessee of a house, warehouse, shop, or agricultural land to stock the leased property with movables of sufficient value to guarantee rent payment for two years or the lease period if shorter, unless rent is paid in advance or other guarantees are provided.

Administrator
An Administrator is a person appointed to manage the estate of a deceased person, responsible for filing an inventory of assets and liabilities with the Court within four months, informing interested parties, paying estate debts, executing legacies, and distributing remaining property to heirs.

Inventory
The Inventory is a formal statement of the assets and liabilities of the estate with an estimate of their value, filed by the administrator with the registry of the Court, and subject to dispute by interested parties within thirty days.

Deceased
The Deceased (also referred to as the testator or Alwarith) is the person whose death gave rise to the estate, whose papers disclose claims and debts, and whose property is subject to administration and division among heirs.

Registry Of The Court
The Registry of the Court is the official office where the administrator files the statement of assets and liabilities of the estate.

Elam Charei
Elam Charei (I'lam Shari'i) is a formal legal document certifying a person's inheritance rights, which an heir must produce to the Court in order to obtain a certificate establishing rights in the inheritance.

Legacies
Legacies are testamentary gifts or charges specified in a will that the administrator must execute and pay after the settlement of all debts of the estate.

Interested Party
An Interested Party is any person with a legal interest in the estate who must be informed of the filing of the inventory by registered letter and who may petition the Court regarding disputes within thirty days.

Agricultural Industrial Or Commercial Enterprise
An Agricultural, Industrial or Commercial Enterprise is an economic unit within the estate that constitutes a distinct economic unity and must be allotted as a whole to the most capable heir requesting it.

Family Papers
Family Papers are documents and articles of sentimental value to the heirs owing to their relationship to the deceased, whose division or sale is ordered by the Court in the absence of agreement among the heirs.

Forced Sales
Forced Sales refer to the prescribed legal procedure and delays governing the public auction sale of movable and immovable estate property when heirs do not unanimously agree on an alternative method.

Article 554
Article 554 is a referenced legal provision governing the calculation of amounts payable to creditors when a debt not yet due is made immediately exigible at the request of all heirs.

Extinctive Prescription
Extinctive Prescription is a legal mechanism that extinguishes obligations through the passage of time, with varying periods of fifteen years, five years, three years, or one year depending on the type of obligation.<SEP>Extinctive prescription is a legal mechanism that extinguishes obligations through the passage of time, with a general term of fifteen years and special shorter terms for certain periodic rights.<SEP>Extinctive prescription refers to rules governing the calculation, suspension, and interruption of prescription periods, which are applied by analogy to acquisitive prescription under Article 973.<SEP>A legal mechanism that extinguishes rights through the passage of time, whose rules are applicable to acquisitive prescription where compatible.

Sale Contract
A Sale Contract is an agreement whereby the vendor binds himself to transfer to the purchaser the ownership of a thing or any other propriety right in consideration of a price in money.<SEP>The Sale Contract is the legal agreement between the vendor and the purchaser governing the transfer of ownership of the thing sold in exchange for a price. Its costs, stamp duties, transcription fees, and other expenses are borne by the purchaser in the absence of contrary agreement or usage.

State
The State is the governmental entity to which taxes and dues are owed, with a three-year prescription period applicable to such claims.<SEP>The State is a sovereign entity that owns immovable and movable property which may be allocated for public utility purposes as part of the public domain.<SEP>The governmental entity that acquires ownership of land uncovered by the sea, as stated in Article 919.

Periodic Payments
