Periodic Payments are sums payable at recurring intervals such as rent of buildings and agricultural land, interest, periodical payments, salaries, wages, and pensions, subject to a five-year prescription period even if the debt is admitted by the debtor.

Professional Remuneration
Professional Remuneration refers to sums due to physicians, chemists, lawyers, engineers, experts, receivers in bankruptcy, brokers, professors, and teachers for work within the scope of their professions or expenses incurred, subject to a five-year prescription period.

Taxes and Dues
Taxes and Dues are financial obligations owed to the State, subject to a three-year prescription period that runs from the end of the year for which they are due or from the date of relevant legal proceedings.

Prescription Interruption
Prescription Interruption is a legal mechanism that halts and restarts the prescription period, triggered by legal proceedings, summons, attachment, creditor claims in bankruptcy, or express or tacit admission by the debtor.

Prescription Suspension
Prescription Suspension is a legal mechanism that halts the running of prescription when there is a bar preventing the creditor from claiming his right, including moral bars, lack of legal representation for incapable persons, absent persons, or convicted criminals.

Natural Obligation
A Natural Obligation is a residual moral obligation that remains upon the debtor even after the legal obligation has been extinguished by prescription.<SEP>A type of obligation that exists without direct legal enforcement, determined by the judge in the absence of legal provision. A debtor cannot claim restitution of what was voluntarily given to discharge a natural obligation. No natural obligation can be contrary to public policy.<SEP>A type of obligation whose performance cannot be enforced, but which may serve as a valid cause for a civil obligation; a debtor cannot claim restitution of what was voluntarily given to discharge it.

Sale by Sample
Sale by Sample is a type of sale where the thing sold must conform to the sample, and the burden of proof lies with the party in whose custody the sample deteriorated or perished.

Sale upon Trial
Sale upon Trial is a type of sale where the purchaser has the option to accept or refuse the thing sold within an agreed or reasonable time, and silence after the trial period is equivalent to acceptance.

Sale Subject to Tasting
Sale Subject to Tasting is a type of sale where the purchaser may accept the thing sold and must declare acceptance within a time fixed by agreement or custom, with the sale only concluded upon such declaration.

Book II: Specific Contracts
Book II: Specific Contracts is a section of the civil code dealing with specific named contracts, including contracts regarding ownership.

Chapter VI: Proof of Obligations
Chapter VI: Proof of Obligations is a chapter of the civil code covering Articles 389 through 417, all of which have been repealed.

One-Year Prescription Rights
One-Year Prescription Rights refer to claims that are prescribed after one year, including rights of action of merchants and manufacturers for things supplied, hotel and restaurant proprietors for accommodation and food costs, and workmen, servants, and wage earners for their pay and supplies.

Oath of Payment
The Oath of Payment is a procedural requirement where a person claiming the one-year prescription must swear that the debt has actually been paid; the Judge directs this oath ex officio, and if the debtor is deceased, it may be directed to the heirs or their guardians.

Prescription Calculation
Prescription Calculation refers to the rule that prescription periods are computed in days rather than hours, the first day is not counted, and the period is completed when the last day has ended.

Prescription Commencement
Prescription Commencement governs when the prescription period begins to run, namely from the day the debt becomes due, from the realization of a suspensive condition, from the date of eviction in warranty claims, from the expiration of a term for future debts, or from when the creditor is in a position to express his will.

Third Party
In legal contexts, a Third Party is any person or entity who is not an original party to a contract, agreement, or legal obligation between two primary parties. The concept of a Third Party arises across a wide range of civil and contractual situations, consistently referring to an external participant whose rights, obligations, and interactions with the primary parties are governed by specific legal provisions.

In the realm of obligations and contracts, a Third Party may assume the role of a new debtor or a new creditor through the mechanism of novation, as described in Article 352. A Third Party may also make payment on behalf of a debtor and, upon doing so, may be subrogated into the rights of the creditor. However, while a Third Party may acquire rights under a contract through a stipulation for a Third Party—gaining a direct right against the promisor—they generally do not acquire obligations under a contract to which they are not a party. A Third Party may also serve as a beneficiary of consideration under Article 497 or as a debtor in the contribution of debts under Article 513, and may be affected by partnership publication formalities under Article 506.

In property-related matters, a Third Party may hold an existing right over a thing sold at the time of sale, which is enforceable against the purchaser and may cause disturbance in the purchaser's enjoyment. A Third Party may also acquire possession of property, such as a good-faith purchaser at a market or public sale, and may be subject to restitution claims. Additionally, in the context of property disposition, the lawful interest and lifetime of a Third Party—being a person other than the one disposing of property or the one in whose favor it is disposed—may serve as valid grounds for an inalienability clause under Article 823.

With respect to security interests, a Third Party is a person not party to a mortgage agreement; a mortgage is effective against Third Parties only if the deed or judgment establishing the mortgage has been inscribed before the Third Party acquires real rights on the property, subject to bankruptcy provisions. Similarly, in the context of a pledge, a Third Party may be chosen by the contracting parties to hold the pledged thing, and their rights are preserved under the law even as the pledge confers rights against all persons.

A Third Party may also play a role in matters of lease, where an external party may claim rights over the leased property or commit trespass or disturbance. In such cases, the lessee may take legal action against the Third Party in the lessee's own name for damages and possessory actions. Furthermore, a Third Party who is not a contracting party may practice fraudulent misrepresentation or duress; the victim of such Third Party acts may demand avoidance of the contract only if the other contracting party was aware or should have been aware of the fraud or duress, as specified in Articles 126 and 128.

Renunciation of Prescription
Renunciation of Prescription refers to the rule that a debtor cannot renounce the benefits of prescription before acquiring the right to invoke it, nor agree to a term different from that fixed by law, but may renounce even tacitly after acquiring the right, provided the renunciation does not prejudice creditors.

Written Document
A Written Document establishing a right referred to in Articles 376 or 378 extends the prescription period for that right to fifteen years instead of the original shorter period.<SEP>The required form of evidence for establishing a compromise, which can only be proved by a written document or by an official proces-verbal.

Heirs and Guardians
Heirs and Guardians are persons who may be directed to take the oath of payment when the debtor is deceased, declaring either that they do not know of the existence of the debt or that they know it has been paid.

Article 670
Article 670 is a legal provision requiring the concessionaire of a public utility service who enjoys a de jure or de facto monopoly to observe strict equality between consumers regarding services rendered and rates charged, while permitting special treatment involving rate reduction if granted to all applicants fulfilling general conditions, and prohibiting granting advantages to some consumers while refusing them to others, with liability for compensation for discrimination disturbing fair competition.

Article 671
Article 671 is a legal provision stipulating that rates laid down by the public authority have force of law with respect to contracts between the concessionaire and consumers, that the parties cannot depart from them by agreement, and that modified rates apply without retroactive effect from the date fixed by the act of ratification.

Article 672
Article 672 is a legal provision stating that any irregularity or mistake in applying rates to individual contracts is subject to rectification, entitling the consumer to recover excess payments or the concessionaire to collect shortfalls, with the right of recovery barred by prescription after one year from collection.

Article 673
Article 673 is a legal provision requiring consumers of water, gas, electricity, and power distribution services to tolerate short interruptions necessary for upkeep, while permitting the concessionaire to repudiate responsibility for abnormal interruptions caused by force majeure or fortuitous events, including strikes under certain conditions.

Article 674
Article 674 is a legal provision defining a contract of service as one whereby one contracting party undertakes to work in the service and under the supervision or control of the other party in consideration for remuneration.

Article 675
Article 675 is a legal provision stating that the provisions of the Contracts of Service section apply only insofar as they are not inconsistent with special laws relating to service, which define categories of workers excluded from these provisions.

Debtor
A Debtor (المدين) is the person or party legally obligated to fulfill, perform, or pay a debt or obligation to a creditor. The debtor's core duty is to deliver or perform the object of an obligation, and may be compelled to specific performance. When the degree of quality of the object is unspecified and cannot be determined by usage or circumstances, the debtor must supply an article of average quality. In monetary obligations, the debtor is bound only to the actual figure stated in the contract. The debtor is always liable for fraud or gross negligence and may be held liable for damages upon non-performance or delay. The debtor enjoys several rights, including the designation of which debt to discharge, the right to demand receipts, the right to make a judicial deposit, and the right of retraction of tender under specified conditions. In alternative obligations, the debtor holds election rights. A debtor cannot claim restitution of voluntary payments made to discharge a natural obligation.

The debtor may invoke defenses against an assignee that were available against the assignor, as well as defenses arising from the contract of assignment. The debtor may also invoke prescription as a defense, and may interrupt prescription by expressly or tacitly acknowledging the debt. In the case of a litigious right that has been assigned, the debtor may extinguish the assigned right by paying the assignee the actual price paid, together with expenses and interest. The debtor may be replaced through novation or delegation by a third party. Revocation of a third-party stipulation does not liberate the debtor vis-à-vis the stipulator unless expressly agreed.

In the context of mortgages and secured obligations, the debtor is the person obligated to pay the secured debt underlying the mortgage. The mortgagor may be the debtor or a third party acting in the debtor's interest. If mortgaged property perishes or deteriorates without the mortgagor's fault, the debtor may either furnish adequate security or pay the debt in full before it falls due. After the debt has fallen due, the debtor may transfer the mortgaged property to the creditor in payment of the debt. The debtor's property may also be subject to privileged rights, including general and special privileges covering obligations such as wages, alimony, taxes, and rent, and may be subject to execution to satisfy outstanding debts, expropriation proceedings, and judgment charges. The debtor may lodge an appeal against an order authorizing a judgment charge before the judge who gave the order or before the Court of First Instance.

A debtor who holds the right of redemption under an annuity may be compelled to redeem if payment defaults occur, securities prove insufficient, or insolvency arises. In the context of suretyship, the debtor's failure to perform triggers the surety's obligation, and the debtor may be required to offer a solvent surety residing in Egypt or adequate real security. If the debtor becomes bankrupt, the creditor must prove the debt.

A debtor may be declared bankrupt or insolvent if assets are insufficient to meet obligations, and is subject to penalties for willful insolvency or the concealment of property. Insolvency may result in the forfeiture of term benefits. Upon cessation of insolvency, the debtor may reclaim previously discharged debts.

Article 676
Article 676 is a legal provision applying contract of service rules to the relationship between masters and canvassers, commercial representatives, commercial travellers, assurance agents, and other intermediaries even if remunerated on commission, and granting departing commercial representatives the right to commission on orders resulting from their efforts during service.

Article 677
Article 677 is a legal provision stating that a contract of service does not require any special form unless law or administrative regulations provide otherwise.

Article 678
Article 678 is a legal provision allowing contracts of service to be concluded for a specific service, a fixed period, or an indefinite duration, and granting a worker the right to resiliate without compensation after five years with six months prior notice for contracts exceeding five years.

Article 679
Article 679 is a legal provision stating that a fixed-period contract terminates automatically upon expiration of its term, and that continued performance by both parties after expiration deems the contract renewed for an indefinite duration.

Article 680
Article 680 is a legal provision stating that a contract for a specific work terminates upon completion of the agreed work, and that if the work is renewable by nature and the contract continues, it is deemed impliedly renewed for the period necessary to perform the same work again.

Article 681
Article 681 is a legal provision establishing the presumption that the performance of services is made for remuneration when such services are not customarily performed gratuitously or fall within the scope of the performer's profession.

Article 682
Article 682 is a legal provision governing the determination of salary when not specified in contracts or factory regulations, prescribing a hierarchy of applicable rates for similar work, trade custom, local custom, and judicial determination according to equity.

Article 683
Article 683 is a legal provision enumerating sums that form an integral part of an employee's salary for purposes of computing the attachable portion, including commissions, percentages on sales, cost of living allowances, gratuities, fidelity bonuses, and family allowances.

Article 684
Article 684 is a legal provision deeming tips to form part of salary only in industries where customary and subject to regulation, and recognizing tips as salary when collected in a common fund and distributed under employer supervision, including hotels and restaurants where salary may consist solely of tips and food.

Article 685
Article 685 is a legal provision outlining the obligations of the worker, including performing work personally with reasonable care and obeying the employer's orders related to the agreed work provided such orders do not violate the contract, law, or public morals.

Concessionaire of Public Utility Service
The Concessionaire of Public Utility Service is the entity that operates a public utility service, potentially enjoying a de jure or de facto monopoly, and is bound to observe equality among consumers, apply legally prescribed rates, rectify rate irregularities, and may repudiate responsibility for service interruptions caused by force majeure.

Consumer
The Consumer is a customer who receives services from the Concessionaire at rates collected in accordance with the conditions stipulated in the concession contract and applicable laws.<SEP>The Consumer is the user of public utility services who is entitled to strict equality in services and rates, may receive special rate treatment if conditions are met, and must tolerate short service interruptions for maintenance purposes.

Public Authority
The Public Authority is the body that lays down the rates applicable to contracts between the concessionaire and consumers, which have force of law.

Section II: Contracts of Service
Section II: Contracts of Service is a chapter of the legal code containing provisions governing employment relationships, including contract formation, remuneration, duration, and the obligations of workers and employers.

Principle of Equality
The Principle of Equality is a legal doctrine requiring the concessionaire of a public utility to treat all consumers equally in services rendered and rates charged, while permitting general special treatment and prohibiting selective advantages.

Worker
The Worker is a party to a contract of service who undertakes to perform work under the supervision or control of an employer in exchange for remuneration, with obligations including personal performance and obedience to lawful orders.

Employer
The Employer, also referred to as the master, is a party to a contract of service who supervises or controls the worker and undertakes to pay remuneration.

Commercial Representative
The Commercial Representative is an intermediary who works under the orders and supervision of an employer, may be remunerated on a commission basis, and retains the right to commission on orders resulting from their efforts even after leaving service.

Commercial Traveller
The Commercial Traveller is a type of intermediary working under employer supervision, remunerated potentially on commission, with similar post-employment commission rights as the commercial representative.

Canvasser
The Canvasser is an intermediary who works under employer supervision and may be remunerated on a commission basis, to whom contract of service provisions apply.

Strike
A Strike is considered a fortuitous event under Article 673 if the concessionaire proves it occurred without fault and that replacement of strikers or avoidance of consequences was not possible.

Assurance Agent
The Assurance Agent is an intermediary who works under the orders and supervision of a master, to whom contract of service provisions apply even if remunerated on a commission basis or working for multiple employers.

Fortuitous Event
A Fortuitous Event is an unforeseen occurrence within the operation of a public utility service that could not have been anticipated or whose consequences could not have been avoided by vigilant management, serving as grounds for the concessionaire to repudiate responsibility for abnormal service interruptions.

Fair Competition
Fair Competition is the natural competitive balance between parties that must not be disturbed by discriminatory practices of the concessionaire, as referenced in Article 670.

Special Laws Relating to Service
Special Laws Relating to Service are legislative enactments that take precedence over the general provisions of Section II on Contracts of Service and define the categories of workers to which those provisions do not apply.

Contract Of Pledge
A possessory pledge that secures not only the capital of the debt but also, in the same rank, necessary preservation expenses, compensation for defect losses, contract and inscription costs, enforcement costs, and accrued interest, as defined under Article 1111.

Extinguishment Of A Pledge
The termination of pledge rights, occurring upon extinguishment of the secured debt, renunciation by the pledgee, union of pledge and ownership rights in one person, or loss or extinguishment of the pledged thing or right, as governed by Articles 1112 and 1113.

Pledge Of An Immovable
A type of pledge (antichresis) involving immovable property, requiring both delivery of the pledged immovable to the pledgee and inscription of the contract for validity against third parties, governed by Articles 1114–1116.

Pledge Of A Movable
A type of pledge involving movable property, requiring a written contract with an established date adequately setting out the secured debt amount and pledged object for validity against third parties, governed by Articles 1117–1122.

Good Faith
Good Faith is a foundational legal principle requiring that parties act honestly, fairly, and without fraud in their legal dealings. At its core, it binds contracting parties not only to the express terms of their agreements but also to everything deemed a necessary sequel according to law, usage, and equity. Good faith operates as both a general standard of conduct and a specific legal state of mind applied across a wide range of civil law contexts.

In the realm of contractual obligations, good faith governs the performance of contracts and the handling of mistakes. A party who has committed a mistake cannot exploit it in a manner contrary to good faith, and the mistaken party remains bound by the intended contract if the other party is prepared to perform it. Good faith also serves as a legal condition enabling creditors and particular successors in title to avail themselves of a hidden contract or to establish the simulation of a contract by which they were prejudiced.

In property and possession law, good faith describes an honest belief in the legitimacy of one's possession at the time of acquisition. A possessor acting in good faith is one who is unaware of infringing upon another's right, and this state is always presumed by law. Good faith possession serves as a basis for acquiring ownership and fruits, limits liability for loss or deterioration, and affects the duration required for acquisitive prescription. Among multiple lessees competing for the same property, a lessee who in good faith transcribes a lease before another takes possession obtains preference. Good faith is also evaluated by courts when resolving disputes over mingled movables in accordance with the rules of equity.

Good faith extends significant protections to third parties and creditors. A third party who acquires a real right on an immovable in good faith is shielded from the supplement of price action. Similarly, a purchaser who acknowledges or compromises with a third party's claim while acting in good faith preserves warranty rights. In mortgage law, a mortgage constituted by an owner whose title is later annulled, resiliated, or abolished remains valid in favor of a mortgagee creditor who acted in good faith at the time of the mortgage's conclusion. Good faith also protects third parties acquiring rights during the interval between the extinguishment and revival of a mortgage, and is a required state of honest belief for a creditor seeking a judgment charge over immovable property.

In the context of unjust enrichment and payment, a good faith recipient of undue payment is bound only to return what was actually received, reflecting the law's recognition that honest conduct should limit the scope of restitutionary liability.

Pledge Of Debts
A type of pledge involving debt instruments, requiring notification to or acceptance by the debtor for validity, and possession of the debt title by the pledgee for validity against third parties, governed by Articles 1123–1129.

Privileged Rights
Priority rights established by law for certain claims, introduced as Chapter IV of the legal code, granting a first-ranking priority to specified rights.

Article 1111
A legal provision stating that a contract of pledge secures not only the capital debt but also necessary preservation expenses, compensation for defect losses, contract and inscription costs, enforcement costs, and accrued interest subject to Article 230.

Article 1112
A legal provision stating that a right of pledge is extinguished upon extinguishment of the secured debt and is revived if the cause of extinguishment disappears, without prejudice to third-party rights acquired in good faith during the interval.

Article 1113
A legal provision enumerating causes of pledge extinguishment: renunciation by the pledgee with legal capacity, union of pledge and ownership rights in one person, and loss of the pledged thing or extinguishment of the pledged right.

Article 1114
A legal provision requiring inscription of the pledge contract, in addition to delivery of the immovable, for a pledge of an immovable to be valid against third parties, applying the mortgage inscription rules.

Article 1115
A legal provision permitting a pledgee of an immovable to lease it to the pledgor while maintaining validity against third parties, with inscription or marginal notation requirements depending on when the lease is agreed.

Article 1116
A legal provision obliging the pledgee of an immovable to maintain it, pay necessary preservation expenses, annual taxes, and charges, with the right to deduct these from collected fruits; the pledgee may abandon the pledge to free himself of these obligations.

Article 1117
A legal provision requiring a written contract with an established date, adequately specifying the secured debt amount and pledged object, for a pledge of a movable to be valid against third parties, with creditor rank fixed by the established date.

Article 1118
A legal provision applying the possession rules of material movables and bearer securities to pledges of movables, protecting good faith pledgees even if the pledgor lacked disposal authority, and protecting good faith third-party holders.

Article 1120
A legal provision permitting the pledgor to apply to the Judge for authorization to sell the pledged thing at an advantageous price even before debt maturity, with the Judge fixing sale conditions and ordering deposit of the price.

Article 1121
Article 1121 is a legal provision referenced in Article 1129 that governs the sale or allocation of a pledged debt to the pledgee.<SEP>A legal provision granting the unpaid pledgee the right to apply to the Judge for authority to sell the pledged thing by public auction or at market value, or to appropriate it in payment of the debt at a value estimated by experts.

Article 1122
A legal provision stating that the preceding pledge provisions apply unless incompatible with commercial laws, provisions relating to authorized lending institutions, or special laws and regulations governing pledge of movables.

Article 1123
A legal provision requiring notification to or acceptance by the debtor for validity of a debt pledge, and possession of the debt title by the pledgee for validity against third parties, with pledge rank fixed by the date of notification or acceptance, as provided for in Article 305.

Article 1124
A legal provision allowing nominative bonds and bonds payable to order to be pledged through the special transfer procedure prescribed by law, provided the transfer is stated to be by way of pledge, without need for notification.

Article 1125
A legal provision prohibiting the pledge of debts that cannot be assigned or attached.

Article 1126
A legal provision granting the pledgee the right to collect interest and periodic payments on pledged debts, offsetting collected amounts first against expenses, then interest, then capital, and obliging the pledgee to protect the pledged debt and promptly inform the pledgor of collections.

Article 1127
A legal provision allowing the debtor of a pledged debt to raise against the pledgee defenses regarding the validity of the secured debt and defenses against the original creditor, to the same extent as in cases of debt assignment.

Article 1128
A legal provision requiring the debtor of a prematurely due pledged debt to discharge it to both pledgee and pledgor jointly, with the pledge transferring to the deposited amount, and obliging both to cooperate on investment and creation of a new pledge in favor of the pledgee.

Article 1129
Article 1129 establishes that if the pledged debt and the secured debt fall due, the unpaid pledgee may collect the pledged debt, demand its sale, or request its allocation in accordance with Article 1121, paragraph 2.<SEP>A legal provision permitting the unpaid pledgee, when both the pledged debt and secured debt fall due, to collect from the pledged debt up to the amount owed, or demand its sale or allocation in accordance with Article 1121 paragraph 2.

Article 305
A referenced legal provision governing notification or acceptance procedures for debt pledges, cited in Article 1123.

Section IV
A section titled "Certain Kinds of Pledge" covering pledges of immovables (antichresis), movables, and debts, encompassing Articles 1114–1129.

Secured Debt
The debt guaranteed by a contract of pledge, whose extinguishment causes the pledge to be extinguished and whose revival revives the pledge, referenced throughout Articles 1111–1129.

Third Parties In Good Faith
Persons who acquire rights legally and in good faith over pledged property, whose rights are protected during the interval between extinguishment and revival of a pledge, or through possession of movables, as stated in Articles 1112, 1113, and 1118.

Debtor Of A Pledged Debt
The original debtor of a debt that has been given in pledge, who may raise defenses against the pledgee, must discharge the debt jointly to the pledgee and pledgor if it falls due prematurely, and may be notified of the pledge as per Articles 1127 and 1128.

Nominative Bonds
Registered bonds that may be pledged in accordance with the special legal procedure prescribed for their transfer, provided the transfer is stated to be by way of pledge, as stated in Article 1124.

Bonds Payable To Order
Order bonds that may be pledged through the special legal transfer procedure, provided the transfer is stated to be by way of pledge, without need for notification, as stated in Article 1124.

Bearer Securities
Securities held by the bearer, whose possession rules apply to the pledge of movables, referenced in Article 1118.

Material Movables
Tangible movable property whose possession rules apply to the pledge of movables, referenced in Article 1118.

data.entity_name: Institutions Authorized To Lend Money On Pledge
data.content:
Institutions Authorized To Lend Money On Pledge
Lending institutions authorized by law to accept pledges, whose special provisions take precedence over general pledge provisions as stated in Article 1122.

Pledged Thing
The property (movable, immovable, or debt instrument) given as security under a contract of pledge, subject to preservation, inscription, and enforcement rules throughout the articles.

Warranty Against Dispossession
Warranty Against Dispossession is a legal guarantee obligating the vendor to protect the purchaser against loss of ownership of the thing sold to a person with superior legal title. It may be increased, restricted, or abolished by special agreement between the contracting parties, but any clause restricting it is void if the vendor fraudulently conceals the rights of a third party.

Total Dispossession
Total Dispossession is the complete loss of the thing sold to a person legally entitled to it, entitling the purchaser to claim the value of the thing at the time of dispossession, legal interest, the value of restored profits, useful and superfluous expenditures, litigation costs, and general compensation for losses and missed profits.

Partial Dispossession
Partial Dispossession is the partial loss or encumbrance of the thing sold, where the purchaser may claim the same remedies as total dispossession if the loss is severe enough that the purchaser would not have entered the contract, provided the thing sold and its profits are returned; otherwise, the purchaser may only claim compensation for the loss sustained.

The Thing Sold
The Thing Sold is the object or property that is the subject of the sale contract between the vendor and the purchaser. It must possess the qualities guaranteed by the vendor and be free of defects diminishing its value or usefulness at the time of delivery.

Judicial Sale
Judicial Sale is a sale conducted through a judicial process in which no warranty against defects applies to the thing sold.

Administrative Sale by Auction
Administrative Sale by Auction is a sale conducted through an administrative auction process in which no warranty against defects applies to the thing sold.

Fraudulent Concealment
Fraudulent Concealment is the intentional and fraudulent hiding of defects in the thing sold or of the rights of a third party by the vendor, which renders void any clause excluding or restricting the warranty and prevents the vendor from invoking the prescription period.

Legal Interest
Legal Interest is the statutory interest accruing on amounts owed by the vendor to the purchaser, such as the value of the thing sold at the time of dispossession or the refund of the price paid, calculated from the time of dispossession or from the date of formal summons.

Article 443
Article 443 is a legal provision setting forth the claims available to the purchaser in case of total dispossession, including the value of the thing sold, legal interest, value of restored profits, useful and superfluous expenses, litigation costs, and general compensation.

Article 444
Article 444 is a legal provision governing the purchaser's remedies in case of partial dispossession or encumbrance of the thing sold, allowing full claims under Article 443 if the loss is severe, or limited compensation otherwise.

Article 447
Article 447 is a legal provision defining the vendor's warranty liability for defects in the thing sold that diminish its value or usefulness, holding the vendor liable even for unknown defects but excluding defects known or discoverable by the purchaser through reasonable inspection.

Article 459
Article 459 is a legal provision establishing the vendor's right of retention, allowing the vendor to withhold the thing sold until payment of the price, and extending this right when the purchaser loses the benefit of the payment term under Article 273.

Article 273
Article 273 is a referenced legal provision regarding the loss of the benefit of the payment term by the purchaser, referenced in Article 459 as a condition for the vendor's extended right of retention.

Article 445
Article 445 is a legal provision allowing the contracting parties to increase, restrict, or abolish the warranty against dispossession by special agreement. It presumes the vendor stipulated no warranty against an apparent or disclosed servitude, and renders void any clause restricting warranty if the vendor intentionally conceals the rights of a third party.

Article 446
Article 446 is a legal provision establishing that, notwithstanding a clause excluding warranty, the vendor remains liable for any dispossession resulting from the vendor's own acts, and any contrary agreement is void. The vendor must also refund the value of the thing sold if dispossession results from a third party's act, unless the purchaser knew the grounds or purchased at own risk.

Article 448
Article 448 is a legal provision exempting the vendor from liability for defects that are customarily tolerated.

Article 449
Article 449 is a legal provision requiring the purchaser to inspect the thing sold upon delivery and give notice of any covered defect to the vendor within a reasonable time, failing which the purchaser is deemed to have accepted the thing sold. For hidden defects, notice must be given immediately upon discovery.

Article 450
Article 450 is a legal provision entitling the purchaser to bring a warranty action in accordance with Article 444 when timely notice of a defect has been given to the vendor.

Article 451
Article 451 is a legal provision confirming that a warranty action exists even if the thing sold has perished, regardless of the cause of destruction.

Article 452
Article 452 is a legal provision prescribing a one-year limitation period for warranty actions from the time of delivery, even if the defect is discovered later, unless the vendor agrees to a longer period. The vendor cannot invoke this prescription if fraudulent concealment is proven.

Article 453
Article 453 is a legal provision permitting the contracting parties to increase, restrict, or abolish the warranty by specific agreement, while rendering void any clause abolishing or restricting the warranty if the vendor intentionally and fraudulently conceals defects.

Article 455
Article 455 is a legal provision governing the vendor's warranty of proper working for an agreed period, requiring the purchaser to notify the vendor of a defect within one month of its appearance and to commence an action within six months of notification, on pain of forfeiture of warranty rights.

Article 456
Article 456 is a legal provision stating that, subject to contrary agreement or custom, the price is payable at the place of delivery, and if not payable at delivery, payment must be made at the purchaser's domicile on the due date.

Article 457
Article 457 is a legal provision establishing that the price is payable at the time of delivery and granting the purchaser the right to retain the price when disturbed by a third party or threatened with dispossession, while allowing the vendor to demand payment upon supplying security. It also applies when the purchaser discovers a defect.

Article 458
Article 458 is a legal provision stating that the vendor is not entitled to legal interest on the price unless the purchaser has been placed in default by formal summons or the thing sold is productive of fruits and has been delivered. The purchaser acquires revenues and increases of the thing sold and bears its charges from the time of sale.

Article 460
Article 460 is a legal provision assigning the risk of loss of the thing sold to the purchaser while the vendor exercises the right of retention, unless the loss results from an act of the vendor.

Article 461
Article 461 is a legal provision establishing that in the sale of commodities or movable effects with an agreed payment term, the sale is automatically dissolved without summons if the price is not paid on the due date, at the vendor's option and subject to contrary agreement.

Article 462
Article 462 is a legal provision assigning the costs of the deed of sale, stamp duties, transcription fees, and all other expenses to the purchaser in the absence of contrary agreement or usage.

Judge
The Judge (القاضي) is a judicial authority and officer vested with broad discretionary powers across numerous areas of civil law. As the primary judicial decision-maker, the Judge is responsible for deciding cases using various sources of law and determining the applicable law in matters involving persons of unknown or plural nationality.

In procedural and prescription matters, the Judge may not invoke prescription on his own initiative but may direct oaths in one-year prescription cases and presides over all legal proceedings related to prescription. The Judge also has authority to grant extensions of time, such as allowing administrators additional time to file inventory statements when justified by circumstances.

In the realm of contractual and obligations law, the Judge plays a central role. The Judge may grant additional time to debtors, reject rescission applications for minor breaches, and assess damages in light of prevailing circumstances while determining the appropriate method of compensation. The Judge is empowered to reduce excessively onerous contractual obligations arising from exceptional and unpredictable events, modify leonine conditions in contracts of adhesion, and reduce obligations to reasonable limits. Under Article 224, the Judge may also reduce the amount of damages agreed upon between contracting parties. Furthermore, the Judge fixes reasonable times for the term of obligations, determines the object of obligations when parties fail to elect, and adjudicates matters related to insolvency and conditional obligations.

Regarding damages, penalties, and natural obligations, the Judge determines the existence of natural obligations in the absence of legal provisions, orders specific performance, fixes damages, and authorizes enforcement actions. The Judge may increase penalties or reduce damages based on circumstances, including reducing damages for a voluntary agent's mistakes when justified. In cases of dispossession where the donor intentionally concealed the cause, the Judge may award equitable compensation to the donee.

In partnership and corporate matters, the Judge evaluates the seriousness of reasons for dissolution, appoints liquidators when partners cannot agree, and authorizes a partner's retirement from a partnership. The Judge also oversees wakf (waqf) property matters, specifically authorizing leases exceeding three years and supervising the Nazir's leasing activities, with the Nazir required to obtain the Judge's permission for such long-term leases.

The Judge exercises authority over judicial custody, appointing receivers, reducing excessive betting stakes, and making decisions regarding the termination and administration of custody arrangements. In employment and remuneration matters, the Judge fixes salaries in accordance with equity when no applicable rates or customs exist, determines the nature and extent of work to be performed, and may designate a trustworthy person to receive information necessary to verify the accuracy of a master's profit-sharing account on behalf of a worker.

In property and structural matters, the Judge is empowered under Article 962 to order the suspension or continuance of threatening works and to require adequate guarantees. Under Articles 859 and 860, the Judge may order the sale of a lower storey, order the execution of urgent repairs, and enforce structural obligations between storey owners. The Judge also determines the method of repayment of expenses in usufruct arrangements, may order the removal of property from a usufructuary, and may declare the extinction of a usufruct. In mortgage matters, the Judge fixes the portion of property to which a mortgage is transferred after partition and may order the cessation of acts that could result in loss or deterioration of mortgaged property. Additionally, under Article 1000, the Judge may be delegated by the President of the Court to draw up a hekr deed.

Action of Revendication
Action of Revendication is a legal action brought to recover ownership of the thing sold, the costs of which the purchaser may claim from the vendor under Article 443, provided the vendor was notified of the action in accordance with Article 440.

Dissolution of Sale
Dissolution of Sale is a legal remedy that terminates the sale contract, mentioned in Articles 443 and 461 as an alternative basis for the purchaser's action against the vendor, and as the automatic consequence of non-payment in commodity sales.

Annulment of Sale
Annulment of Sale is a legal remedy that voids the sale contract, mentioned in Article 443 as an alternative basis for the purchaser's action against the vendor, distinct from warranty claims for dispossession.

Proper Working Warranty
Proper Working Warranty is a specific type of warranty under Article 455 whereby the vendor guarantees the functionality of the thing sold for a specified period, subject to the purchaser's obligation to notify defects within one month and commence an action within six months of notification.

Notice of Defect
Notice of Defect is the purchaser's obligation under Articles 449 and 455 to inform the vendor of any defect discovered in the thing sold within a reasonable time or within one month, respectively, failing which the purchaser is deemed to have accepted the thing sold and forfeits warranty rights.

Commodities and Movable Effects
Commodities and Movable Effects are categories of movable property the sale of which is subject to automatic dissolution without summons if the price is not paid on the due date, as provided under Article 461.

Founder (Waqif)
The Founder is the person who established the wakf and may, if serving as Nazir, lease wakf property for more than three years without the judge's authority.

Sole Beneficiary
The sole beneficiary is the single person entitled to the benefits of the wakf, who may also serve as Nazir with the privilege of leasing wakf property beyond three years without judicial authorization.

Loan for Use (Ariyah)
A loan for use is a contract by which the lender undertakes to hand over to the borrower, without valuable consideration, a non-consumable thing for use during a specific time or for a specific purpose, to be restituted after use.

Lender (Mu'ir)
The lender is the party in a loan for use who delivers a non-consumable thing to the borrower and must reimburse necessary preservation expenses, but does not generally warrant against dispossession or hidden defects unless agreed or deliberately concealed.

Borrower (Musta'ir)
The borrower is the party in a loan for use who receives a non-consumable thing, must use it according to the contract or its nature, bears normal maintenance expenses, and must restitute the thing after use with due care.

Contract for Work (Muqawalah)
A contract for work is an agreement where one contracting party undertakes to perform a piece of work or service in consideration for remuneration which the other party undertakes to pay.

Contractor (Muqawil)
The contractor is the party who undertakes to perform work or a service, may supply materials or labor alone, and is responsible for the quality of materials and proper execution of the work.

Master of the Work (Rabb al-Amal)
The master of the work is the party who commissions the work, pays the remuneration, may supply materials, and is entitled to receive the completed work.

Architect (Muhandis Mi'mari)
The architect is a professional who prepares building plans and may supervise their execution, bearing joint and several liability with the contractor for ten years for structural defects, or limited liability for defects in plans alone if not supervising execution.

Subcontractor
The subcontractor is a contractor working under the main contractor, against whom the main contractor may have rights of recourse as stated in Article 651.

Article 634
Article 634 provides that general lease provisions apply to wakf leases insofar as they are not incompatible with the preceding special wakf rules.

Article 635
Article 635 defines a loan for use as a contract for gratuitous lending of a non-consumable thing for a specific time or purpose.

Article 636
Article 636 obligates the lender to deliver the thing lent in its condition at the time of contract conclusion and to leave the borrower in possession during the loan period.

Article 637
Article 637 requires the lender to reimburse the borrower for necessary preservation expenses, while useful expenses follow the rules for bad-faith possessors.

Article 638
Article 638 limits the lender's liability for dispossession and hidden defects unless the lender deliberately concealed them or gave an express warranty.

Article 639
Article 639 restricts the borrower to using the thing lent only in the manner prescribed by contract, nature, or custom, and prohibits assigning use to third parties without the lender's authority.

Article 640
Article 640 provides that the borrower bears normal maintenance expenses without right of refund, and may remove additions made to the thing lent if restored to original condition.

Article 641
Article 641 requires the borrower to exercise the same care as for personal property but not less than a reasonable person, and holds the borrower liable for loss even from fortuitous events if personal property was preferentially saved.

Article 642
Article 642 requires the borrower to restitute the thing lent at the end of the loan in its current state at the place it was received, absent contrary agreement.

Article 643
Article 643 governs termination of the loan for use upon expiration of the agreed term, completion of purpose, or at the lender's demand if no term is fixed, and permits early restitution by the borrower unless prejudicial to the lender.

Article 644
Article 644 allows the lender to terminate the loan for use at any time if the lender has an urgent unforeseen need, the borrower misuses the thing, or the borrower becomes insolvent.

Article 645
Article 645 provides that a loan for use ends with the death of the borrower unless otherwise agreed.

Article 646
Article 646 defines a contract for work as one party's undertaking to perform work or service for remuneration to be paid by the other party.

Article 647
Article 647 allows the contractor to supply labor only or both labor and materials, with the master responsible for materials in the former case.

Article 648
Article 648 makes the contractor responsible for and warrants the good quality of materials when the contractor supplies them.

Article 649
Article 649 requires the contractor to care for master-supplied materials, use them with technical skill, account for their use, and refund the value of materials rendered unfit due to neglect or lack of skill.

Article 650
Article 650 allows the master to demand resiliation of the contract or assign the work to another contractor at the first contractor's cost if defective performance is not corrected within a reasonable period, or immediately if correction is impossible.

Article 651
Article 651 imposes joint and several liability on the architect and contractor for ten years for total or partial demolition of constructions or permanent works, including defects endangering solidity, running from the date of delivery.

Article 652
Article 652 limits the architect's liability to defects resulting from plans when the architect only prepares plans without supervising execution.

Article 653
Article 653 renders void any clause seeking to exclude or restrict the warranty of the architect and the contractor.

Article 654
Article 654 prescribes warranty actions after three years from the date of destruction or discovery of defects.

Article 209
Article 209 is a referenced legal provision governing the handing over of works to a replacement contractor at the original contractor's cost.

Three-Year Lease Limit
The three-year lease limit is the maximum duration for which the Nazir may lease wakf property without judicial authorization, applicable even to successive contracts.

Ten-Year Warranty (Decennial Liability)
The ten-year warranty is the period during which the architect and contractor are jointly and severally liable for total or partial demolition of constructions and defects endangering solidity, running from delivery of the works.

Section II: Loan for Use
Section II covers the legal provisions governing loans for use, including obligations of the lender and borrower, and termination rules, spanning Articles 635 through 645.

Section I: Contracts for Work
Section I covers contracts for work and concessions of public utility services, including obligations of the contractor and master, spanning Articles 646 through 654.

data.entity_name: Chapter III: Contracts for the Hire of Services
data.content:
Chapter III: Contracts for the Hire of Services
Chapter III is the legal chapter covering contracts for the hire of services, including contracts for work and concessions of public utility services.

Article 655
Article 655 provides that once the contractor has completed the work and placed it at the disposal of the master, the master must take delivery of it as soon as possible in accordance with customary practice. If the master refuses without lawful cause to take delivery despite being summoned by formal notice, the work is deemed to have been delivered to the master.

Will (الوصية)
A legal instrument for transferring property upon death, governed by Mohammedan Law and specific legislation, as established in Articles 915–917 of the civil code.

Testator (الموصى)
A person who makes a testamentary disposition or will; the division made by the testator becomes irrevocable upon the testator's death.

Heirs (الورثة)
Persons entitled to inherit from a deceased person's estate under the rules of inheritance, including contingent heirs who may predecease the deceased.

Estate (التركة)
The total property and obligations left by a deceased person, subject to division, debts, and winding-up procedures.

Mohammedan Law (الشريعة الإسلامية)
The Islamic legal system that governs wills alongside statutory laws on wills, as referenced in Article 915.

Division by Disposition (Mortis Causa)
A method of dividing property that takes effect upon death, which may always be revoked during the testator's lifetime and becomes irrevocable upon death, as governed by Articles 909–913.

Rules of Inheritance (قواعد الميراث)
The legal rules determining how property not included in a division devolves in common upon heirs.

Accession (الالتصاق)
A legal mechanism for acquiring property through natural or artificial attachment, covering both immovable and movable property as addressed in Articles 918–931.

Accession to Immovable Property (الالتصاق بالعقار)
Rules governing ownership of buildings, plantations, alluvium, and other works on land, including rights and obligations of land owners and third parties.

Accession to Movable Property (الالتصاق بالمنقول)
Rules governing ownership when movable properties belonging to different owners become mingled and cannot be separated without deterioration.

Alluvium
Land formed gradually and imperceptibly by a river through sediment deposits, belonging to riparian owners under Article 918.

River
A natural watercourse that creates alluvium for riparian owners and may displace or uncover land and form islands in its channel.

Sea
A body of water that may cover or uncover land; land uncovered by the sea belongs to the State under Article 919.

Lake and Pond (البحيرات والبرك)
Bodies of still water whose adjoining land owners do not acquire ownership of land uncovered by the retreat of these waters under Article 920.

Creditors of the Estate (دائنو التركة)
Persons to whom the estate owes debts; unsecured creditors may take action on alienated immovable property of the estate if their claims are recorded in accordance with the law.

Third Party (أجنبي)
A person other than the land owner who may carry out works or constructions on land belonging to another, with varying rights depending on good faith and consent.

Land Owner (مالك الأرض)
The owner of land who holds presumptive ownership of buildings, plantations, and works above or below the ground, and has specific rights and obligations regarding constructions by third parties.

Court (المحكمة)
The judicial body that resolves disputes related to accession, mingled movables, and encroachment, deciding matters according to rules of equity.

Contract (العقد)
A method of acquiring ownership and other real rights in movable and immovable property, as referenced in Article 932.

Article 909
A legal provision stating that division by disposition (mortis causa) may always be revoked and becomes irrevocable on the death of the testator.

Article 910
A legal provision stating that property not included in a division devolves in common on the heirs in accordance with the rules of inheritance.

Article 911
A legal provision stating that if a contingent heir predeceases the deceased, the divided part allotted to that heir devolves in common on the other heirs.

Article 912
A legal provision stating that general rules of division, except those relating to lesion, apply to division by disposition (mortis causa).

Article 913
A legal provision allowing any heir to call for a division of the estate in accordance with Article 895 when estate debts are not included or creditors do not agree.

Article 914
A legal provision granting unsecured creditors the right to take action on alienated or charged immovable property of the estate if their claims are recorded by law.

Article 915
A legal provision stating that wills are governed by Mohammedan Law and laws on wills.

Article 916
A legal provision deeming legal dispositions made during a terminal illness with the object of making a gift as testamentary dispositions governed by rules applicable to wills.

Article 917
A legal provision deeming a disposition to an heir as testamentary when the disposer retains possession and enjoyment of the property during his lifetime.

Article 922
A legal provision establishing the presumption that all buildings, plantations, and works on land were carried out by the land owner at the owner's expense.

Article 923
A legal provision stating that constructions made with another's materials become the land owner's property if removal would cause serious damage or if recovery proceedings are not commenced within one year.

Article 924
A legal provision granting the land owner the right to demand removal or retention of works erected by a third party who knew the land was not theirs.

Article 925
A legal provision addressing works carried out by a third party in good faith, limiting the land owner's remedies to payment of value or increased land value.

Article 928
A legal provision allowing a court to compel an adjoining land owner to transfer ownership of encroached land to a neighbor who built in good faith.

Article 931
A legal provision stating that when two movables of different owners are mingled inseparably, the court decides the matter according to rules of equity.

Article 932
A legal provision stating that ownership and other real rights in movable and immovable property transfer by contract.

Illness Immediately Preceding Death (مرض الموت)
A terminal illness during which any legal disposition made with the object of gifting is deemed a testamentary disposition governed by the rules applicable to wills, as established in Article 916.

Good Faith (حسن النية)
A legal principle affecting the rights and remedies available to land owners and third parties in construction and accession disputes, referenced in Articles 925, 928, and 931.

Riparian Owners (الملاك المجاورين)
Owners of land adjoining a river who acquire ownership of alluvium formed gradually and imperceptibly by the river under Article 918.

Islands (الجزر)
Land formations created in a river's channel whose ownership is regulated by special laws under Article 921.

Light Constructions (المنشآت الصغيرة)
Temporary structures such as sheds, shops, and shelters erected on another's land without the intention of permanent maintenance, which remain the property of the person who erected them under Article 929.

data.entity_name: Laws on Wills (القوانين الصادرة في شأنها)
data.content:
Laws on Wills (القوانين الصادرة في شأنها)
Statutory legislation governing wills alongside Mohammedan Law, as referenced in Article 915.

Debts of the Estate (ديون التركة)
Financial obligations of a deceased person's estate that must be addressed during division; if not included in the division or if creditors do not agree, any heir may call for a new division under Article 913.

Materials (المواد)
Building materials belonging to a person other than the land owner, used in constructions on the land, whose ownership and recovery rights are governed by Articles 923 and 930.

data.entity_name: Buildings, Plantations, and Works (بناء أو غراس أو منشآت)
data.content:
Buildings, Plantations, and Works (بناء أو غراس أو منشآت)
Constructions, plantations, and other structures existing above or below ground, presumed to have been carried out by the land owner at the owner's expense under Article 922.

Article 918
A legal provision stating that alluvium formed gradually and imperceptibly by a river belongs to the riparian owners.

Article 919
A legal provision stating that land uncovered by the sea belongs to the State and no one may encroach upon the sea shore except to restore covered property boundaries.

Article 920
A legal provision stating that owners of lands adjoining still waters such as lakes and ponds do not acquire ownership of uncovered land nor lose ownership of overflowed land.

Article 921
A legal provision stating that ownership of land displaced or uncovered by a river and of islands formed in its channel is regulated by special laws.

Article 926
A legal provision stating that when a third party carries out works with permission of the land owner, the land owner cannot demand removal and must pay one of two prescribed amounts.

Article 927
A legal provision referring to Article 982 for the payment of compensation addressed in Articles 924, 925, and 926.

Article 929
A legal provision stating that light constructions such as sheds, shops, and shelters erected on another's land without permanent intent belong to the person who erected them.

Article 930
A legal provision stating that when a third party carries out works with another's materials, the material owner cannot claim restitution but may seek compensation from both the third party and the land owner.

Article 895
A legal provision referenced in Article 913 as the basis for division of an estate when debts are unresolved or creditors do not agree.

Article 982
A legal provision referenced in Article 927 governing the payment of compensation for works addressed in the accession provisions.

Egyptian Nationality
Egyptian nationality is a legal status governed by a special law, determining who is considered a national of Egypt.

Legal Personality
Legal personality commences from the time a child is born alive and ends at death. The law also determines the rights of a child en ventre de sa mere.

Domicile
A domicile is the place where a person habitually resides. A person may have more than one domicile at the same time or may have none.

Moslem Law
Moslem law (Islamic law) is applied to cases involving missing persons and absent persons in the absence of special laws.

Consumable Things
Consumable things are those whose utility consists in their consumption or disposal by reason of their destined use, including things destined for sale in commercial establishments.<SEP>Consumable things are those whose utility, by reason of their destined use, consists in their consumption or disposal. All things destined for sale in commercial establishments are deemed consumable.<SEP>Items that are consumed through use, which a usufructuary who has provided security may use provided they are replaced upon termination of the usufruct.

Fungibles
Fungibles are things that can be replaced by one another in payment and are customarily estimated in trade by number, measure, volume, or weight.<SEP>Fungibles are things which can be replaced one by another in payment and which are customarily estimated in trade by number, measure, volume or weight.

Wakfs
Wakfs are recognized as one of the categories of juristic persons under the Egyptian Civil Code.

Missing Person
A missing person is subject to provisions contained in special laws, or in the absence of such laws, Moslem law. The domicile of a missing person is the domicile of the legal representative.

Absent Person
An absent person is subject to provisions contained in special laws, or in the absence of such laws, Moslem law. The domicile of an absent person is the domicile of the legal representative.

Birth And Death Registers
Birth and death registers are official records used to establish birth and death, regulated by a special law.

Family
The family of a person is composed of relatives. Persons having a common ascendant are deemed to be relatives.

Direct Lineal Relationship
Direct lineal relationship is the relationship existing between ascendants and descendants, calculated by ascending to the common ancestor and counting each relative excluding the common ancestor.

Collateral Relationship
Collateral relationship is the relationship existing between persons who have a common ascendant without one of them being a descendant of the other, calculated by ascending from one descendant to the common ancestor then descending to the other.

Special Domicile
A special domicile may be elected for the performance of a specific legal act, and the election must be evidenced by writing.

Natural Guardianship
Natural guardianship is one of the legal regimes governing persons deprived of full or partial legal capacity, subject to conditions and rules laid down by law.

Legal Guardianship
Legal guardianship is one of the legal regimes governing persons deprived of full or partial legal capacity, subject to conditions and rules laid down by law.

Curatorship
Curatorship is a legal regime governing persons deprived of full or partial legal capacity, subject to conditions and rules laid down by law.

Religious Groups And Communities
Religious groups and communities that the state has recognized are classified as juristic persons under Egyptian law.

Commercial And Civil Corporations
Commercial and civil corporations are recognized as juristic persons under the Egyptian Civil Code.

Associations And Foundations
Associations and foundations created in accordance with the provisions of the Egyptian Civil Code are classified as juristic persons.

First Name And Family Name
Every person must have a first name and a family name, and the family name of a person is bestowed upon his children. Acquisition and change of family name are governed by special legislation.

Personal Liberty
Personal liberty is a fundamental right that no person can renounce, as established in Article 49.

Personality Rights
Personality rights are rights inherent in a person's personality. A person whose personality rights have been unlawfully infringed shall have the right to demand cessation of the infringement and compensation for any damage sustained.

Name Rights
Name rights protect a person whose right to the use of his name is unlawfully disputed or whose name is unlawfully used by another, entitling that person to demand cessation and compensation.

Trade Or Profession Domicile
The place where a person exercises a trade or profession is considered as his domicile as regards matters carried on in connection with such trade or profession, as stated in Article 41.

Person Under Legal Disability
A person under legal disability is a category alongside minors, missing persons, and absent persons whose domicile is the domicile of the legal representative. A person in a similar legal position to a minor who has attained eighteen years shall have a special domicile for acts the law considers capable of performing.

data.entity_name: Things Outside The Ambit Of Trade
data.content:
Things Outside The Ambit Of Trade
Things outside the ambit of trade by their very nature are things that cannot be objects of exclusive possession. Things outside the ambit of trade by law are things which cannot be objects of proprietary rights, as stated in Article 81.

Rights In Non-Material Things
Rights in respect of non-material things are regulated by special laws, as stated in Article 86.

Provinces (Mudirias)
Provinces (mudirias) are administrative divisions of the state recognized as juristic persons under Egyptian law, along with towns and villages, in accordance with conditions fixed by law.

Proprietary Rights
Proprietary rights are rights over things that may be the object of such rights, provided the things are not outside the ambit of trade by their nature or by virtue of law.

Pledged Debt
The Pledged Debt is a debt used as security for another debt, which the pledgee may collect, sell, or allocate upon maturity if unpaid, as governed by Article 1129.

Chapter IV: Privileged Rights
Chapter IV of the legal code deals with privileged rights (حقوق الامتياز), comprising general provisions and the classification of different kinds of privileges.

Section I: General Provisions
Section I of Chapter IV covers general provisions governing privileged rights, including the definition, ranking, scope, and enforceability of privileges, as established in Articles 1130 through 1136.

Privileged Right
A Privileged Right (privilege) is a right of preference granted by law to a particular right by reason of its quality, as defined in Article 1130. No right is privileged except by virtue of a provision of the law.

General Privileges
General Privileges are privileged rights that extend to all movable and immovable property of the debtor, as stated in Article 1132. They are not subject to publication and do not give a right of tracing property into the hands of subsequent holders, even over immovables.

Special Privileges
Special Privileges are privileged rights limited to a specific movable or immovable property only, as defined in Article 1132.

State Treasury
The State Treasury (الخزانة العامة) is the government financial entity to which sums are due for taxes, duties, and other dues. Privileges securing sums due to the State Treasury over immovables are not subject to publication and rank prior to any other privilege over immovables or mortgages and prior to general privileges, as established in Articles 1134 and 1139.

Holder in Good Faith
The Holder in Good Faith (حائز حسن النية) is a person who possesses a movable without knowledge of any defect in title. A privilege cannot be set up against a holder in good faith of a movable, as established in Article 1133.

Costs of Legal Proceedings
Costs of Legal Proceedings (المصروفات القضائية) are expenses incurred in the common interest of all creditors for the preservation and sale of the debtor's property. They have the highest-ranking privilege and are payable in priority to any other claim, including privileged or mortgage-secured claims, as established in Article 1138.

Article 1130
Article 1130 defines a privilege as a right of preference granted by law to a particular right by reason of its quality, and states that no right is privileged except by virtue of a provision of the law.

Article 1131
Article 1131 provides that the rank of a privilege is fixed by law, that unranked privileged rights rank after all privileges provided for in the chapter, and that privileged rights of the same rank are paid rateably.

Article 1132
Article 1132 states that general privileges extend to all movable and immovable property of the debtor, while special privileges are limited to a specific movable or immovable.

Article 1133
Article 1133 provides that a privilege cannot be set up against a holder in good faith of a movable, deems the lessor and hotel proprietor as holders for purposes of the article, and allows a creditor to apply for judicial custody of movables if misappropriation is feared.

Article 1134
Article 1134 makes mortgage provisions applicable to privileged rights over immovable property, while providing exceptions for general privileges and State Treasury privileges, which are not subject to publication and rank prior to all other immovable privileges or mortgages.

Article 1135
Article 1135 provides that provisions applying to the loss or deterioration of mortgaged property apply also to privileges.

Article 1136
Article 1136 states that in the absence of a contrary provision, privileges are extinguished in the same way and in accordance with the same rules as a mortgage or a pledge.

Section II: Kinds of Privileges
Section II of Chapter IV enumerates the specific kinds of privileged rights, including general privileges and special privileges over movables, as detailed in Articles 1137 through 1144.

Article 1138
Article 1138 grants a privilege over the price of property for costs of legal proceedings incurred in the common interest of all creditors for preservation and sale, payable in priority to any other claim.

Article 1139
Article 1139 grants a privilege to sums due to the State Treasury for taxes, duties, and other dues, payable out of the proceeds of charged property before all other rights except costs of legal proceedings.

Article 1140
Article 1140 grants a privilege over a movable for expenses incurred for its preservation and necessary repairs, ranking after costs of legal proceedings and sums due to the State Treasury, with inter se ranking in inverse order of dates incurred.

Article 1141
Article 1141 grants a privilege over all of the debtor's property for wages due to servants, clerks, and workmen for the last six months, sums due for food and clothing supplied to the debtor and dependents for the last six months, and alimony due to family members for the last six months.

Article 1142
Article 1142 grants a privilege over the crop for sums disbursed for seeds, manure, fertilizers, insecticides, cultivation, and harvesting, all of the same rank, and a similar privilege over agricultural implements.

Article 1143
Article 1143 grants a lessor's privilege over attachable movables and crops on the leased property for rent and other sums due under the lease, enforceable for two years, with provisions for sub-lessees and removal of goods.

Article 1144
Article 1144 grants a hotel proprietor a privilege over the effects brought by a traveller into the hotel for sums due for accommodation, provisions, and expenses, with the same rank as the lessor's privilege.<SEP>Article 1144 establishes that sums due to hotel proprietors by a traveller for accommodation, food, and expenses are secured by a privilege over the effects brought by the traveller to the hotel or its annexes, and that the hotel proprietor may object to removal of such effects if unpaid.

Article 1137
Article 1137 is a transitional provision stating that, in addition to the privileges established by special provisions of the law, the rights enumerated in the following articles are privileged.

Compensation (Set Off)
Compensation (set off) is a legal mechanism allowing a debtor to extinguish mutual debts with a creditor, provided both debts are for money or fungibles of like nature and quality, are not in dispute, and are due and enforceable.

Release Of Obligation
Release of obligation is a voluntary discharge of a debtor by the creditor, completed upon reaching the debtor's knowledge and subject to the rules governing gifts.

Impossibility Of Performance
Impossibility of performance is a legal ground for extinguishing an obligation when the debtor establishes that performance has become impossible due to causes beyond the debtor's control.

Original Obligation
The original obligation is the pre-existing obligation that is extinguished and replaced by a new obligation through novation, along with its accessories.

New Obligation
The new obligation is the replacement obligation created through novation, which must be free from grounds of nullity and may or may not inherit the securities of the original obligation.

Current Account
A current account is a financial arrangement in which mere entry of a debt does not constitute novation, but fixing and agreeing the balance does.

Promissory Note
A promissory note is a written debt instrument whose subscription in respect of a pre-existing debt does not, by itself, constitute novation.

Article 353
Article 353 provides that novation can only be effected if both the original and new obligations are free from grounds of nullity, and if the original obligation arises from a voidable contract, the new obligation must aim to confirm and replace it.

Article 354
Article 354 states that novation is not presumed and must be expressly agreed or clearly inferred from circumstances, and does not result merely from changes to the date, place, or mode of performance, or from modifications to securities or interest rates.

Article 355
Article 355 provides that mere entry of a debt in current account does not effect novation, but fixing and agreeing the balance does, with special securities maintained unless otherwise agreed.

Article 356
Article 356 establishes that novation extinguishes the original obligation with its accessories and substitutes a new obligation, with securities not transferred unless provided by law, agreement, or the intention of the parties.

Article 357
Article 357 sets out conditions for transferring real securities to the new obligation, differing based on whether novation results from a change of debt, debtor, or creditor, and requires compliance with registration provisions.

Article 358
Article 358 provides that suretyship, whether real, personal, or joint and several, is only transferred to the new obligation with the consent of the sureties and co-debtors.

Article 359
Article 359 defines delegation as occurring when a debtor procures the creditor's acceptance of a third party who undertakes to pay in the debtor's stead, without requiring a prior debt between the debtor and the third party.

Article 360
Article 360 provides that delegation with an agreement to substitute a new obligation constitutes novation by change of debtor, liberating the original debtor provided the new obligation is valid and the new debtor is not insolvent.

Article 361
Article 361 states that the new debtor's obligation towards the creditor is valid even if the obligation towards the original debtor is void or contestable, subject to a right of recourse against the original debtor.

Article 362
Article 362 grants the debtor a right to compensation of mutual debts with the creditor, provided both are for money or fungibles of like nature, are not in dispute, and are due and enforceable.

Article 363
Article 363 allows compensation even when the places of payment differ, but requires the debtor to compensate the creditor for any resulting loss.

Article 364
Article 364 specifies exceptions to compensation, including claims for restitution of unjustly deprived property, deposited or lent items, and rights not liable to attachment.

Article 366
Article 366 allows compensation even after the prescription period has expired, provided the period had not expired when compensation first became possible.

Article 367
Article 367 prohibits compensation to the detriment of rights acquired by third parties, including after seizure of property by a third party.

Article 368
Article 368 provides that a debtor who consented to assignment of debt without reserve cannot set up compensation against the assignee, while a debtor who merely received notification of assignment may still do so.

Article 369
Article 369 provides that a debtor who paid despite having a right to compensation cannot invoke securities to the prejudice of third parties, unless unaware of the right.

Article 370
Article 370 establishes that merger extinguishes the debt when creditor and debtor qualities unite in one person, with revival if the cause disappears retroactively.

Article 371
Article 371 provides that obligations are extinguished by voluntary release of the debtor by the creditor, effective upon the debtor's knowledge and void if refused.

Article 372
Article 372 states that release is subject to the rules governing gifts and requires no special form even for obligations originally conditional on a special form.

Article 373
