Article 373 provides that an obligation is extinguished if the debtor proves performance has become impossible due to causes beyond the debtor's control.

Article 374
Article 374 sets the general term of extinctive prescription at fifteen years, subject to special provisions and exceptions in the law.

Article 375
Article 375 prescribes a five-year prescription period for periodic rights such as rent, interest, revenues, wages, and pensions.

Assignment Of Debt
Assignment of debt is a legal mechanism whereby a creditor transfers the creditor's right to a third party (assignee), with implications for the debtor's right to set up compensation depending on whether the debtor consented without reserve or merely received notification.

Right Of Recourse
Right of recourse is the new debtor's legal right to seek redress against the original debtor when the new debtor's obligation towards the original debtor is void or contestable.

Periodic Rights
Periodic rights are rights payable periodically such as rent for buildings and agricultural land, interest, revenues, wages, and pensions, which are subject to a five-year prescription period.

Non-Material Object
A non-material object is an intangible thing; rights in respect of non-material objects are regulated by special laws.

Public Domain
The public domain consists of immovable and movable property owned by the State or public juristic persons and allocated for purposes of public utility. Such property is not alienable, not liable to seizure, nor subject to acquisition by prescription.

Public Juristic Persons
Public juristic persons are legal entities that may own property allocated for public utility purposes, forming part of the public domain.

Declaration Of Intention
A declaration of intention is an expression of will that may be verbal, written, by signs in general use, or by conduct. It becomes effective when it comes to the knowledge of the person for whom it was intended.

Consent
Consent is a fundamental element of contracts, requiring the exchange of concordant intentions between two parties.

Offer
An offer is a proposal made by an offeror that may be accepted to form a contract. An offeror who fixes a time limit for acceptance is bound to maintain the offer until the expiration of that limit.

Offeror
The offeror is the person who makes an offer in contract formation and is bound to maintain the offer within any specified time limit.

Acceptance
Acceptance is the agreement to an offer. An acceptance that goes beyond, restricts, or modifies the offer is deemed a rejection comprising a new offer.

Contract Of Adhesion
A contract of adhesion is a contract where acceptance is confined to adherence to standard conditions drawn up by the offeror and not subject to discussion.

Earnest Money
Earnest money is a payment made at the time a contract is concluded, indicating that either party may withdraw from the contract. The party who paid and withdraws forfeits the earnest money; the party who received it and withdraws must repay double.

Promise To Contract
A promise to contract is an agreement by which parties promise to enter into a particular contract in the future. It is only binding if all essential points and the time for conclusion are stated, and any legally required form must also be observed.

Mandatory
A mandatory is a representative who acts in accordance with the principal's precise instructions. The principal cannot plead the ignorance of the mandatory of circumstances the principal knew or should have known.

Minor Lacking Discretion
A minor lacking discretion has no legal capacity to dispose of property; all acts in law by such a person are deemed void.<SEP>A minor lacking discretion is a person who has no legal capacity to dispose of property; all such acts in law are deemed void as per Article 110.

Discerning Minor
A discerning minor is a minor with discretion whose purely beneficial financial acts are valid, purely harmful acts are void, and mixed acts are voidable for the benefit of the minor.

Sources Of Obligations
Sources of obligations are the origins from which legal obligations arise, with contracts being identified as one such source as outlined in Chapter I of Book I on obligations generally.

Personal Rights
Personal rights, also referred to as obligations, are rights arising from legal relationships between persons, forming the subject of the First Part of the civil law text.

Public Utility
Public utility is the purpose for which immovable and movable property owned by the State or public juristic persons is allocated, thereby making such property part of the public domain. Cessation of allocation for public utility causes the property to lose its public domain status.

Silence As Acceptance
Silence as acceptance is the legal principle that failure to reply is equivalent to acceptance when the offer relates to existing dealings between the parties or when the offer is solely in the interests of the offeree. A contract may also be deemed concluded if the offer is not refused within a reasonable time when no formal acceptance was anticipated.

Self-Dealing
Self-dealing is the prohibition on a representative contracting with himself in the name of the person represented, whether for his own benefit or for that of a third party, without authorization from the principal. The principal may ratify such a contract after the fact.

Undisclosed Representation
Undisclosed representation refers to the situation where a contracting party does not disclose at the time of contract conclusion that he is acting as a representative. The contract only operates in favor of or binds the principal if the third party necessarily knew of the representation or was indifferent to contracting with either the principal or the representative.

Extinction Of Representation
Extinction of representation occurs when a representative's authority has ended. If both the representative and the third party were unaware of the extinction at the time the contract was concluded, the effects of the contract, whether rights or obligations, revert to the principal or his successor in title.

Obligations
Obligations are legal duties arising between persons, treated as equivalent to personal rights, and governed generally in Book I of the civil law framework with contracts identified as a primary source.

Architect
The Architect is responsible for preparing plans and specifications and supervising construction work, and is entitled to separate fees for each of these tasks. The Architect is bound by warranty obligations; any clause excluding or restricting the warranty is void.<SEP>A person entrusted with the construction or design of buildings or other works, entitled to a privilege over such works.

Contractor
The Contractor executes works under a contract for work, is obligated to notify the master of cost overruns, may entrust work to sub-contractors, and is entitled to payment upon delivery. The Contractor is bound by warranty obligations and is responsible for the sub-contractor's work.<SEP>A person entrusted with the erection, reconstruction, repair, or maintenance of buildings or other works, entitled to a privilege over such works.

Sub-contractor
The Sub-contractor is a party to whom the Contractor may entrust the execution of all or part of the work, unless restricted by contract terms or the personal nature of the work.

Workmen
Workmen are workers employed by a Contractor or Sub-contractor in the execution of work who hold direct rights of action against the Master and the main Contractor for sums due.

Contract For Work
A Contract for Work is a legal agreement between a Master and a Contractor for the execution of works, establishing mutual obligations regarding delivery, payment, warranty, and termination, governed by specific legal provisions.

Warranty
Warranty is a legal obligation binding the Architect and the Contractor for the quality and soundness of works. Actions on warranty are prescribed after three years from destruction or discovery of defects, and any clause excluding or restricting the warranty is void.

Sub-contract
A Sub-contract is an arrangement permitting a Contractor to entrust the execution of all or part of the work to a Sub-contractor, subject to contractual restrictions and the requirement that the Contractor remains responsible to the Master.

Concession Of Public Utility Service
A Concession of Public Utility Service is a contract for the management of a public utility service of an economic nature, concluded between an Administrative Authority and a private person or company for a fixed period of exploitation.

Administrative Authority
The Administrative Authority is the governmental body in charge of organizing a public utility service and entering into concession agreements with private persons or companies.

Concessionaire
The Concessionaire is a private person or company entrusted with the exploitation of a public utility service for a fixed period, obligated to provide services to consumers in accordance with the concession terms and applicable laws.

Contractor's Heirs
The Contractor's Heirs are the successors of a deceased Contractor who may continue the contract if they offer sufficient guarantees for the due performance of the work.

Contractor's Estate
The Contractor's Estate is the legal successor to the deceased Contractor's rights, entitled to receive payment from the Master for the value of work already done and expenses incurred for uncompleted work when the contract is dissolved by death.

Unit Price Contract
A Unit Price Contract is a type of contract for work concluded on the basis of an estimate drawn up on a unit price basis, requiring the Contractor to notify the Master of anticipated cost overruns and forfeiting the right to recover excess expenses if notification is not given.

Lump Sum Contract
A Lump Sum Contract is a type of contract for work concluded on a lump sum basis according to a plan agreed with the Master, under which the Contractor has no claim to a price increase even if modifications are made, unless due to the Master's fault or authorized by the Master.

Materials
Materials are the supplies used in the execution of works, whose loss in the event of destruction before delivery falls on the party who supplied them, whether the Master or the Contractor.

Monopoly
Monopoly refers to a de jure or de facto exclusive right held by a Concessionaire over a public utility service, which obligates the Concessionaire to observe strict equality among all consumers in services and rates.

Preemption
Preemption is a legal right that allows a qualified person to substitute themselves in a sale of immovable property in place of the purchaser, subject to specific conditions and procedures laid down in Articles 935 through 948.<SEP>A legal mechanism by which the right of usufruct may be acquired, listed alongside legal disposition and prescription.

Ownership
Ownership is a real right in movables and immovables that can be transferred by contract, subject to provisions regarding identification of the object and publication of real rights.

Preemptor
The Preemptor is the person exercising the right of preemption, who is substituted for the purchaser in all rights and obligations vis-a-vis the vendor upon exercising that right.

Possession
Possession is the central legal concept across these articles, encompassing acquisition, transmission, loss, protection, and effects such as acquisitive prescription.<SEP>Possession is a legal state of control over property that does not result from acts done by mere permission or tolerance, and may be acquired through an intermediary or a legal representative.

Bare Owner
The owner of the property subject to a usufruct, whose ratification of a usufructuary's lease allows it to survive beyond the usufruct period.<SEP>The Bare Owner is the owner of bare property who holds the right of preemption in case of a sale of all or part of the usufruct attached to the bare property, or in case of a sale of the hekr right.

Co-Owner in Common
The Co-Owner in Common is a joint owner of property held in common who holds the right of preemption in case of a sale of a part of the common property to a third party.

Neighboring Owner
The Neighboring Owner is the owner of adjoining property who holds the right of preemption in cases involving buildings, building land, rights of servitude, or land adjoining on two sides with a value of at least half the value of the land sold.

Legal Representative
The Legal Representative is the person authorized to consent on behalf of a life assured who is under legal incapacity, required for the validity of a life insurance contract on such person.<SEP>A legal representative is a person authorized to acquire possession on behalf of a person lacking discretion.<SEP>A Legal Representative is a person who may acquire possession on behalf of a person lacking discretion through legal representation.

Right of Servitude
The Right of Servitude is a legal right over neighboring land that qualifies the Neighboring Owner for preemption when the sold land enjoys a servitude over the neighbor's land or vice versa, as described in Article 936.

Intermediary
An intermediary is a person who exercises possession in the name of the possessor and is obliged to obey the possessor's instructions.<SEP>An Intermediary is a person through whom possession may be exercised, provided the intermediary acts in the name of the possessor and maintains a relationship obliging compliance with the possessor's instructions regarding that possession, as stated in Article 951.

Person Lacking Discretion
A Person Lacking Discretion is an individual who may acquire possession only through the intervention of a Legal Representative, as stated in Article 950.

Liability Arising from Things
A legal section covering the responsibility of persons in charge of animals, buildings, and things requiring special care for damage caused by them, as established in Articles 176–178.

Enrichment Without Just Cause
A legal section establishing that a person who enriches himself without just cause to the detriment of another is liable to compensate for the loss sustained, even if the profit later disappears. Governed by Articles 179–180.

Payment Not Due
A subsection dealing with the restitution of payments made when no obligation existed, including rules on good faith, bad faith, legal capacity, and prescription, as governed by Articles 181–187.

Voluntary Agency
A subsection addressing situations where a person knowingly assumes management of an urgent business of another person without being bound to do so, governed by Articles 188–197.

Effects of Obligations
A chapter dealing with the enforceability of obligations against the debtor and the distinction between civil and natural obligations, governed by Articles 199–202.

Civil Obligation
A legally enforceable obligation for which a natural obligation may constitute a valid cause.<SEP>An enforceable obligation against the debtor, which may arise from a natural obligation as its valid cause.

Article 176
Establishes that a person in charge of an animal, even if not its owner, is liable for any harm done by the animal, even if it strays or escapes, unless the accident was due to a cause beyond control.

Article 177
Establishes liability of a person in charge of a building for damage caused by its collapse, even if partial, unless the accident did not result from negligent maintenance, age, or defect; also entitles endangered persons to seek court authorization for preventive measures.

Article 178
Establishes liability of a person in charge of things requiring special care or of machines for damage caused by them, unless the damage was due to a cause beyond control, subject to special legal provisions.

Article 180
Sets the prescription period for enrichment claims at three years from when the injured party knew of the right and fifteen years from when the right first arose.

Article 181
Establishes that a person who receives what is not owed must return it, except when the payor knew he was under no obligation to pay, unless he was legally incapable or paid under duress.

Article 182
Allows recovery of payment not due if made in performance of an obligation whose cause had not materialized or had ceased to exist.

Article 183
Permits restitution of premature payments if the payor was unaware that payment was not yet due; the creditor may limit restitution to profit gained from the premature payment.

Article 184
Bars restitution of payment made by a third party if the creditor in good faith gave up the document of title, security, or allowed the claim to prescribe; the real debtor must indemnify the third party.

Article 185
Distinguishes between good faith recipients who must return only what they received, and bad faith recipients who must also return interest and profits gained or negligently forfeited from the date of payment or bad faith.

Article 186
Limits the liability of a recipient lacking legal capacity to the extent of his enrichment.

Article 187
Sets the prescription period for restitution claims at three years from when the payor knew of the right and fifteen years from when the right arose.

Article 188
Defines voluntary agency as a situation where a person knowingly and voluntarily assumes management of an urgent business of another person on that person's behalf without being bound to do so.

Article 189
Extends voluntary agency to situations where a person manages another's affairs while managing his own, due to an inseparable connection between the two businesses.

Article 190
Provides that the rules of mandate apply when the person for whom the voluntary agent acts ratifies the agent's act.

Article 191
Imposes a duty on the voluntary agent to continue the work commenced until the principal can manage it and to inform the principal of the intervention.

Article 192
Requires a voluntary agent to exercise the care of a reasonable person and holds him responsible for mistakes; the judge may reduce damages; delegates are jointly and severally responsible.

Article 193
Binds the voluntary agent by the same obligations as a mandatary regarding restitution of what was received and rendering of accounts.

Article 194
Provides that upon the death of a voluntary agent, his heirs are bound by the same obligations as those of a mandatary under Article 717; upon the death of the principal, the agent remains bound to the heirs.

Article 195
Deems the voluntary agent a representative of the principal if he exercised reasonable care; the principal must carry out obligations, indemnify the agent, reimburse expenses with interest, and compensate for loss, though the agent is not entitled to remuneration unless the work falls within his profession.

Article 196
Limits the liability of a legally incapable voluntary agent to the extent of his enrichment, unless the liability results from an unlawful act; the principal remains fully responsible regardless of capacity.

Article 197
Sets the prescription period for voluntary agency claims at three years from when each party knew of his right and fifteen years from when the right arose.

Article 198
Provides that obligations arising directly from the law are governed by the legal provisions that created them.

Article 199
Establishes that an obligation is enforceable against the debtor, but a natural obligation cannot be enforced.

Article 200
Empowers the judge to determine whether a natural obligation exists in the absence of a legal provision, provided it is not contrary to public policy.

Article 201
Prevents a debtor from claiming restitution of what was voluntarily given to discharge a natural obligation.

Article 202
Provides that a natural obligation may constitute a valid cause for a civil obligation.

Person in Charge of Animal
A person who has custody or supervision of an animal and is liable for harm caused by it even if not the owner, unless the harm resulted from a cause beyond control.

Person in Charge of Building
A person who has custody or supervision of a building and is liable for damage caused by its collapse, even if partial, unless it did not result from negligent maintenance, age, or defect.

Person in Charge of Things
A person who supervises things requiring special care or machines and is liable for damage caused by them unless the damage was due to a cause beyond control.

Voluntary Agent
A person who knowingly and voluntarily assumes management of the urgent business of another person without being legally bound to do so, owing duties of care, continuation, and notification.

Payor
A person who makes a payment, who may claim restitution if the payment was not due, was for an unmaterialized obligation, or was made prematurely without knowledge.

The Law
Section V of the legal text, providing that obligations which arise directly and solely in consequence of the law are governed by the provisions of the law giving rise to such obligations, as established in Article 198.

Delegate
A third party to whom a voluntary agent delegates the whole or part of the work he has assumed, and whose acts the voluntary agent is responsible for, without prejudice to the principal's right of direct remedy against the delegate.

Machine
A mechanical device whose supervisor is liable for damage caused by it unless the damage was due to a cause beyond control, as established in Article 178.

Compromise
A legal agreement that can only be established by a written document or an official proces-verbal, which terminates disputes and extinguishes rights and claims finally renounced by the parties.<SEP>A contract by which two parties put an end to an existing dispute or prevent an anticipated dispute through the mutual surrender of part of their respective claims, requiring written documentation and legal capacity.

Right of Management
A limited legal authority that restricts the holder from entering into leases exceeding three years without the consent of the competent authority.

Compromise Nullity
The legal invalidity of a compromise, which is indivisible so that nullity of one part involves nullity of the whole contract, unless the parties agreed the parts are independent.

data.entity_name: Chapter II: Contracts Relating to the Use of a Thing
data.content:
Chapter II: Contracts Relating to the Use of a Thing
A chapter of the civil code that covers contracts for the use of a thing, including leases generally.

Section I: Leases
A section within Chapter II that provides the general legal provisions governing leases, including their elements and effects.

Competent Authority
The authority whose consent is required for a person holding only a right of management to enter into a lease exceeding three years.

Declaratory Effect
The legal effect of a compromise whereby it establishes the rights it covers as declaratory rather than constitutive, and this effect is limited solely to the disputed rights.<SEP>The legal effect of a compromise on the rights it covers, which is declaratory in nature and limited specifically to litigious rights, as stated in Article 554.

Renunciation
The act of giving up rights in a compromise, the wording of which must be strictly interpreted and applies only to rights that form the precise object of the dispute settled by the compromise.

Article 1145
Article 1145 establishes that sums due to a vendor of a movable for price and accessories are secured by a privilege over the movable sold, enforceable as long as the movable preserves its identity, subject to third-party good faith rights and commercial provisions.

Article 1146
Article 1146 provides that co-owners who have partitioned a movable have a privilege over this movable for their respective remedies against each other resulting from partition and for repayment of any difference reverting to them.

Article 1147
Article 1147 establishes that the price and accessories due to a vendor of an immovable are secured by a privilege over the immovable sold, which must be inscribed and its rank is fixed by the date of inscription.

Article 1149
Article 1149 provides that co-owners who have partitioned an immovable have a privilege over it for their respective remedies against each other resulting from partition, including the right to claim payment of any difference, and such privilege must be inscribed.

Hotel Proprietor's Privilege
A legal privilege securing sums due to hotel proprietors over effects brought by travellers, having the same rank as a lessor's privilege, enforceable even on effects not owned by the traveller provided they are not lost or stolen property.

Vendor's Privilege Over Movable
A legal privilege securing sums due to a vendor of movable property over the thing sold, ranking below other movable privileges but enforceable against lessors and hotel proprietors if they had knowledge of the privilege at the time the movable was brought onto their premises.

Vendor's Privilege Over Immovable
A legal privilege securing sums due to a vendor of an immovable over the property sold, requiring inscription notwithstanding transcription of the sale, with rank fixed by the date of inscription.

Co-partitioner's Privilege Over Movable
A legal privilege held by co-owners over partitioned movables for remedies against each other resulting from partition and for repayment of differences, having the same rank as a vendor's privilege.

Co-partitioner's Privilege Over Immovable
A legal privilege held by co-owners over partitioned immovables for remedies and payment of differences, requiring inscription with rank fixed by the date of inscription.

Contractor's And Architect's Privilege
A legal privilege securing sums due to contractors and architects over buildings or works they erected, reconstructed, repaired, or maintained, limited to the increase in value resulting from such works, requiring inscription.

Lessor's Privilege
A legal privilege held by a lessor over leased property, having the same rank as a hotel proprietor's privilege.

Third Party In Good Faith
A person who has acquired for valuable consideration a real right over property sold during a seller's last illness; the provisions restricting such sales do not apply to the prejudice of such third parties.<SEP>A third party who acquires rights over property without knowledge of existing privileges, whose acquired rights are protected against enforcement of such privileges.

Special Privileges Over Immovables
A category of legal privileges applicable to immovable property, encompassing the vendor's privilege, the contractor's and architect's privilege, and the co-partitioner's privilege over immovables.

Effects
The personal belongings brought by a traveller to a hotel or its annexes, which serve as the subject of the hotel proprietor's privilege to secure sums due for accommodation, food, and expenses.

Buildings Or Other Works
Physical structures or constructions that are the subject of the contractor's and architect's privilege, including buildings erected, reconstructed, repaired, or maintained by contractors and architects.

Minor Possessing Discretion
A minor possessing discretion is a person whose contracts and dispositions of property are valid when wholly to their advantage, void when wholly to their disadvantage, and voidable when simultaneously profitable and detrimental, as defined in Article 111.

Interdiction
Interdiction is a court-ordered legal restriction pronounced on persons suffering from insanity, mental derangement, imbecility, or prodigality, which may also be raised by the court in accordance with prescribed rules and procedures, as stated in Article 113.

Insanity
Insanity is a mental condition that, when combined with a registered sentence of interdiction, renders acts entered into by the affected person null, as described in Article 114.

Mental Derangement
Mental derangement is a psychological condition that serves as grounds for court-ordered interdiction and nullification of acts performed after registration of the interdiction sentence, as per Article 114.

Imbecility
Imbecility is a condition for which the court may pronounce interdiction; acts by a person interdicted for imbecility are governed by the same provisions as those for minors possessing discretion, according to Article 115.

Prodigality
Prodigality is a condition of reckless spending for which the court may pronounce interdiction; acts after registration follow the same rules as for minors possessing discretion, as stated in Article 115.

Judicial Adviser
A judicial adviser is a person appointed by the court to assist a deaf and dumb, deaf and blind, or blind and dumb person who cannot express their will, in connection with acts necessary for their interests, as established in Article 117.

Natural Guardian
A natural guardian is a person whose acts on behalf of those under their guardianship are valid within the limits provided by law, as stated in Article 118.

Legal Guardian
A legal guardian is a person whose acts on behalf of those under their guardianship are valid within the limits provided by law, as stated in Article 118.

Curator
A curator is a legal representative whose acts are valid within the limits provided by law, as stated in Article 118.

Essential Mistake
An essential mistake is a mistake of such gravity that, had it not been committed, the mistaken party would not have concluded the contract, as defined in Article 121; it may relate to the quality of the thing or the identity or qualities of the contracting party.

Mistake of Law
A mistake in law is an error regarding legal provisions that may entail the voidability of a contract if it fulfills the same elements as a mistake of fact, unless the law provides otherwise, as per Article 122.

Mistake of Fact
A mistake of fact is an error regarding factual circumstances that, when it meets the criteria of essentiality, may serve as grounds for avoidance of a contract, as referenced in Articles 120 through 122.

Object of Obligation
The object of an obligation is what a debtor must deliver or perform; it may be a future thing but cannot be impossible in itself, and must be determinate as to its kind and quantity, as defined in Articles 131 through 133.

Void Act
A void act is a legal act that has no legal effect, such as acts by a minor lacking discretion, acts by insane persons after registration of interdiction, contracts with impossible objects, or agreements regarding the succession of a living person.

Voidable Act
A voidable act is a legal act that may be annulled at the request of an interested party, including dispositions by a minor possessing discretion that are both profitable and detrimental, acts performed without a required judicial adviser, and contracts affected by mistake, fraud, duress, or lesion.

Civil Code
The Civil Code is the body of law containing Articles 109 through 134 that governs legal capacity, defects of consent, and the object of obligations in contractual matters.

data.entity_name: Mistakes of Calculation and Clerical Mistakes
data.content:
Mistakes of Calculation and Clerical Mistakes
Mistakes of calculation and clerical mistakes are errors that do not affect the validity of a contract but must be corrected, as provided in Article 123 of the Civil Code.

Succession of a Living Person
An agreement with regard to the succession of a living person is void, even if the person consents, except in cases provided for by law, as stated in Article 131 of the Civil Code.

Avoidance of Contract
Avoidance of contract is a legal remedy whereby a contracting party may demand the nullification of a contract on grounds including legal incapacity, essential mistake, mistake of law, fraudulent misrepresentation, duress, or lesion, as referenced across Articles 119 through 129 of the Civil Code.

Special Provisions for Lesion
Special provisions for lesion are legal rules applicable to certain contracts and rates of interest that take precedence over the general lesion provisions of Article 129, as stated in Article 130.

Specific Performance
A legal remedy in Section I of the code that compels a debtor to perform an obligation exactly as specified, provided such performance is possible and not excessively onerous for the debtor.

Compensation in Lieu of Performance
A legal remedy in Section II of the code, awarded when specific performance is impossible, covering losses suffered and lost profits.

Real Right
A property right, including ownership, that may be transferred through obligation, subject to transcription rules. An obligation to transfer a real right includes the duty of delivery and preservation of the article.

Moral Prejudice
Non-material harm for which damages may be awarded. The right to compensation for moral prejudice is not transferable to third parties unless fixed by agreement or subject to legal proceedings. Awards are limited to spouses and relatives up to the second degree for grief caused by death of a victim.

Gross Negligence
A severe degree of carelessness for which a debtor always remains liable. A debtor cannot be contractually discharged from liability for gross negligence, though the debtor may stipulate non-liability for gross negligence of persons employed.

Penalty
A monetary sanction imposed on a debtor who abstains from performing an obligation when specific performance is impracticable unless performed by the debtor personally. The judge may increase the penalty if insufficient to compel performance.

Contractual Obligation
An obligation arising from a contract, where a debtor who has not committed fraud or gross negligence is liable only for damages that could have been normally foreseen at the time of entering into the contract.

Code De Procedure
The procedural law referenced in Article 219 governing the manner in which formal summons may be served by post.

Thief
A person who steals. The thief bears the risk of loss of the stolen thing regardless of how it perishes, as stated in Article 207.

Agreed Damages
Damages fixed in advance by the parties either in the contract or in a subsequent agreement, as provided in Articles 223 and 224. Agreed damages are not due if the debtor proves that the creditor suffered no loss. The judge may reduce the amount of agreed damages.

Sale Of Commodities
A legal concept involving the sale of commodities or movable effects where a term is agreed for payment and delivery; the sale is ipso facto dissolved without summons if the price is not paid upon due date, subject to contrary agreement and at the vendor's option.

Sale With Right Of Redemption
A form of sale in which the vendor reserves the right to take back the thing sold within a fixed time; such a sale is declared void under Article 465.

data.entity_name: Sale Of A Thing Belonging To Another
data.content:
Sale Of A Thing Belonging To Another
A form of sale where a person sells a definite and ascertained thing of which he is not the owner; the purchaser may demand annulment of the sale, and the sale cannot have any effect against the true owner even if the purchaser ratifies the contract.

Sale Of Litigious Rights
A form of sale involving the assignment of a litigious right, defined as a right that is the subject of a court action or serious controversy; the debtor may extinguish the assigned right by paying the assignee the actual price paid plus expenses and interest.

Court Officials
Members of the magistracy, Parquet, lawyers, Greffiers, and bailiffs who are prohibited from purchasing litigious rights within the jurisdiction of the court in which they serve, under penalty of nullity of the sale.

Lawyers
Legal professionals who are prohibited under Article 472 from entering into agreements with their clients regarding litigious rights they have undertaken to defend, under penalty of nullity of the contract.

Sale Of An Inheritance
A form of sale where a person sells an inheritance without giving particulars thereof; the seller only warrants that he is an heir unless otherwise agreed, and transfer of rights requires fulfillment of necessary formalities.

Sale During Last Illness
A sale made by a person during his last illness to an heir or non-heir at a price inferior to the value of the thing sold; it is valid against heirs only if the difference between value and price does not exceed one third of the inheritance, with provisions for ratification or payment to make up two thirds.

Sale By Representative To Himself
A prohibited form of sale where a person representing another by agreement, law, or court order purchases property entrusted to him for sale, unless authorized by a court order; such sales are governed by Articles 479 through 481.

Brokers And Experts
Professionals who are prohibited from purchasing goods entrusted to them for sale or appraisal, either in their own name or through intermediaries, under Article 480.

Exchange
A contract by which contracting parties mutually bind themselves to transfer to each other by way of exchange the ownership of a thing other than money; the provisions governing sale apply to exchange as far as the nature of exchange allows.

Annulment Of Sale
A legal remedy available to a purchaser who was unaware that the thing sold did not belong to the vendor, entitling the purchaser to claim damages even if the vendor acted in good faith, as provided under Article 468.

Future Property Gift
A gift of future property is declared void under Article 492, meaning property not yet owned by the donor at the time of the gift cannot be validly gifted.

Promise Of Gift
A promise to make a gift that is not binding unless made by an authentic document, as provided under Article 490.

Annuity
A perpetual periodic prestation consisting of a sum of money or fixed quantity of fungibles, redeemable at the debtor's will, governed by rules on interest-bearing loans when made for valuable consideration.<SEP>Annuity is a periodic financial payment settled on the life of a person, payable upon occurrence of a specified event or maturity date.

Assured
The Assured is the person who contracts the insurance, pays the premium, and may nominate beneficiaries; the Assured may also surrender or reduce the policy under certain conditions.

Life Assured
The Life Assured is the person whose life is the subject of the life insurance contract; the insurer's obligations depend on events such as the death or survival of this person.

Insurance Contract
An Insurance Contract is an agreement whereby the insurer undertakes to pay the assured or beneficiary a sum of money or annuity upon occurrence of a specified risk, in consideration of a premium or other pecuniary payment.

Policy of Insurance
The Policy of Insurance is the document evidencing the insurance contract, containing general and special conditions, including those relating to reduction, surrender, and forfeiture.

Life Insurance
Life Insurance is a class of insurance in which sums become due upon the occurrence of the event insured against or on a stipulated maturity date, without the need to establish that any loss was suffered.

Insurance Reserve
The Insurance Reserve is a financial reserve associated with a life insurance policy, used in calculating reduced sums assured and amounts payable upon surrender or suicide of the life assured.

Suicide
Suicide is an event affecting the insurer's obligation under a life insurance contract; the insurer is generally released from payment unless suicide resulted from illness causing loss of control or occurred after two years from the contract date.

Section III: Contracts of Insurance
Section III: Contracts of Insurance is the part of the Code containing general provisions and specific rules governing insurance contracts, including life insurance.

The Code
The Code is the legal instrument containing statutory provisions on insurance contracts, annuities, and related matters, with Articles 746 through 764 addressing insurance law.

Lawful Economic Interest
Lawful Economic Interest is any legitimate economic interest a person may have in the non-occurrence of a specified risk, and it constitutes the insurable subject matter under an insurance contract.

Void Conditions
Void Conditions are specific types of clauses in an insurance policy that are legally unenforceable, including forfeiture clauses for breach of law, unreasonable delay-related forfeiture clauses, unclear printed conditions relating to nullity, embedded arbitration clauses, and arbitrary clauses unrelated to the insured event.

Limitation Period
The Limitation Period is a three-year statutory period after which actions arising out of insurance contracts become barred, running from the date of the occurrence giving rise to the action, with exceptions for concealment or late discovery.

Paid-Up Policy
A Paid-Up Policy is a converted insurance policy with a reduced sum assured, obtained by the assured after payment of at least three yearly premiums, in lieu of the original policy.

Indemnification
Indemnification is the principle under which the insurer is only bound to compensate the assured for actual loss arising from the occurrence of the insured risk, limited to the amount insured.

Age Misstatement
Age Misstatement refers to false declarations or errors regarding the age of the life assured, which do not invalidate the insurance but may result in a proportional reduction of the sum assured if the premium paid was lower than required.

Attempted Homicide
Attempted Homicide is an unsuccessful deliberate attempt by the beneficiary to cause the death of the life assured, which grants the assured the right to substitute the beneficiary with another person.

Article 950
Article 950 provides that a person lacking discretion may acquire possession through the intervention of a legal representative.

Article 951
Article 951 regulates possession by intermediary, requiring the intermediary to act in the name of the possessor and obey instructions; it also establishes presumptions about possession on one's own behalf.

Article 952
Article 952 states that possession is transmitted by mutual agreement between possessor and another, without requiring actual delivery, provided the transferee can assume control of the right.

Article 953
Article 953 allows transmission of possession without actual delivery if the possessor continues possession on behalf of a successor in title or the successor continues for his own account.

Article 954
Article 954 equates the handing over of documents relating to goods with delivery of the goods themselves; if documents and goods go to different good-faith recipients, the recipient of the goods has preference.

Article 955
Article 955 provides that possession is transmitted with all its features to a universal successor in title, and a special successor may add the original possessor's possession to his own for legal effect.

Article 956
Article 956 provides that possession ceases when the possessor abandons actual control or loses it in any other way.

Article 957
Article 957 states that temporary obstacles do not terminate possession, but possession ceases if the obstacle continues for a full year due to a new possession against the possessor's will.

Article 958
Article 958 grants a person who loses possession of an immovable the right to claim reinstatement within one year; secret loss starts the period from discovery.

Article 959
Article 959 provides that a person who possessed for less than a year may recover possession if the dispossessor lacks a better possession; possession by violence allows restitution within one year in all cases.

Article 960
Article 960 allows a dispossessed person to take proceedings for recovery of possession even against a good-faith possessor of the property.

Article 961
Article 961 grants a possessor of an immovable for a full year the right to take proceedings for discontinuance of disturbance within the following year.

Article 962
Article 962 allows a possessor of an immovable for a full year to apply to the Judge for suspension of threatening new works, and the Judge may order a guarantee in either outcome.

Article 963
Article 963 provides that when several persons claim possession of the same right, the person with actual possession is provisionally presumed possessor unless acquisition was wrongful.

Article 964
Article 964 establishes the presumption that the possessor of a right is its rightful possessor until the contrary is proved.

Article 965
Article 965 defines good faith in possession, stating that a possessor unaware of infringing another's right is in good faith; good faith of a juristic person depends on its representative; good faith is always presumed.

Article 966
Article 966 provides that good faith ceases when the possessor becomes aware of infringement or when defects are notified in legal proceedings; usurpation by violence is deemed bad faith.

Article 967
Article 967 states that possession retains the character it had at the time of acquisition, subject to proof to the contrary.

Article 968
Article 968 establishes acquisitive prescription, allowing a possessor of a movable or immovable without ownership to acquire title after fifteen years of uninterrupted possession.

Article 969
Article 969 reduces the acquisitive prescription period to five years for possession in good faith and by virtue of a just title over an immovable; a just title must be duly transcribed.

Article 970
Article 970 requires thirty-three years of possession for acquiring wakf property and hereditary rights by prescription; state and public entity property cannot be acquired by prescription.

Article 971
Article 971 establishes the presumption that present possession existed during the intervening time if proven at an ascertained previous time.

Article 972
Article 972 prohibits acquiring by prescription contrary to one's title but allows it if the nature of possession changes by act of a third party or adverse claim against the owner.

Article 973
Article 973 makes rules of extinctive prescription applicable to acquisitive prescription regarding calculation, suspension, interruption, and renunciation, subject to compatibility.

Acquisitive Prescription
Acquisitive prescription is the legal mechanism by which prolonged uninterrupted possession leads to acquisition of ownership or real rights, with periods of five, fifteen, or thirty-three years depending on circumstances.<SEP>A legal mechanism by which a person acquires ownership of property through continuous possession over a specified period of time, subject to rules on suspension, interruption, and calculation of the period.

Just Title
A just title is a duly transcribed document of title emanating from a person who is not the owner, required for the shortened five-year acquisitive prescription period.<SEP>A lawful basis or reason for acquiring possession, which, together with good faith, enables a possessor to acquire ownership of movables.

Successor In Title
A successor in title is a person who receives possession from a prior possessor, either universally or under a special title, and may add prior possession to his own.

Three Possessory Actions
The three possessory actions are legal remedies for the protection of possession, including reinstatement of possession, discontinuance of disturbance, and prevention of threatened disturbance.

Article 974
Article 974 provides that whatever the duration of acquisitive prescription, it is suspended under certain conditions; the article appears truncated in the source text.

Carrier
A carrier is a person to whom goods are entrusted, and documents issued in respect of such goods are equivalent to delivery of the goods themselves under Article 954.

Competent Minister
The Competent Minister is the authority empowered under Article 970 to administratively remove encroachments on state property and public entity property.

Hereditary Rights
Hereditary rights are a category of rights that can only be acquired by prescription after thirty-three years of possession, as prescribed by Article 970.

Violence
Violence is a means of dispossession that constitutes bad faith under Article 966 and entitles the dispossessed possessor to restitution within one year in all cases under Article 959.

Disturbance
Disturbance is an interference with the possession of an immovable, against which a possessor of at least one year may seek legal proceedings for discontinuance under Article 961.

Liquidator
A person appointed by the majority of partners or by the judge to carry out the liquidation of partnership property, restricted from undertaking new business except as necessary to complete prior transactions.

Dissolution
The legal termination of a partnership, triggered by unanimous partner agreement, court order for non-performance, or a partner's retirement, after which liquidation is required.

Liquidation
The legal process of winding up partnership affairs involving payment of creditors, settling outstanding debts, and distributing remaining assets among partners according to their capital contributions and profit shares.

Partnership Property
The assets of the partnership that are subject to liquidation and partition among all partners after satisfaction of creditors and deduction of outstanding obligations.

Loan for Consumption
A contract by which the lender undertakes to transfer ownership of a sum of money or other fungible to the borrower, who must return an equal thing in amount, kind, and quality at the end of the loan.

Borrower
The party to a loan for consumption who receives ownership of money or fungibles and is obligated to return an equivalent, pay agreed interest, and may terminate the contract with six months' notice after six months from the loan date.

Redemption
The right of the debtor to extinguish an annuity by repaying the capital sum, exercisable at any time subject to notice requirements and a maximum deferral period of fifteen years.

Dispute
A conflict or anticipated conflict between parties that may be resolved through compromise by the mutual surrender of claims, extinguishing the rights and claims that have been renounced.

Retirement
The right of a partner to withdraw from the partnership by giving previous notice to co-partners, provided the retirement is free of fraudulent intent and not at an unsuitable time.

Exclusion
The legal process by which a partner may be expelled from the partnership by court order when that partner's presence has given rise to objections to extending the partnership or when that partner's actions constitute grounds for dissolution.

Loan for Use
A type of loan referenced in Article 540 whose provisions apply when a loan made without valuable consideration results in dispossession of the loaned thing.

Hidden Defect
A defect in the loaned thing not apparent at the time of the loan, which triggers different remedies depending on whether the loan is for valuable consideration or gratuitous, and whether the lender deliberately concealed it.

Securities
Collateral or guarantees promised by the debtor to the creditor in the context of an annuity, the disappearance of which or failure to supply can compel the debtor to redeem.

Sale
A legal concept referenced in Article 540 whose provisions apply when a loan made for valuable consideration results in dispossession of the loaned thing.

Bearer Warrant
A negotiable document transferable by delivery, which may be acquired by a possessor in good faith or subject to recovery claims if lost or stolen.

Right of Usufruct
A legal right granting a person the use and enjoyment of another's property and its fruits, which may be acquired by legal disposition, preemption, or prescription.

Right of Use
A limited real right permitting a person to use another's property, classified alongside the right of usufruct and the right of occupation.

Right of Occupation
A real right allowing a person to occupy or reside in a property, classified alongside the right of usufruct and the right of use.

Natural Fruits
Products naturally generated by property, deemed collected from the moment of their separation.

Industrial Fruits
Products generated through human labor on property, deemed collected from the moment of separation.

Legal Fruits
Revenue or income derived from property through legal relationships, deemed collected day by day.

Necessary Expenditure
Essential costs incurred for the preservation of property, which the owner is obligated to reimburse to the possessor upon restitution.

Advantageous Expenditure
Costs that enhance the value of property, governed by the provisions of Articles 924 and 925 regarding reimbursement.

Luxurious Expenditure
Non-essential ornamental costs incurred on property, for which the possessor cannot claim repayment but may remove the works if the property is restored to its original condition.

Standing Crops
Crops growing on land subject to a usufruct at the time of its termination, for which the usufructuary or heirs may retain the land until harvest upon payment of rent.

Suspension of Prescription
The halting of the running of the acquisitive prescription period, which occurs whenever a qualifying cause for suspension exists, regardless of the length of the prescription period.

Interruption of Prescription
The breaking of the acquisitive prescription period, occurring when the possessor abandons or loses possession even by the act of a third party, unless possession is recovered or legal proceedings are initiated within one year.

Normal Charges
Regular recurring costs and maintenance expenses in respect of property subject to a usufruct, which the usufructuary is obligated to bear during the continuance of the usufruct.

Abnormal Expenses
Extraordinary costs and heavy repairs not arising from any fault of the usufructuary, which the owner is obligated to bear, with the usufructuary required to pay interest on amounts expended by the owner.

Public Funds
Government securities in which the proceeds from the sale of movable property subject to a usufruct are invested when no security is given, with the income thereof paid to the usufructuary.

Heir
A successor who may inherit the right to retain possession of land with standing crops until harvest after the death of the usufructuary, subject to payment of rent for that period.

Legal Disposition
A legal act by which the right of usufruct may be acquired or created.

Article 717
Article 194 references Article 717 to determine the specific obligations of the heirs of a voluntary agent, applying the same rules as those for the heirs of a mandatary.
